profile.summary: A single paper's benchmark of how well six single-cell foundation models recover gene regulatory networks without any training, compared with three classical network inference methods. Networks are built from six BEELINE single-cell RNA-seq datasets from mouse and human and checked against four kinds of reference network. A second task, dynamic transition probing, asks whether a model can move early-cell expression profiles towards later states. It is for researchers choosing a foundation model, or a way of reading one, for network inference.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Section 2.1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark asks which part of a single-cell foundation model carries gene regulatory information and how that compares with conventional inference. Three readings of each model are compared: cosine similarity of the pretrained gene token embeddings (costok), cosine similarity of final-layer hidden states (coshid), and last-layer attention scores (attn). The inferred networks are scored at the edge level, the transcription factor (TF) level and the topology level. A second task, dynamic transition probing, tests whether a model's learned gene relationships can drive early-cell expression towards the observed late-cell state without temporal supervision.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 1, 2.1 to 2.3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Six BEELINE datasets are used: mouse dendritic cells (mDC), three mouse haematopoietic stem-cell lineages (mHSC-E, mHSC-GM, mHSC-L), human mature hepatocytes (hHep) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Raw data were preprocessed with the BEELINE protocol. Genes whose expression varies with pseudotime were selected with a generalised additive model and Bonferroni correction (corrected P < 0.01). Two TF-prioritised gene sets were then built: TFs+500 and TFs+1000 keep all significant TFs plus the top 500 or 1000 most dynamically variable non-TF genes. Main results use TFs+500. Reference networks are cell-type-specific ChIP-seq, non-specific ChIP-seq, STRING functional interactions and OmniPath. Table 2 gives the TF and gene counts and network density for each dataset, gene set and reference.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1; Appendix A.1, Table 2

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every method outputs ranked gene pairs. Scoring is restricted to TF-target candidates: the source gene must be a reference TF and the target must be in the reference gene set. Edges are ranked by absolute weight, and the top K edges, with K equal to the number of reference edges, give the early precision. The early precision ratio (EPR) divides this by the edge density of the candidate space, and the AUPRC ratio divides the average precision by the same density, so values above 1 beat random ranking. Main-text results average over the six datasets and three references (STRING, non-specific ChIP-seq and OmniPath); cell-type-specific ChIP-seq is reported in the appendix only, because every method was near random on it. TF-level F1 and five graph metrics, compared with STRING through a normalised closeness score, are secondary analyses. For dynamic transition probing, early and late cells are the lowest and highest 20% pseudotime quantiles, and the score is directional accuracy on the 30% of genes with the largest observed change; mDC is left out of the aggregate comparison.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 2.2, 3.1, 3.4; Appendices B.2, B.3, C, D.1

sections.title: Dynamic transition probing
sections.body: Continuous-value models (scGPT, scFoundation, scPRINT) start from the mean expression vector of early cells and pass the state repeatedly through the model, with an exponential moving average (alpha = 0.9). Rank-driven models (Geneformer, LangCell, scCello) start from ranked gene tokens and accept random token swaps that raise the masked-token likelihood, 8 proposals per iteration. The model never receives time labels, pseudotime or late-cell profiles. A gene counts as correct when the sign of the predicted change matches the observed early-to-late change. As a control, the scGPT analysis was repeated with randomly initialised weights.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.4; Appendices C.1 and C.2

strengths.text: All methods share one preprocessing, one candidate gene set, one graph-construction rule and one set of references and metrics, so the three ways of reading a model are compared on equal terms.

Four reference types with different evidence (ChIP-seq of two kinds, STRING, OmniPath) are scored separately, and the complete per-dataset tables for both gene sets are printed in the appendix, including the near-random cell-type-specific ChIP-seq results.
The dynamic probing task includes a randomly initialised scGPT control, which the authors use to show that the signal depends on pretraining rather than the iteration itself.

limitations.text: The authors state that reference networks are incomplete and biased towards well-studied genes, and every method was near random against cell-type-specific ChIP-seq, so that reference is left out of the main comparison.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Section 4

limitations.text: Only zero-shot use is tested, and the extraction strategies are deliberately simple; the authors say fine-tuning or head-selective attention might recover more signal.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Section 4

limitations.text: The paper names no code, data release or leaderboard, and reports no seeds or confidence intervals, so the results cannot be rerun from public files. It is a preprint not certified by peer review.

profile.summary: A single paper's test of whether the cell embeddings of scGPT and Geneformer are useful without any further training (zero-shot). Embeddings are scored on five human single-cell RNA-seq datasets for separating known cell types and for mixing batches, against 2,000 highly variable genes, Harmony and scVI; a third analysis checks how well each model performs its own pretraining reconstruction task. It is for researchers deciding whether to use a single-cell foundation model's embeddings directly, without fine-tuning.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results and discussion; Methods

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The study asks whether single-cell foundation models produce cell embeddings that work without task-specific training, which matters in exploratory work where labels are unknown and fine-tuning is not possible. It scores three things: how well the embedding separates known cell types, how well it removes batch effects while keeping biology, and how well each model performs its own masked-language-model pretraining task of reconstructing gene expression.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Background; Results and discussion

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Five human datasets are used: Pancreas (16k cells, 14 labels, 6 batches, combining 5 studies), PBMC 12k (9 labels, 2 batches), PBMC 95k (10 labels, 1 batch), a cross-tissue Immune atlas (330k cells, 45 labels, 12 batches) and Tabula Sapiens (483k cells, 177 labels, 27 batches). The models are Geneformer and four scGPT variants: randomly initialised, and pretrained on kidney, blood and bone marrow, or whole-human data. Baselines are 2,000 highly variable genes (HVG), and scVI and Harmony trained on each dataset. Some evaluation data were seen in pretraining: part of Pancreas (GEO GSE84133) by Geneformer, and Tabula Sapiens and Immune by scGPT. The authors scored both the full Pancreas set and its non-overlapping subset and report that results were consistent.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Models and baselines' and 'Datasets'; Additional file 1 sheets TableS1 and TableS2

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Scoring largely follows Luecken et al. (scIB, version 1.0.4). Cell-type separation uses the average silhouette width (ASW) and AvgBIO, the mean of ASW, NMI and ARI, with NMI and ARI computed on Louvain clusters at the best of 20 resolutions. Batch mixing uses a batch integration score (silhouette with respect to batch, averaged across cell types, subtracted from 1) and the principal component regression (PCR) score; their mean is the Average Batch Score. All scores are on a 0 to 1 scale, higher is better. Scores are computed on the full embedding dimensions and again after UMAP projection. For reconstruction, all genes are left unmasked; scGPT is scored by mean squared error against a mean-prediction baseline and Geneformer by Pearson correlation between true and predicted rankings against an average-ranking baseline.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Evaluation metrics', 'Biological preservation scores', 'Batch mixing scores', 'Reconstructing gene expression'; Code availability

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The README's quick start clones the repository, downloads a data archive from figshare, and starts a Jupyter server in the published Docker image. The evaluation is run from three notebooks: one for scGPT, one for Geneformer and one for the HVG and scVI baselines. The code needs an NVIDIA GPU because scGPT requires flash-attention.

profile.summary: DEKOIS 2.0 is a virtual screening benchmark: for each target it asks how well a method ranks experimentally validated active compounds above property-matched decoys. The official page offers 81 target sets for download; Shen et al. describe each set as 40 actives from BindingDB and 1200 decoys selected from ZINC. It is used by developers of docking, scoring and co-folding methods to compare enrichment of actives.
profile.summary_source_locator: dekois.com page: list of targets; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark measures early recognition in structure-based virtual screening: given a protein target and a library of 40 known actives mixed with 1200 decoys, can a method place the actives near the top of its ranking. Because the decoys are chosen to match the actives' physicochemical properties, a method cannot succeed simply by preferring, for example, heavier or more lipophilic molecules. Shen et al. use it as their primary reference set for comparing AlphaFold3-like co-folding methods with conventional docking programs.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Introduction; Results 'Evaluation of AF3's built-in confidence scores on DEKOIS2.0 dataset'; Methods 'Datasets'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each target set pairs actives taken from BindingDB with decoys selected from ZINC and matched on molecular properties, giving an actives-to-decoys ratio of 1 to 30. The official page lists 81 targets, spread across kinases, proteases, nuclear receptors, GPCRs and other enzyme families, and offers the target sets in three download parts plus a ligands download. The page does not print a version string, a licence or a construction protocol; the construction details on this page come from Shen et al.'s description. Shen et al. also used the protein templates and initial ligand conformers that come with the dataset rather than preparing their own.
sections.source_locator: dekois.com page: downloads and list of targets; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets' and 'Complex structure prediction'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a ranking of each target's library. Shen et al. score rankings with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), BEDROC with alpha = 80.5, which weights the top 2% of the ranking to 80% of the score, and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%. Per-target values are then summarised across targets, with the mean marked in their box plots. Their comparison runs on 79 of the 81 targets, because two targets (pygl-in and pygl-out) were dropped as too costly to model; values for one tool, SurfDock, were taken over from earlier work and cover all 81 targets. There is no central leaderboard: each paper publishes its own numbers.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'; Methods 'Datasets'; Fig. 1 caption

facts.value: As reported by Shen et al.: five docking programs (Glide SP, AutoDock Vina, GOLD CHEMPLP, Surflex-Dock, LeDock) and five machine-learning docking tools (Gnina, TankBind, KarmaDock, CarsiDock, SurfDock), with the values for all but AF3, Protenix, Boltz-2 and Gnina taken over from earlier studies.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None in the benchmark itself, and Shen et al. warn that it is a problem here: the set was released over ten years before their study and its template structures may overlap AlphaFold3's training data, so they built the separate GPCRrecent set. They also say Boltz-2's affinity numbers on DEKOIS2.0 are likely over-estimated, because Boltz-2 took affinity data from the same public databases that DEKOIS 2.0 draws on. In place of a split control they computed, for each active compound, its minimum Tanimoto similarity (ECFP4) to any PDB ligand, as the paper words it, and re-calculated the metrics at varying similarity thresholds.

facts.value: No replicates or intervals are asked for. Shen et al. report the spread across targets with box plots and mark the mean; the co-folding predictions were run with one fixed random seed (seed = 1).

strengths.text: The actives are experimentally validated measurements from BindingDB, and the decoys are matched on physicochemical properties, so simple property bias does not by itself produce enrichment.

81 target sets spanning many protein families are downloadable from the official page, with the protein templates and ligand conformers included, so methods that need a prepared structure can be run without extra preparation.

strengths.text: Shen et al. describe it as widely used for both physics-based and machine-learning docking tools, which is why results from different papers can be put side by side; they take ten tools' values from earlier work.

profile.summary: One paper's harmonised benchmark of six single-cell and spatial foundation models (Nicheformer, CellPLM, scGPT-spatial, GenePT, scELMo, Novae) across scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics and Perturb-seq data. Five tasks are scored under shared metrics: zero-shot clustering, clustering after continual pretraining, supervised cell type annotation, marker-gene concordance and perturbation prediction. It is for researchers choosing which foundation model, if any, to use for a given modality and task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark asks when a foundation model's representation actually helps biological inference, and whether the answer holds across modalities. Clustering tasks ask whether an embedding separates reference cell types or spatial domains; the supervised task asks whether fine-tuning or adapting a model on labels gives accurate annotation; the marker-gene task asks whether clusters found in the embedding recover the same differentially expressed genes as the reference labels; the perturbation task asks whether a representation supports predicting post-perturbation expression for perturbations not seen in training. The authors report that model rankings shifted with modality, preprocessing, tokenisation, biological prior, domain shift and metric choice, and that no model dominated.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; Methods 'DEG Analysis' and 'Perturbation Prediction'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Three scRNA-seq datasets are used: ATAA (ascending aortic tissue from 11 individuals, 11 major cell types), BMMC (the NeurIPS 2021 challenge CITE-seq subset, bone marrow mononuclear cells from 12 healthy donors, 45 annotated cell types) and HS (human splenic dendritic cells, seven subtypes). Four spatial datasets are used: HBCA1 (10x Visium human breast cancer, 20 domain labels), MHPC (mouse hippocampus, Slide-seqV2, 14 domain labels), MOSTA (mouse organogenesis Stereo-seq, section E9.5 E1S1, 12 anatomical regions) and SEAAD (middle temporal gyrus MERFISH, 27 aged donors, a 140-gene panel, 24 annotated cell types). All spatial datasets except SEAAD came from the BenchmarkST data resource. Three Perturb-seq datasets in K562 cells are used: Adamson (87 single-gene perturbations), Norman (131 two-gene and 105 single-gene perturbations) and Replogle (genome-wide CRISPR interference). Reference labels are the original studies' annotations. Each model is run with its own recommended preprocessing, so the harmonisation is in the tasks, splits and metrics rather than in one shared input pipeline.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'; Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Clustering: embeddings are clustered with Leiden, sweeping the resolution until the number of clusters matches the number of reference labels, and scored with adjusted Rand index (ARI), normalised mutual information (NMI) and silhouette score; k-means results are reported in the supplement for models that originally used it. Continual pretraining repeats this after two epochs of self-supervised adaptation on the target dataset, with other hyperparameters at each model's defaults. Supervised annotation uses a stratified 8:2 train and test split, 7:1:2 where a validation set is needed, and is scored with accuracy, precision, recall, macro F1, macro PR-AUC and macro ROC-AUC. Marker-gene concordance takes the top 20 differentially expressed genes per Leiden cluster and per reference cell type with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests in Scanpy, and compares the sets with pairwise Jaccard indices. Perturbation prediction follows a scGPT-style GEARS framework with the standard simulation split, and is scored with mean squared error and Pearson correlation over all genes and over the top 20 differentially expressed genes per condition, plus the same measures on the change from control. The paper fixes random seeds at 42; the GenePT-w folder's README also lists pytorch_lightning.seed_everything(202310).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering', 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering', 'Cell type annotation', 'DEG Analysis', 'Perturbation Prediction'

sections.title: Task coverage differs by model
sections.body: Not every model runs every task. Novae is evaluated on spatial transcriptomics only. Perturbation prediction is restricted to CellPLM, scGPT-spatial, GenePT-w and scELMo, because Nicheformer and Novae provide no comparable workflow for the GEARS setting. Supervised annotation is restricted to datasets with cell-level labels: the three scRNA-seq datasets and the single-cell-resolution SEAAD MERFISH atlas, and for SEAAD a section-wise split is used to avoid leakage between train and test. Two tasks had to be implemented by the authors where the original model did not support them: Nicheformer's cell type annotation, Novae's annotation through a frozen encoder plus a small classifier, and CellPLM's continual pretraining, because its repository provided no such pipeline.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering', 'Cell type annotation', 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering', 'Perturbation Prediction'

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The code is public under the MIT licence and organised by model, one directory each for CellPLM, Nicheformer, scGPT-spatial, GenePT, scELMo and Novae, with each directory holding the model's codebase plus the notebooks or scripts that run the shared tasks. The GenePT folder's README lists three notebooks, one per task, the Python packages they need, and the gene embedding pickle they read from a local data folder. The repository documents no installation or command-line entry point, so running a task means opening the relevant notebook and supplying the dataset.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Overview and License; GenePT/README.md: Contents, Requirements, Data Layout

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Ten datasets. scRNA-seq: ATAA (11 individuals, 11 major cell types), BMMC (12 healthy donors, 45 annotated cell types), HS (seven dendritic-cell subtypes). Spatial: HBCA1 (20 domains), MHPC (14 domain labels), MOSTA E9.5 E1S1 (12 anatomical regions), SEAAD (27 aged donors, 140-gene panel, 24 annotated cell types). Perturb-seq in K562: Adamson (87 single-gene perturbations), Norman (131 two-gene and 105 single-gene perturbations), Replogle (genome-wide CRISPR interference). Cell counts are not printed in the text.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: By task. Clustering tasks have no split: the whole dataset is embedded and clustered. Supervised annotation uses a stratified 8:2 train and test split, with the training part cut 7:1 into train and validation where a model needs one (7:1:2 overall), except SEAAD, which is split section-wise with two sections held out as validation. Perturbation prediction uses the GEARS standard simulation split with seed 42, so test perturbation conditions are unseen in training.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Cell type annotation' and 'Perturbation Prediction'

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Clustering: ARI, NMI and silhouette score, higher is better. Supervised annotation: accuracy, precision, recall, macro F1, macro PR-AUC and macro ROC-AUC, higher is better. Marker-gene concordance: Jaccard index between top-20 gene sets, higher is better. Perturbation prediction: Pearson correlation (higher is better) and mean squared error (lower is better), over all genes and over the top 20 differentially expressed genes, and the same on the change from control.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering', 'Cell type annotation', 'DEG Analysis', 'Perturbation Prediction'

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The six foundation models are compared with each other; ground-truth annotations and ground-truth-label marker genes are the references. Ground-truth UMAPs were made with Scanpy on 2,000 highly variable genes and 40 principal components, but the result tables report no non-foundation-model baseline such as PCA or scVI.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Ground truth visualisation'; Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks'

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Per task, and partial. Perturbation prediction uses the GEARS simulation split so that test conditions are unseen. SEAAD annotation is split by tissue section to avoid leakage between train and test. Overlap between the evaluation datasets and each model's pretraining corpus is not controlled or reported; the authors say current foundation models remain vulnerable to domain shift.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Perturbation Prediction' and 'Cell type annotation'; Introduction

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None reported: no replicates, repeated splits or confidence intervals are described. The paper states a random seed of 42 for splits and stochastic steps; the GenePT-w folder's README also lists pytorch_lightning.seed_everything(202310).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering' and 'Cell type annotation'; GenePT/README.md: Requirements

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A cell for clustering and annotation (a spot or cell with tissue coordinates for the spatial datasets), and a held-out perturbation condition for perturbation prediction, scored over a shared gene set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering' and 'Perturbation Prediction'

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human and mouse. Human: ATAA aortic tissue, BMMC bone marrow, HS spleen, HBCA1 breast cancer, SEAAD brain, and the K562 Perturb-seq screens. Mouse: MHPC hippocampus and MOSTA embryo.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: scRNA-seq and CITE-seq; spatial transcriptomics by 10x Visium, Slide-seqV2, Stereo-seq and MERFISH; Perturb-seq genetic screens including CRISPR interference. Labels are the original studies' expert or marker-based annotations.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Each model's own documented inputs, prepared by its own recommended preprocessing: raw counts for Nicheformer, library-size normalised and log1p counts for CellPLM, vocabulary-aligned binned expression for scGPT-spatial, normalised counts combined with text-derived gene embeddings for GenePT-w and scELMo, and spatial coordinates with neighbourhood graphs for Novae. Genes outside a checkpoint's vocabulary are discarded.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering', per-model paragraphs

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Three settings are scored: zero-shot (frozen pretrained embeddings), continual pretraining (two epochs of self-supervised adaptation on the target dataset), and supervised annotation with each model's default or recommended set-up: most models are fine-tuned, GenePT-w uses a k=7 nearest-neighbour vote on its embeddings, and Novae trains a small classifier on a frozen encoder.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks', 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering', 'Cell type annotation'; GenePT/README.md: cell_type_annotation.ipynb

strengths.text: Tasks, splits, clustering procedure, metrics and seeds are the same across models, and where the Leiden resolution could bias the comparison it is swept to match the number of reference labels.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering' and 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering'

strengths.text: Perturbation metrics are computed on one shared gene set per dataset, the intersection of the dataset's genes with every evaluated model's vocabulary, so differences are not driven by unequal gene coverage.

The per-model implementation details are written out, including checkpoints, batch sizes, learning rates, masking ratios and where the authors had to implement a task the original model did not provide.
The code that runs the tasks is public under the MIT licence, organised per model.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Data and Tool Availability; LICENSE; README.md: Overview

limitations.text: No non-foundation-model baseline is reported in the result tables: the models are compared with each other and with ground-truth labels, so a reader cannot see whether a simple method such as highly variable genes or PCA would match them. Highly variable genes are used only for the ground-truth UMAPs.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Ground truth visualisation'; Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks'

limitations.text: Overlap between the evaluation datasets and the models' pretraining corpora is not checked, so a model may be scored on cells it was pretrained on.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'; Introduction

limitations.text: No replicates or intervals are reported; the paper fixes its seeds at 42 and the GenePT-w README also lists a seed of 202310. The authors' own finding is that rankings shift with preprocessing and metric choice, so small differences between models should not be read as decisive.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering'

limitations.text: Coverage is uneven and partly author-implemented: Novae is spatial only, perturbation prediction covers four of the six models, and the Nicheformer and Novae annotation tasks and the CellPLM continual pretraining pipeline were written by the authors because the original models did not provide them.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Cell type annotation', 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering', 'Perturbation Prediction'

profile.summary: CACHE #3 is a blinded prospective challenge: 23 computational teams each picked up to 100 commercially available compounds for the macrodomain 1 of SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3, the organisers had them synthesised and assayed, and a separate hit evaluation committee scored the confirmed binders for quality and chemical novelty. The 1739 selected compounds all went through a fluorescence displacement screen and crystal soaking, and subsets went on to dose response and surface plasmon resonance, and teams whose compounds bound could then nominate up to 50 analogues each in a second round. It shows what current hit-finding workflows achieve on a target whose answers were not known in advance.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; Results 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse' and 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: CACHE is a series of challenges meant to show, prospectively and under a time limit, what computational hit-finding can do and what machine learning adds. Teams submit compound selections before any testing, so no retrospective tuning is possible. For CACHE #3 the target was Nsp3-Mac1, and the brief was stricter than binding alone: participants were asked for compounds with a novel chemical scaffold and no carboxylic acid. What is measured is therefore both whether a workflow finds confirmed binders and whether those binders are chemically new.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: A new protein target is nominated every few months and applications are ranked by double-blind peer review, each applicant scoring five others' proposed methods, with the ranking reviewed by an independent Applications Review Committee; the top 25 applicants are then invited to submit, within three months, a list of 100 drug-like ligand candidates from Enamine REAL. For CACHE #3, 23 of the 25 participants submitted within the required two-month window, and their selections, ranging from 41 to 99 molecules each, came to 1739 compounds, which Enamine synthesised and shipped. The library is therefore made by the participants, not by the organisers, and the labels come from the assays that follow. For reference, 161 Nsp3-Mac1 ligands had been published before the challenge.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Computational Workflows Were Diverse' and 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Round 1: all 1739 compounds were tested at 100 micromolar in a homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF) assay measuring displacement of an ADP-ribose conjugated peptide. 302 compounds that reduced the binding signal by 30% or more in at least one of two duplicates, or gave ambiguous data, went to a limited three-point dose response at 25, 50 and 100 micromolar, leading to 166 compounds tested by surface plasmon resonance (SPR); 28 compounds from nine participants were confirmed in a six-point SPR dose response and advanced. In parallel all 1739 compounds were soaked with crystallised Nsp3-Mac1, giving complex structures for 44, all binding at the ADP-ribose site; three of those were rescued as hits but not advanced. Round 2: 296 analogues of the 28 advanced compounds, from nine teams, were synthesised and tested; after HTRF and dynamic light scattering for solubility, 158 compounds plus 16 crystallography-rescued Round 1 molecules went to six-point SPR, giving 84 confirmed hits, each then counter-screened against the macro 1 domain of PARP14 to check specificity. Each of the 28 Round 1 hits, and the three rescued with a measurable dissociation constant, was given an activity score for signal quality and chemical soundness, and three chemists on the Hit Evaluation Committee voted a separate novelty score from 0 to 3. Teams were also asked to predict the actives in the merged library of all 1739 Round 1 compounds, which puts every workflow on the same library; confirmed hits scoring above 15 were grouped into four chemically novel Tier 1 compounds and 25 Tier 2 compounds judged not novel, and each workflow's selection was normalised as the aggregated score of its predicted actives divided by the number it predicted.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging', 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds', 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'; Figure 6 caption

sections.title: What the organisers concluded
sections.body: Over 85% of the designed molecules were chemically novel, but the best confirmed hits were structurally similar to previously published compounds, and the active molecules largely mimicked the adenine ring of ADP-ribose. Nine of the 23 workflows delivered at least one Round 1 compound scoring above 15, and only four of those produced a compound the committee judged novel. The paper classifies the seven best-performing workflows two ways. The Introduction says two included a deep learning step, one used a random forest classifier as a preliminary filter and the remaining four were purely physics-based. The abstract says two used compounds selected by physics-based screening to train machine learning models and four used exclusively physics-based approaches, and that three pharmacophore searches and one fragment growing strategy were also part of the seven. The organisers conclude that machine learning augments but does not consistently outperform physics-based methods, and that there is no single best method for rapid computational hit-finding.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; Results 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'; Conclusion

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: No fixed library: the data are made during the challenge. Round 1 is the 1739 compounds the 23 participating teams selected from Enamine REAL and Enamine synthesised, with 41 to 99 molecules per team. Round 2 is 296 analogues of the 28 advanced compounds. The merged Round 1 library of all 1739 compounds is also used as a common prediction set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse', 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'; Figure 6 caption

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train, validation or test split. The design is prospective and blinded: predictions are submitted before any compound is made or tested, within a time limit (three months in the general format, and the CACHE #3 participants submitted within the required two-month window).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Computational Workflows Were Diverse'

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Expert scores rather than a single statistic, all higher is better: an activity score per confirmed hit for signal quality and chemical soundness, a novelty score from 0 to 3 voted by three chemists, the best and aggregated Round 1 score per team, and for the merged-library prediction the aggregated score of the compounds a workflow predicted active divided by the number it predicted.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'; Figure 6 caption

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The reference points are the other teams' workflows and the previously published chemistry: 161 Nsp3-Mac1 ligands were in the literature before the challenge, the 10 published carboxylate-free ligands with a Ki below 100 micromolar all shared a bi- or tricyclic adenine-mimetic ring, and five of those had Ki values in a similar range to the new hits. The organisers also compare against the earlier CACHE #1 and #2 rounds.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging'; Introduction

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The design is the control: targets and libraries are set by the organisers and every prediction is submitted before testing, so there is nothing to memorise. It is not a control against prior knowledge of the target: the organisers note that the binding features of the ADP-ribose site were well documented at the outset and that 161 ligands had been published, and the confirmed hits largely reused the known adenine-mimetic chemotype.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging' and 'Trends and Strategies from the Best Performing Computational Workflows'

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Experimental replication rather than statistical intervals: the primary HTRF screen was run in two duplicates, compounds were taken through dose response and then an orthogonal SPR assay, Round 2 resupplied 17 parent molecules to check that a signal was not limited to one batch, and hits were counter-screened against PARP14. No confidence intervals or seeds are reported for the computational workflows.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging' and 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'; Introduction

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A commercially available compound selected by a team, later labelled by assay; the unit of comparison is a workflow, and chemical series group the confirmed compounds.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: The target protein is viral: macrodomain 1 of SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3, with human PARP14 used as the antitarget in the counter-screen. Constructs were expressed in Escherichia coli.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods 'Protein Expression and Purification'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence displacement of an ADP-ribose conjugated biotin peptide as the primary screen; limited three-point and six-point dose response; surface plasmon resonance on a Biacore 8K with dissociation constants from 1:1 steady-state affinity; dynamic light scattering for compound solubility; and X-ray crystallography by ligand soaking, with coordinates deposited in the Protein Data Bank under group deposition G_1002327.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Homogeneous Time-Resolved Fluorescence (HTRF)', 'Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR)', 'Dynamic Light Scattering', 'Crystallography'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Anything the team chooses, as long as the compounds come from the Enamine REAL catalogue and the selection is submitted in time. All 23 workflows used docking at some point; 17 included a machine learning step, eight molecular dynamics, five binding free energy methods, four pharmacophore searches guided by multiple PDB-bound molecules, and two quantum mechanics. Participants were also asked, though not required, to check their molecules against the badapple chemical liability filter.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Computational Workflows Were Diverse' and 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse'

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Inapplicable as a model setting: this is a prospective human-and-software competition, not a fixed dataset a model is trained or probed on. Teams built whatever workflow they chose, several trained machine learning models on docking scores from their own physics-based screens, and the organisers note that most top teams also inspected the selected molecules by eye.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Discussion

strengths.text: It is prospective and blinded: compounds are chosen before synthesis and testing, so a workflow cannot be tuned to known answers, and every selection is actually made and assayed.

Confirmation is layered: a primary displacement assay in duplicate, dose response, an orthogonal SPR measurement, solubility by light scattering, crystal soaking of all 1739 compounds, an analogue round to test whether a scaffold holds, and a counter-screen against a related protein.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging' and 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'

strengths.text: The merged-library prediction puts every workflow on the same 1739 compounds, which allows a comparison that the teams' own differing selections do not.

strengths.text: All molecular structures with their properties and activities are published in machine-readable supplementary tables, and the crystal structures are deposited in the Protein Data Bank.

profile.summary: PLABench scores protein-ligand binding affinity prediction with the training leakage taken out. It runs nine sequence-based and structure-based models over the same targets with the same metrics, and varies the input structure so that pose quality can be told apart from model quality. Its arms are Davis and KIBA under warm-start, cold-target and cold-drug five-fold cross-validation, two CASP16 ligand series, and a ChEMBL35 test set with every ligand within ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.85 of any ligand in fourteen audited training corpora removed. It is for anyone comparing affinity predictors who needs to know how much of a reported score comes from overlap with training data.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs; Results; ChEMBL35

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark measures how well a model predicts binding affinity when the easy routes are closed. Three things are varied deliberately: the split, so that a target or a drug unseen in training can be scored separately; the training overlap, so that scores on ligands similar to training compounds can be separated from scores on the rest; and the input structure, through a four-rung pose ladder, so that a structure-based model's errors can be attributed to the pose it was given rather than to the model. Protein-family breakdowns show where each model is accurate.
sections.source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs, Results, Per-family accuracy; results/README.md: casp16/ and leakage

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Davis and KIBA use the folds MixingDTA defined, five folds in three regimes, with train, validation and test for the warm-start arm and both cold-start arms. The test folds ship as CSV and everything else in the pickle format MixingDTA released, with a script to export the rest as CSV. CASP16 uses two ligand series, with 140 compounds in total for stage 1, converted to pKd from the Prediction Center's target files, and a size-weighted average across them. ChEMBL35 is cut from the Shimizu et al. release; the published arm removes every test ligand within ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.85 of any ligand in fourteen audited training corpora and then drops targets left with fewer than ten ligands, leaving 4,862 ligands over 71 targets, against an unfiltered arm of 7,650 ligands over 84 targets. Standardised affinity tables for CASF-2013, CASF-2016 and two CSAR-HiQ sets are included, and the structures the benchmark scored are AlphaFold3 predictions for ChEMBL35 and CASP16 and Boltz-2 predictions for CASP16, CASF and CSAR-HiQ. The data are on Zenodo in four archives, 1.4 GB to download and 5.8 GB unpacked, with a per-path record of origin and licence in data/SOURCES.tsv. Corpora the authors may not redistribute (PDBbind v2020, CSAR-HiQ structures, the CASF core sets, the CASP16 stage-2 complexes) are linked rather than shipped: 46 of the 68 dataset configs run from the deposit as it stands.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Results, Data, Davis and KIBA cross-validation, License; Zenodo record 22716174

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every arm except the Davis and KIBA cross-validation runs through one Hydra entry point, python run_benchmark.py with a model and a dataset config; there is one config per model and 68 dataset configs, one per combination of input source, benchmark and evaluation mode. Predictions land under outputs/<model>/<dataset>/latest/ and are scored in a separate analysis environment by scripts/collect_results.py, which writes results/benchmark_summary.csv (one row per model and dataset), results/per_target_evaluation.csv and results/benchmark_failures.csv, after which scripts/weighted_summary.py aggregates the first two into target-count-weighted summaries. The reported metrics are RMSE, Pearson, Spearman and the concordance index for Davis and KIBA; Kendall tau for the CASP16 ranking arms; and MSE, RMSE, Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, Rm2 and the concordance index for ChEMBL35. The Davis and KIBA rows come instead from the dedicated cross-validation collector, which averages the five folds. Runs that produce no usable prediction are recorded with a reason rather than dropped.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Running a benchmark, Results, Davis and KIBA cross-validation; results/README.md: top-level tables

sections.title: The leakage audit
sections.body: The audit is published as files, not just as a statement. For each of fourteen training corpora there is one table giving every benchmark ligand's highest ECFP4 Tanimoto against that corpus and whether its InChIKey skeleton appears there, after desalting and neutralisation; the filter cuts on the row-wise maximum across the fourteen. A per-corpus summary separates the ligands a corpus reaches on its own from the rows attributed to it as the closest analogue, so the first column does not sum to the number of removed rows. Further tables cover how the drop rate moves with the threshold, how much of the overlap is target-conditioned, which ligands match a training compound exactly, and how much protein sequence the benchmark shares with the corpora. The README reports that SAIR, built from ChEMBL 35, reaches Tanimoto 0.85 against 32.7% of the unfiltered benchmark, 2,413 of the 2,735 rows the similarity cut removes. CASP16 gets the same audit plus a stricter version that requires protein, ligand and affinity label to match before calling a row leaked.
sections.source_locator: results/README.md: leakage; README.md: ChEMBL35

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone with submodules, because the nine model sources are git submodules under forks/, each pinned to a plabench branch holding the exact upstream commit that was benchmarked plus the patches needed to run it. Each model needs its own conda environment, exported under environments/, since their dependencies conflict, and the analysis scripts get a tenth. Weights that PLABench trained are fetched by scripts/download_checkpoints.sh, which has the address and SHA256 baked in; third-party weights are never re-uploaded and are fetched and verified by scripts/download_third_party.sh. Benchmark inputs and structures come from the Zenodo data deposit. A run is then one Hydra command with a model and a dataset, scored afterwards in the analysis environment.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Install, Checkpoints, Data, Running a benchmark, Environments

strengths.text: The leakage audit is reproducible from published files: one table per training corpus with every benchmark ligand's highest similarity, the row-wise cut that defines the filtered set, and the threshold sensitivity beside it.

Every model is rerun by the benchmark rather than quoted, in its own conda environment, from a fork pinned to the upstream commit that was benchmarked, with the external tool versions and the per-model runtime stack written out.

profile.summary: SCMBench compares 23 methods for integrating single-cell multi-omics data, 19 domain-specific models and four foundation models (scGPT, UCE, Geneformer, scFoundation), on three paired and two unpaired RNA and ATAC datasets from four organs and two species, plus a triple-omics dataset and simulated data with increasing batch effects. Thirteen metrics cover integration accuracy, biological conservation (biomarker detection, differentially accessible regions, enriched motifs, trajectory conservation) and batch correction. It is for researchers choosing an integration tool, and for model developers who want to know where foundation models stand on this task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline'; Figure 1 caption; README.md: Downstream tasks

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark asks whether an integration method puts cells from different omics into one latent space that keeps the biology. Three groups of questions are asked: can cell types be told apart in the joint embedding (integration accuracy), does the embedding preserve informative features and dynamics (biomarker genes, differentially accessible chromatin regions, enriched motifs, developmental trajectories), and does it remove batch effects without over-correcting. Both paired data, where the two omics are measured in the same cells, and unpaired data, where they come from different cells, are covered, and the authors state that unpaired alignment is the harder case.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline'; Figure 1 caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Three paired datasets (PBMC-10k from 10x Multiome, 9631 cells; Chen-2019 SHARE-seq mouse cortex, 9190 cells; Ma-2020 SHARE-seq mouse skin, 32231 cells) and two unpaired datasets (Muto-2021 human kidney, 19985 RNA and 24205 ATAC cells; Yao-2021 mouse MOp, 69727 RNA and 54844 ATAC cells) are used, with a triple-omics mouse cortex dataset adding DNA methylation and a Chen-Traj subset of 1469 cells for trajectory work. Datasets were picked for species, organ, sample size, batch effects and sequencing technique. Ma-2020 and Muto-2021 carry batch effects and are partitioned by batch, then sampled to 2500 cells per batch for the batch-effect experiments, with the originals kept for the imbalanced case. Features are filtered with Scanpy's seurat_v3 flavour to 80,000 peaks and 8000 genes. Simulated paired data come from scMultiSim: 10,000 cells, 3000 genes and peaks, three batches, with batch effect size varied across 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 and 3. Because pretrained foundation models cannot take ATAC peaks, chromatin accessibility is turned into a gene-centric activity matrix with MAESTRO's ATACCalculateGenescore, weighting peaks by distance to transcription start sites; Seurat4's GeneActivity and BABEL translation are evaluated as alternatives.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results and Methods 'Datasets and preprocessing', 'Real data preprocessing', 'Simulated data generation'; Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each method produces latent embeddings and cell-type inferences, which are then scored. Integration accuracy uses four metrics, mean average precision (MAP), normalised mutual information, average silhouette width and the adjusted Rand index, with the overall score the mean of the four; all metrics are higher is better. Biological conservation is scored by consistency rather than by a single truth: cell types are annotated from each method's embedding with a k-nearest-neighbour classifier, the top 100 differentially expressed genes per cell type are taken with Scanpy's rank_genes_groups t-test, and the Jaccard similarity index of marker sets is averaged across cell types and method pairs to give that method's biomarker score. The same construction is applied to the top 100 differentially accessible regions and to motifs enriched in them with GimmeMotifs. For PBMC-10k there is also a recall against curated CellMarker 2.0 markers. Trajectory conservation uses a TC score against the original data's lineage. Batch correction uses iLISI, kBET, graph connectivity and batch-ASW. Datasets with batch information are split into smaller ones before computing integration metrics, and the overall box plots are across datasets, n = 5 for paired and n = 6 for unpaired.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Figure 2 caption, Methods 'Evaluation metrics' and 'Biomarkers Detection Consistency'; README.md: Downstream tasks

sections.title: How foundation models are handled
sections.body: Only scGPT came with an implementation for paired multi-omics integration, with both fine-tuning and zero-shot modes; UCE, Geneformer and scFoundation were modified by the authors to produce embeddings for each omics separately in a zero-shot way. Several adaptation strategies are then benchmarked as if they were separate methods: an adapter that feeds foundation model embeddings into scVI's framework (FM-scVI), fine-tuning at different transformer depths, parameter-efficient tuning, and training from scratch with only the pretrained gene token embeddings. The authors report that pretrained weights did not help substantially against training from scratch on this task, that scGPT's blood-specific model generally beat its whole-human model, and that foundation models generally underperform the domain-specific models, with UCE the only one able to handle the mouse Yao-2021 data. Foundation models are left out of the triple-omics comparison because continuous methylation beta values do not match the sparse counts they were trained on.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline', 'Benchmarking data integration on both paired and unpaired datasets', and the adaptation section

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds the benchmark package, the data preprocessing instructions, the per-method wrappers and the evaluation pipelines. Methods are grouped into four environments by language and version, each created by its own installation script, because the tools conflict. Data are preprocessed to one h5ad format with the same keys. A method is then run as a script taking the RNA and ATAC h5ad files and writing per-omics embedding CSVs plus a run-info file; Python methods and R methods have the same argument shape. Downstream evaluation is documented separately in the evaluation folder.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Directory structure, Installation, Quick start, Data preprocessing, Downstream tasks

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Six real datasets plus simulations. Paired: PBMC-10k (9631 cells), Chen-2019 (9190), Ma-2020 (32231). Unpaired: Muto-2021 (19985 RNA, 24205 ATAC cells), Yao-2021 (69727 RNA, 54844 ATAC cells). Triple-omics mouse cortex (2317 ATAC, 3377 methylation, 55803 RNA cells) and a Chen-Traj trajectory subset of 1469 cells. Simulated: 10,000 cells, 3000 genes and peaks, three batches at six batch-effect sizes.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet; Paper: Methods 'Simulated data generation'

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train and test split: integration is unsupervised and every method is run on the whole dataset, then its embedding is scored. Instead the data are partitioned by batch where batches exist: Ma-2020 and Muto-2021 are split by batch and sampled to 2500 cells per batch for the batch-effect experiments, and datasets with batch information are split into smaller ones before the integration metrics are computed. For unpaired results the authors report a single batch (Muto-2021-Batch1) to remove batch effects from the accuracy comparison.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Real data preprocessing'; Figure 2 caption; Results on unpaired datasets

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Thirteen metrics, all higher is better. Integration accuracy: MAP, NMI, ASW, ARI, with the overall score their mean. Biological conservation: Jaccard similarity index for biomarker detection, for differentially accessible regions and for enriched motifs, a recall against CellMarker 2.0 markers for PBMC-10k, and a trajectory conservation (TC) score. Batch correction: iLISI, kBET, graph connectivity and batch-ASW.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Downstream tasks; Paper: Results and Methods 'Evaluation metrics'

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The 19 domain-specific models are the reference points for the four foundation models: statistical methods PCA, MOFA, bindSC, LIGER, online-iNMF, scMoMaT, MMD-MA, Pamona, UnionCom, Harmony, Seurat4 and Seurat5, and deep learning methods scMDC, scJoint, GLUE, Cobolt, scVI, TotalVI and DeepMAPS. Seventeen of the methods can be applied to unpaired data, and seven handle the triple-omics case.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline' and the unpaired and triple-omics results; Supplementary Data 1 Method sheet

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None described for pretraining overlap: the paper does not report whether the benchmark datasets appear in the foundation models' pretraining corpora. The controls it does apply are about batch effects rather than leakage: partitioning and subsampling batched datasets, reporting one batch for unpaired accuracy, and adding simulated data at six batch-effect sizes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Real data preprocessing' and 'Simulated data generation'; Results on batch correction

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Spread across datasets rather than repeated runs: the overall scores are box plots with median and quartiles over individual dataset scores, n = 5 for paired and n = 6 for unpaired. The authors also report critical difference diagrams and significance reports, and state that the top methods are not significantly separated, for example that GLUE ranks first but does not significantly outperform scJoint, and that scJoint's lead on the unpaired data is not statistically significant.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 2 caption; Results on paired and unpaired integration

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A cell, embedded in a joint latent space; for paired data the same cell carries both omics, for unpaired data the two omics come from different cells that must be aligned.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Benchmarking data integration on both paired and unpaired datasets'; Figure 1 caption

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human and mouse: PBMC-10k and Muto-2021 are Homo sapiens, Chen-2019, Ma-2020, Yao-2021, the triple-omics set and Chen-Traj are Mus musculus. The authors note that most foundation models, trained mainly on human data, scale poorly to mouse, and that UCE was the only one that could handle the mouse Yao-2021 data.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet; Paper: Results on unpaired datasets and the adaptation section

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Single-cell transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility, by 10x Multiome, SHARE-seq, snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq and 10x v3, plus snmC-seq DNA methylation and Drop-seq RNA in the triple-omics set. Labels are the datasets' own cell-type annotations; marker references come from CellMarker 2.0.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet; Paper: Methods 'Biomarker Detection with Prior Knowledge'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Paired or unpaired RNA and ATAC matrices in one h5ad format with the same keys, filtered to 80,000 peaks and 8000 genes. Foundation models cannot take ATAC peaks because of their token limits, so they receive a gene-centric activity matrix computed by MAESTRO's ATACCalculateGenescore; Seurat4 GeneActivity and BABEL translation are tested as alternatives and neither uniformly wins.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results on activity matrices, Methods 'Real data preprocessing'; README.md: Data preprocessing

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: All of them, and the comparison of settings is part of the benchmark. Domain-specific models are fitted to each dataset. Foundation models are run zero-shot, fine-tuned (scGPT at different transformer depths), parameter-efficiently tuned, trained from scratch with only pretrained gene token embeddings, and combined with scVI as an adapter (FM-scVI); each adaptation is benchmarked as a standalone method.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline' and the adaptation section; Figure 2 caption

strengths.text: Significance is reported, not just ranking: critical difference diagrams show overlapping groups, and the authors say in the text where a lead is not statistically significant.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results on paired and unpaired integration

strengths.text: The foundation model setting is not taken for granted: three models were adapted to the task, several adaptation strategies are benchmarked as separate methods, and the alternatives to the MAESTRO activity matrix are tested rather than assumed.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results on activity matrices and on adaptation

strengths.text: The spread of conditions is wide: paired, unpaired and triple-omics real data from two species and four organs, with simulated data at six batch-effect sizes and a computational efficiency comparison of time and memory.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Figure 1 caption, Figure 2 caption, Results on triple-omics

strengths.text: Code and environments are public under the MIT licence, with one installation script per method group and an archived release on Zenodo.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Installation; LICENSE; Zenodo record 19050984; Paper: Code availability

limitations.text: The biomarker, differentially accessible region and motif scores measure agreement between methods, not correctness: each method's score is the average Jaccard similarity of its marker sets with the other methods'. Only the PBMC-10k recall against CellMarker 2.0 compares with outside knowledge, and the authors note it cannot credit novel or unannotated markers.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Biomarkers Detection Consistency' and 'Biomarker Detection with Prior Knowledge'

limitations.text: The foundation models are not fed their native input: chromatin accessibility reaches them as a gene activity matrix because of token limits, which the authors call a reasonable strategy with several feasible alternatives rather than a settled choice.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results on activity matrices

limitations.text: Coverage is uneven: 17 of 23 methods run on unpaired data, seven on triple-omics, foundation models are excluded from the triple-omics comparison, and Yao-2021 has no activity matrix because the computation ran out of memory, so not every method has a score on every dataset.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results on unpaired and triple-omics; Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet

limitations.text: Data are not redistributed and are subsampled: every dataset is fetched from its original repository, and the batched datasets are cut to 2500 cells per batch so that a wide range of methods could run, so the published scores are not on the full data.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Data availability; Methods 'Real data preprocessing'

profile.summary: This is the evaluation the HyCell technical report runs: frozen, zero-shot embeddings of eleven pretrained single-cell models, plus PCA of the counts, scored on seven human atlases that were excluded from HyCell's pretraining corpus. Each embedding is scored for biological conservation and batch correction with scIB metrics and for annotation transfer to a held-out batch, combined into one score S. Every model was rerun by the authors on the same cells with one scoring implementation, so the figures are comparable within this report.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report: Abstract; Section 3.1; README.md: Recorded result

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The question is whether a pretrained model's frozen embedding of a cell is useful without further training: does it separate the curated cell types, does it mix cells from different donors, laboratories and chemistries, and can a simple classifier trained on some batches annotate a held-out batch from it. The report motivates this by noting that independent evaluations find zero-shot embeddings often separate cell types no better than PCA of the counts, so PCA fitted to each atlas is included as a reference without pretraining.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 1; Section 3.1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Seven atlases with raw integer counts and curated cell-type labels are used: the integer-count parts of the scIB integration benchmarks for human immune cells (32,484 cells, 9 batches, 16 cell types), pancreas (10,963 cells, 5 batches, 14 types) and lung (9,701 cells, 4 batches, 11 types); peripheral blood mononuclear cells from two 10x runs (12,039 cells, 2 batches, 9 types); the healthy donors of the MultiVINE human brain vasculature atlas (21,155 cells, 10 donors, 14 types); a stratified 40,322-cell sample of the cross-tissue immune atlas spanning 17 tissue sites, 12 donors and three 10x chemistries, with 45 cell types; and a 41,140-cell sample of the Asian Immune Diversity Atlas (5 sites, 32 types). Batches are the unit held out in annotation transfer and the label the batch metrics use. Every dataset and collection contributing cells to these atlases, and to a separate development set of eight tissues used for the design choices, was removed from HyCell's pretraining corpus, taking the Census from 95.0 million cells in 555 datasets down to 79.5 million in 532.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1 and Table 2; Section 2.5

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: All embeddings are scored by one implementation built on scib-metrics, on the absolute scale with no rescaling across methods. Biological conservation is the mean of seven scIB metrics: isolated-label score, NMI and ARI of k-means and of Leiden clusters against the cell types, cell-type silhouette and cLISI. Batch correction is the mean of five: batch silhouette, iLISI, kBET, graph connectivity and principal-component regression. Annotation transfer holds out each batch in turn, trains a logistic-regression classifier and a 15-nearest-neighbour classifier on the remaining batches, and reports macro-F1 averaged over held-out batches. The composite score is S = 0.3 Bio + 0.2 Batch + 0.25 LR + 0.25 kNN, which weights the scIB total (0.6 Bio + 0.4 Batch) and annotation transfer equally. Atlases are weighted equally in all averages.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1, Metrics

sections.title: Which systems are compared, and under what conditions
sections.body: Ten published models are compared with HyCell: Stack, SCimilarity, scFoundation, UCE, Tahoe-x1, TranscriptFormer, scGPT, Geneformer V2, STATE and scPRINT, each run by the authors with its released weights and default inference settings on the same cells, plus PCA fitted to each atlas. The conditions are not identical, and the report says so: Stack encodes sets of 256 cells and the authors encode each batch together, so Stack uses batch labels at inference; SCimilarity and scPRINT were trained with cell-type labels; PCA is fitted to each atlas; and HyCell embeds each cell from its counts alone. The report marks these cases in its tables and states that Stack also draws on the other cells of a sample at inference, which helps sample-level tasks that this benchmark does not include.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1 Models; Section 3.2; README.md: Recorded result

sections.title: Downstream analyses on one atlas
sections.body: Beyond the scores, the report applies the frozen embeddings to the cross-tissem immune atlas, where cells of the same state come from 12 donors, 17 tissue sites and three chemistries. The 2,778 CD4 T cells (1,343 naive or central-memory, 1,435 effector or effector-memory) are split in two by k-means on each embedding; with HyCell the groups are 85% naive and 96% effector (ARI 0.64) and nearly independent of chemistry, while every other embedding reaches at most ARI 0.031 and seven of them follow chemistry instead. Diffusion pseudotime on the 3,751 cells of four B-cell to plasma-cell states (1,440, 572, 618 and 1,121) is correlated with stage at Spearman 0.937 for HyCell, the highest of all embeddings, and eight of the ten published models order the stages less faithfully than PCA. The decoder is used to read gene programs back from embeddings, with decoded and counted fold changes correlated at Spearman 0.81 over the 12,879 genes detected in at least 1% of either state.
sections.source_locator: Report: Sections 4, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The hycell package installs from the repository subdirectory with pip, and its weights (64 MB) ship inside the package, so it runs without network access once installed. Embedding is one call on an AnnData object of raw counts, or one command-line call on an h5ad file, and the embedding can then be used as any representation in scanpy. Decoding and fine-tuning have their own calls, and four example scripts plus a 512-cell test file from the scIB lung atlas come with the package. The report's own scores are reproduced bit for bit on a CUDA GPU with flash-attn, verified on all seven evaluation atlases, 167,804 cells. What the package does not provide is the benchmark harness itself: the scIB and annotation-transfer scoring of the eleven models is not among the published scripts.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Install, Embed, Decode, Fine-tune, Examples, Reproducibility

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Seven atlases: Immune (32,484 cells, 9 batches, 16 cell types), Pancreas (10,963, 5, 14), Lung (9,701, 4, 11), PBMC (12,039, 2, 9), Brain (21,155, 10 donors, 14), Cross-tissue immune (40,322, 12 donors, 45) and AIDA (41,140, 5 sites, 32). The README states the seven together come to 167,804 cells.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 2; README.md: Reproducibility

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No training split for the embedding tasks: every model embeds all cells of an atlas and the embedding is scored. Annotation transfer holds out each batch in turn and trains on the remaining batches, averaging macro-F1 over held-out batches; for the atlases without a study-level batch column the batch label is the donor or the site, as Table 2 gives: 10 donors for Brain, 12 donors for Cross-tissue immune and 5 sites for AIDA. The held-out status of the atlases themselves is a pretraining exclusion, not a split: every contributing dataset and collection was removed from HyCell's corpus.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1, Metrics and Table 2; Section 2.5

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Four reported quantities, all higher is better: Bio (mean of seven scIB biological-conservation metrics), Batch (mean of five scIB batch-correction metrics), LR and kNN (macro-F1 of annotation transfer with logistic regression and with a 15-nearest-neighbour classifier), combined as S = 0.3 Bio + 0.2 Batch + 0.25 LR + 0.25 kNN. The downstream analyses use ARI, NMI and Spearman correlation.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1, Metrics; Sections 4.1 to 4.3

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Ten published models (Stack, SCimilarity, scFoundation, UCE, Tahoe-x1, TranscriptFormer, scGPT, Geneformer V2, STATE and scPRINT) and PCA fitted to each atlas on 2,000 highly variable genes of the log-normalised counts with 50 components. For the fine-tuning table, the frozen-embedding classifiers are the baseline for the fine-tuned annotator.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1, Models; README.md: Fine-tune

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: One-sided. The seven atlases were excluded from HyCell's own pretraining corpus, dataset and collection by dataset and collection, and a separate development set of eight tissues was used for all design choices. The report does not state whether the ten published comparators were pretrained on cells of these atlases, and several of them are trained on CELLxGENE data, so the exclusion is established for HyCell only.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 2.5; Section 3.1

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None is printed. The tables give single values per model and atlas, with no replicates, seeds or intervals; the only averaging is over held-out batches within annotation transfer, over donors in two downstream analyses, and over the seven atlases.
facts.source_locator: Report: Tables 3 and 4; Section 3.1; Section 4.2

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A cell, represented by a frozen embedding; scores are computed per atlas and then averaged with equal weight.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 1; Section 3.1

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human only. The atlases are human immune, pancreas, lung, blood, prefrontal cortex, cross-tissue immune and Asian Immune Diversity Atlas cells, and HyCell's vocabulary is 36,495 human genes.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1; README.md: Inputs

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing on several platforms: inDrop and Smart-seq2 for the pancreas atlas, Drop-seq for the lung atlas, 10x Chromium for PBMC, vascular-enriched prefrontal cortex for the brain atlas, and three 10x chemistries across 17 tissue sites for the cross-tissue immune atlas. Labels are the atlases' curated cell-type annotations.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 2; Section 3.1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Raw integer counts of human genes, with all measured genes passed rather than a highly variable subset, because the measured zeros are drawn from the genes present in the input. Genes are matched to the 36,495-gene vocabulary by Ensembl gene id and otherwise by symbol; genes outside it are dropped and duplicates summed. HyCell receives no batch or donor labels at inference; Stack, as run here, does receive batch labels.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Inputs, Method; Report: Section 3.1

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot frozen embeddings for the headline comparison, with simple classifiers trained on top for annotation transfer. The README adds a separate fine-tuning result in which the encoder and a linear head are trained with cross-entropy on a labelled reference; that table covers four atlases and HyCell only, not the comparators.
facts.source_locator: Report: Abstract; README.md: Fine-tune

strengths.text: Every model was rerun by the authors on the same cells with released weights and default settings, and all embeddings were scored by one implementation on the absolute scale, so the figures within the report are not collected from different papers.
The differing conditions are declared rather than hidden: the tables mark batch-grouped inference and training with cell-type labels, and the text names which models those are.

The embeddings that were scored can be reproduced: the package carries its weights, and the README states the embeddings match the report bit for bit on a CUDA GPU with flash-attn, verified on all seven atlases.
A reference without pretraining is included and reported per atlas, so the reader can see where pretrained embeddings beat PCA of the counts and where they do not.

limitations.text: It is developer-run: the authors of the model under test chose the atlases, the metrics and the composite weights and ran every comparator themselves. There is no independent harness, and the benchmark scoring code is not among the published scripts.
limitations.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1; README.md: Examples

limitations.text: The held-out claim is established for HyCell only: the seven atlases were removed from its pretraining corpus, but the report does not say whether the ten comparators were trained on cells of these atlases.
limitations.source_locator: Report: Section 2.5; Section 3.1

limitations.text: Models run under different conditions: Stack receives batch labels at inference, SCimilarity and scPRINT were trained with cell-type labels, and PCA is fitted to each atlas, so the single score column mixes settings. No uncertainty is printed for any value.
limitations.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1 Models; Table 3

limitations.text: Only cell-level tasks are measured. Tasks defined per sample, such as predicting a donor's disease state, are not included, and the report notes that Stack's use of the other cells of a sample helps exactly those tasks.
limitations.source_locator: Report: Section 3.2; README.md: Recorded result
