profile.summary: This is the retrieval evaluation reported in the MSAlign paper, not a separate suite. Given a tandem mass spectrum and a candidate set of 256 molecules pulled from PubChem by mass, a method must rank the true structure first; recall at 1, 5 and 20 is reported. The current version of the paper scores Spectraverse and MassSpecGym under two splits, a chemical-formula split the authors recommend and MassSpecGym's harder MCES split, and reports methods that need the target formula separately from those that do not. It is for developers of spectrum-to-structure methods who need results that are comparable across models and splits.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper v3: Abstract; Section 5.1; Table 3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is molecule retrieval from a tandem mass spectrum: the method scores each molecule in a candidate set against the spectrum, and is judged on whether the true structure appears at the top of the ranking. The paper frames this as the tractable version of metabolite identification, and treats the choice of data split as part of what is being measured, because splits trade leakage against distribution shift. A second contribution is therefore a measure of how far a split moves the test distribution from the training distribution.
sections.source_locator: Paper v3: Abstract; Sections 2 and 4

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The current version uses two open benchmarks: MassSpecGym, 231,104 curated and standardised spectrum and molecule pairs, and Spectraverse, 488,797 pairs with broader coverage of adducts and ionisation modes, more than half of its spectra from adducts other than [M+H]+. The paper warns that pair counts overstate chemical diversity because the same molecule recurs under different ionisation conditions, and gives unique molecule counts in an appendix table. The first version of the paper also used NPLIB1, the smallest benchmark at 10,633 spectrum and molecule pairs. Candidate sets follow MassSpecGym's standardised protocol: molecules are drawn from PubChem's 118M compounds whose mass matches the target within 10 ppm, prioritising databases of decreasing metabolite relevance, and the pool is cut to 256 candidates per spectrum, which the paper says are typically structurally close to the target.
sections.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 5.1 'Supervised Datasets' and 'Candidates Sets'; Paper v1: Section 5.1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Recall at 1, 5 and 20 over the 256-candidate pool is the reported metric, higher is better. Methods that assume the target's molecular formula is known are reported in a separate block, because in practice the formula has to be estimated; MSAlign is also run in that setting by filtering candidates to those matching the ground-truth formula, which cuts the pool to about 100. The main split is by chemical formula, so that train, validation and test molecules have distinct formulas, with results averaged over three random seeds of the splitting algorithm; MassSpecGym's official MCES split is reported as well, averaged over its two variants obtained by swapping validation and test, because generating new MCES splits is expensive and the validation set is used for calibration and checkpoint selection. The repository states the ranking rules: candidate 0 is the target, padded candidates score minus infinity, a negative tied with the target ranks ahead of it, fusion weights are calibrated on validation data and metrics come from test data, and results across splits are macro-averaged.
sections.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3 and Section 5.1 'Data Splitting and seeds'; Section 5.2; README.md: Evaluation rules

sections.title: The split-shift measure
sections.body: Rather than argue about splits, the paper measures them. Each spectrum and molecule pair is encoded as the concatenation of an L2-normalised spectrum embedding and an L2-normalised molecule embedding, and the sliced Wasserstein distance between the training and test distributions is computed with the POT library using 100 random projections, then divided by the value from a random split so that a random split scores 1. On MassSpecGym the MCES and Murcko splits induce the largest shift and the formula and 2D InChIKey splits sit in between; the authors recommend the formula split because it is strictly more challenging than InChIKey, two molecules with the same InChIKey necessarily having the same formula, and still reflects deployment. The repository exposes this as its own command.
sections.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 4, Table 2; README.md: Measure train-test distribution shift

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository reproduces both the MSAlign models and the baselines. Datasets are downloaded and prepared per split and seed, or the prepared archives are downloaded from Zenodo with a checksum check. The four frozen input representations (DreaMS spectra, MolDeBERTa molecules, Morgan fingerprints, with spectrum bins computed on demand) are precomputed on a GPU, MolDeBERTa being a gated Hugging Face model that needs its terms accepted and a token set. One command then trains a model on one split, another evaluates the selected checkpoint once on the test candidates, and a third calibrates and evaluates the score fusion. A separate playground environment scores a spectrum against candidate SMILES from a pretrained checkpoint without any training data.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Applying pretrained MSAlign to my data; Reproducing the training experiments, steps 1 to 6

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: In the current version, two: MassSpecGym (231,104 spectrum and molecule pairs) and Spectraverse (488,797 pairs). The first version also used NPLIB1 (10,633 pairs). Unique molecule counts, rather than pair counts, are given in an appendix table that was not read here.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 5.1 'Supervised Datasets'; Paper v1: Section 5.1

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two kinds. The main split is by chemical formula, so train, validation and test molecules have distinct formulas, averaged over three random seeds of the splitting algorithm; the repository prepares five seeds, formula_seed0 to formula_seed4. The second is MassSpecGym's official MCES split, which requires molecules in different folds to have an edit distance of at least 10, averaged over its two validation and test swapped variants. The paper's shift measure also covers random, InChIKey, Murcko scaffold and Murcko histogram splits.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Sections 4 and 5.1; Table 2; README.md: step 1 and MassSpecGym MCES splits

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Recall at 1, 5 and 20 (R@1, R@5, R@20) over the candidate pool, higher is better, reported as percentages with a standard deviation over the splits. Ties count against the method: a negative tied with the target ranks ahead of it. The split-shift analysis reports a normalised sliced Wasserstein distance, where 1 is a random split and larger means more shift.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3 and Table 2 captions; README.md: step 4 and Evaluation rules

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: In the current version, DeepSet, JESTR, Emb-Cos and the two MSAlign variants in the no-formula block, and MIST, MVP and FLARE in the block that needs the target formula, with MSAlign plus candidate filtering alongside them. The first version also reported FFN and SAIL. The repository's model zoo holds reproductions of DeepSets, EmbCos, JESTR, FLARE and MVP.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3; Paper v1: Table 3; README.md: Repository layout

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split itself, and it is measured rather than asserted. Molecules in train, validation and test have distinct chemical formulas in the main setting, which the paper argues is strictly stronger than an InChIKey split, and the induced distribution shift is quantified by the normalised sliced Wasserstein distance. The paper's point is that stricter splits such as MCES prevent leakage at the cost of a large shift, with MCES test sets forming a distinct cluster away from the training data.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 4; Section 5.1

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Standard deviation over three random seeds of the formula split for the main arms, and over the two swapped variants for the MCES split. The split-shift table reports mean and standard deviation over five splits, except MCES which has two.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3 and Table 2 captions; Section 5.1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A tandem mass spectrum paired with its true molecule, scored against a candidate set of 256 molecules drawn by mass; candidate 0 is the target.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 5.1 'Candidates Sets'; README.md: Evaluation rules

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Inapplicable: the examples are mass spectra of small molecules and their candidate structures, not sequences or cells from a species. The datasets are described by their coverage of adducts and ionisation modes rather than by organism.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 5.1 'Supervised Datasets'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) spectra, with candidate structures taken from PubChem. Spectraverse covers more than 50% of spectra from adducts other than [M+H]+.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Sections 2 and 5.1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The spectrum and the candidate molecules. Whether the target's molecular formula may be used divides the table into two blocks: the paper reports formula-using methods separately because in practice the formula is unknown and must be estimated, and MSAlign's filtered variant uses the ground-truth formula to cut the pool to about 100 candidates. The frozen representations used by MSAlign are DreaMS for spectra and MolDeBERTa or Morgan fingerprints for molecules, with binned spectra as the simple alternative.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3 caption, Section 3, Section 5.3; Paper v1: Section 5.2

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training on the benchmark's own training split: every model, MSAlign and the baselines, is trained on the training fold of each split, with the validation fold used for checkpoint selection and for calibrating the score fusion, and the test fold evaluated once. Pretrained foundation models (DreaMS, MolDeBERTa) are used as frozen encoders inside this training.
facts.source_locator: README.md: steps 3, 4 and 6, Evaluation rules; Paper v3: Section 3

strengths.text: The split is treated as a measurable choice rather than a convention: a normalised sliced Wasserstein distance quantifies the shift each splitting rule induces, and the paper states which rule it adopts and why.
Methods that need the target's molecular formula are kept in a separate block, so a reader does not compare an oracle-assisted method with one that works from the spectrum alone.
Every number has a spread: standard deviation over three formula-split seeds, or over the two swapped MCES variants, with the reason for the latter stated.

The code is public under the MIT licence with reproductions of the baselines, the prepared data and checkpoints on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, and the ranking rules written out, including how ties are handled.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Evaluation rules and Repository layout; LICENSE; Zenodo record 23372807

limitations.text: This is one paper's evaluation, not a maintained suite: there is no leaderboard, and the arms changed between versions. The first version reported four dataset arms including NPLIB1 and the baselines FFN and SAIL; the current version reports three arms without NPLIB1 and a different baseline set, so figures from the two versions are not interchangeable.
limitations.source_locator: Paper v1: Table 3 and Section 5.1; Paper v3: Table 3 and Section 5.1

limitations.text: Scores are tied to the candidate set: the paper states that its NPLIB1 results use the 256-candidate pool it built and cannot be compared with retrieval performance on different candidate sets, and the formula-filtered variant scores on a pool of about 100.
limitations.source_locator: Paper v1: Section 5.2

limitations.text: The baselines are the authors' own reruns and some fall below their published numbers: the paper notes JESTR performing slightly below its original report, echoing issues raised in public implementations, and a similar trend for FLARE, while simpler baselines improved when trained for more epochs.
limitations.source_locator: Paper v1: Section 5.2

limitations.text: Reproducing it is gated and heavy: a CUDA GPU, several uv environments including a separate one for the graph baselines on a DGL wheel limited to Linux, Python 3.11 and CUDA 12.1, and a Hugging Face token for the gated MolDeBERTa model whose terms must be accepted.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Training environments; Applying pretrained MSAlign to my data

run_guide.summary: Prepare one dataset and split, precompute the frozen representations, train the model on that split, and evaluate the selected checkpoint once on the test candidates.
prerequisites: Python 3.11 and uv, and a CUDA GPU; the graph baselines need a DGL wheel built for Linux, Python 3.11 and CUDA 12.1.
Access to the gated MolDeBERTa model on Hugging Face, with its terms accepted and HF_TOKEN set.
Multiple CPU cores for building the candidate sets, or the prepared archives from Zenodo instead.
The repository code is MIT; the prepared data on Zenodo are CC BY 4.0, and the external datasets and pretrained models keep their own licences.

steps.title: Get the code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/KrzakalaPaul/MSAlign-NeurIPS2026.git
cd MSAlign-NeurIPS2026
git checkout --detach 97e201b1dd61e792d9086815192f7518a0b62ed8
steps.explanation: The README's clone and cd lines; the checkout line was added here to pin the commit this page was read at.

steps.title: Install the training environment
steps.explanation: The core environment covers MSAlign training, evaluation, score fusion, DeepSets and EmbCos. Preprocessing and the graph baselines are separate extras in the README.

steps.title: Get the prepared data
steps.explanation: Downloads the prepared dataset, splits and candidate maps from the Zenodo record, verifying the published checksum. The alternative is download_data.py followed by prepare_data.py per split and seed, which builds the candidate sets locally.

steps.title: Precompute the representations
steps.shell:
export HF_TOKEN=hf_your_token_here
python precompute_representations.py massspecgym \
  --candidate-map official_candidates_by_mass
steps.explanation: Generates DreaMS embeddings, MolDeBERTa embeddings and packed Morgan fingerprints; spectrum bins are computed on demand and DreaMS runs in its own environment automatically. Needs a GPU and the token for the gated model.

steps.title: Train on one split
steps.shell:
python train_msalign.py \
  --config massspecgym_formula \
  --dataset massspecgym \
  --candidate-map official_candidates_by_mass \
  --split formula_seed0 \
  --output-checkpoint checkpoints/dreams_moldeberta/massspecgym__official_candidates_by_mass__formula_seed0.ckpt \
  --no-logger
steps.explanation: The README's command for the paper's model on one formula split. Validation recall at 1 selects the saved checkpoint and the test fold is not touched here.

steps.title: Evaluate on the test candidates
steps.explanation: Scores the selected checkpoint once on the test candidates and writes a JSON result file. For the fused model, fuse_and_eval.py calibrates the weights on validation candidates and writes results/fusion.csv.

outputs: A JSON result file per evaluated checkpoint, and results/fusion.csv for the fused scores, with score tensors cached under cache/MSAlign_fusion.
For the split-shift command, a row per dataset, split and encoder pair in sliced_wasserstein/results.csv.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The detached checkout line was added here; the README does not pin a commit.
The MolDeBERTa model is gated, so the precompute step cannot run without accepting its terms.
Reproducing the published table needs the five formula seeds for both datasets plus the two MCES variants, not the single run shown here.

The version matters: version 1 (2026-05-19) reports four arms, NPLIB1, Spectraverse, MassSpecGym formula split and MassSpecGym MCES split, with baselines including FFN and SAIL; version 3 (2026-11-02) drops NPLIB1, reports three arms and a different baseline set, and renames the fused model. The record's protocol list includes NPLIB1 arms and entries labelled MSAlign v2; no saved file here uses the label v2, so those are left unmatched. profile.summary: BacBench is a multi-task benchmark for machine-learning models of bacterial genomics. A model embeds genomes or their genes and proteins, and the embeddings are scored on five active tasks: essential gene prediction, operon identification from long-read RNA sequencing, protein-protein interaction, antibiotic resistance prediction and phenotypic trait prediction; a sixth task, strain clustering, is deprecated but kept in the repository. The datasets are published on Hugging Face in DNA and protein-sequence form, and the repository holds the embedding and evaluation scripts for each task. It is for developers of bacterial genome, DNA and protein language models who want one comparison across tasks and across the bacterial tree of life.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs; Task overview

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Each task asks whether a model's representation of a genome carries a particular kind of biological information. Essential gene prediction and protein-protein interaction are per-gene or per-protein questions answered from gene or protein embeddings. Operon identification asks whether neighbouring genes belong to one transcriptional unit, from per-gene embeddings grouped by contig. Antibiotic resistance and phenotypic traits are whole-genome questions answered from a pooled genome embedding. The tasks therefore test different granularities of the same representation.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Task overview

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The datasets are curated from public databases and published on Hugging Face, each in DNA and protein-sequence form: essential genes from the Database of Essential Genes, operons from long-read RNA sequencing, protein-protein interaction labels from STRING, antibiotic resistance and phenotypic traits from genome collections. Sizes differ by orders of magnitude, from 59.2 MB for the essential-gene protein sequences to 38.8 GB for the antibiotic-resistance protein sequences, so the README recommends streaming the large ones. The splits ship inside the data: the essential-gene and PPI parquet files carry a split column with train, validation and test values, while the operon dataset has a test split only. Row counts on the dataset cards are genomes: 37 train, 9 validation and 9 test genomes for essential genes, 159, 49 and 53 for the small PPI set, and 5 test genomes for operons. As of 2026-05-13 the essential-gene and PPI tasks use a phylogeny-aware split by genus. The package also includes functions to download genomes from NCBI or GenBank and preprocess GBFF, GFF and FNA files into the required format.
sections.source_locator: README.md: News, Datasets, Download and preprocess genomes; PPI README: Data; Hugging Face dataset cards

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Running a task has two stages. First a model embeds the dataset: run_embed_prot_seqs.py or run_embed_dna.py writes a parquet file of embeddings, with options for whole-genome aggregation and a pooling method for the genome-level tasks. Then a per-task script reads that parquet file and scores it. Reading the scripts rather than their names: the essential-gene script takes the split straight from the parquet file's split column, trains a classifier, computes AUROC and average precision per genome with torchmetrics, reports the median across genomes for validation and test, selects the checkpoint on validation AUROC, and repeats the whole run for random states 1, 2 and 3, writing one parquet file of results. The operon script is unsupervised: it explodes the data by contig, scores each adjacent gene pair by the cosine similarity of the two embeddings rescaled to 0 to 1, sets the score to zero when the two genes are on different strands, concatenates the pairs of a strain, and computes ROC AUC and average precision per strain with scikit-learn, printing the mean and standard deviation. The antibiotic-resistance script defaults to split = genus with 0.7, 0.1 and 0.2 train, validation and test proportions, falling back to stratified or plain shuffled splits when a group split cannot be made, and reports classification metrics or, in regression mode, the coefficient of determination and the Pearson correlation. PPI is binary classification with STRING combined scores thresholded at 0.6 by default, scored per genome by AUROC and average precision.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Embedding genomes, Model evaluation; run_train_cls.py; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py; train_and_predict_linear.py; PPI README

sections.title: What the operon score actually computes
sections.body: The operon task is worth reading closely because it is not a trained probe. For each contig the script turns the annotated operon membership into a binary label per adjacent gene pair, one when the two genes share an operon. The prediction is the cosine similarity between the two genes' embeddings, mapped from minus one to one onto zero to one, with one exception: when the two genes lie on different strands the score is set to zero, a strand veto. Scores and labels are then pooled per strain and scored by ROC AUC and average precision. Intergenic distances are computed in the script but are not used in the prediction.
sections.source_locator: run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py: operon_prot_indices_to_pairwise_labels, predict_pairwise_operon_boundaries, run

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install the package from a clone, optionally with the fast-attention extra on a GPU machine. Load the task's dataset from Hugging Face, streaming the large ones. Embed it with the protein or DNA script, naming the model checkpoint and, for the genome-level tasks, adding whole-genome aggregation and a pooling method. Then run the task's evaluation script on the resulting parquet file. The README notes that embedding and most full benchmark runs need GPU hardware and task-specific input files, and the task READMEs give the per-task dataset and label-file locations.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Usage, Embedding genomes, Model evaluation, Large dataset tips

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Five active task datasets on Hugging Face, each in DNA and protein-sequence form, with sizes the README prints: essential genes (59.2 MB protein, 92.2 MB DNA), operon identification (15.3 MB protein, 24 MB DNA), protein-protein interaction (792 MB protein and 985 MB DNA for the 261-genome small version, 58 GB for the large protein-only version with more than 10k genomes), antibiotic resistance (38.8 GB protein, 54.9 GB DNA) and phenotypic traits (36 GB protein, 51.1 GB DNA). The dataset cards give genome counts: 37 train, 9 validation and 9 test for essential genes; 159, 49 and 53 for the small PPI set; 5 test genomes for operons.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Datasets; Hugging Face dataset cards

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Per task, and carried in the data. The essential-gene and PPI parquet files hold a split column with train, validation and test values, which the scripts read directly; since 2026-05-13 those two tasks use a phylogeny-aware split by genus. The operon dataset has a test split only and its evaluation trains nothing. The antibiotic-resistance and phenotypic-trait scripts make their own splits at run time, defaulting to split = genus with proportions 0.7 train, 0.1 validation and 0.2 test, and falling back to a stratified or plain shuffled split when a group split cannot be made.
facts.source_locator: README.md: News; run_train_cls.py; train_and_predict_linear.py; PPI README: Data; operon dataset card

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC and average precision (AUPRC), higher is better, are the metrics for the essential-gene, operon and PPI tasks, computed per genome or per strain and then summarised: the essential-gene script reports the median across genomes, the operon script the mean and standard deviation across strains. The antibiotic-resistance script adds a regression mode reporting the coefficient of determination and the Pearson correlation (higher is better for both).
facts.source_locator: run_train_cls.py; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py; train_and_predict_linear.py

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The benchmark publishes no numeric results of its own; its reference points are the supported models, which the README lists with checkpoint, objective, parameter count, dimension and maximum context: Mistral-DNA, DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer, ProkBERT, Evo, Evo2, ESM-2, ESM-C, ESMPlusPlus, ProtBert, gLM2, BacLM, Bacformer and Bacformer Large. A model leaderboard for each task is on the to-do list.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Benchmarked models; To-do-list

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: A phylogeny-aware split by genus for the essential-gene and PPI tasks since 2026-05-13, and split = genus as the default group for the antibiotic-resistance and phenotypic-trait scripts, so genomes of one genus do not appear in both training and test. The group split has fallbacks that drop to a stratified or plain shuffled split when it cannot be made, which removes the control for that run. No sequence-identity cut-off is described.
facts.source_locator: README.md: News; train_and_predict_linear.py: _split_indices

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Repeated runs and per-genome spread, task by task. The essential-gene script runs the whole training and test cycle for random states 1, 2 and 3 and keeps the random state in the output. The antibiotic-resistance and phenotypic-trait scripts accept a list of seeds and default to one seed. The operon script prints the standard deviation across strains. No confidence intervals are computed.
facts.source_locator: run_train_cls.py; train_and_predict_linear.py; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: Depends on the task: a gene or protein for essential-gene prediction, an adjacent gene pair within a contig for operon identification, a protein pair for PPI, and a whole genome for antibiotic resistance and phenotypic traits. Dataset rows are genomes, with gene-level fields nested inside and exploded by the scripts.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Task overview; run_train_cls.py; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Bacteria, across the bacterial tree of life; the essential-gene dataset card carries species, genus and family fields per genome, and the genus is what the phylogeny-aware splits group on. No individual species list is printed in the files read.
facts.source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph; essential-gene dataset card features

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Public database annotations rather than one assay: gene essentiality from the Database of Essential Genes, operon structure from long-read RNA sequencing, interaction labels from the STRING database's combined score, and antibiotic resistance and phenotypic trait labels from genome collections. Inputs are assembled genome sequences and their annotated genes and proteins.
facts.source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph, Datasets; PPI README

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence or protein sequence, whichever modality a model takes, with the datasets published in both; mixed-modality models (gLM2, BacLM) can use either but not both at once in the current implementation. Embedding granularity is set by flags: per-gene or per-protein embeddings, or whole-genome aggregation with a pooling method for the genome-level tasks. Context limits are the model's own, listed in the model table.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Datasets, Embedding genomes, Benchmarked models

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Three settings appear. Zero-shot: the operon task and the PPI unsupervised evaluation score embeddings directly with no training. Linear or shallow probes: a classifier is trained on frozen embeddings for essential genes, PPI, antibiotic resistance and phenotypic traits. End-to-end fine-tuning: the essential-gene folder also holds fine-tuning scripts for protein, DNA and mixed-modality language models, which load the Hugging Face datasets directly.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Model evaluation, Task overview; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py; essential-gene folder listing in the task README

strengths.text: One pipeline covers many model families: fourteen checkpoints across DNA, single-protein, whole-genome protein and mixed-modality models are supported by the same embedding scripts, with their parameter counts, dimensions and context lengths tabulated.
The splits are shipped in the data rather than left to the user for the essential-gene and PPI tasks, and are grouped by genus, so the same split can be reused across models.
The datasets are published under Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face in both DNA and protein form, and the repository code is Apache-2.0, so both halves of a run are redistributable.

The package also covers getting the data in: it can download genomes from NCBI or GenBank by taxid or assembly id and extract protein and DNA information from GBFF, GFF and FNA files into the format the models expect.

limitations.text: The repository prints no numeric results and no leaderboard: a model leaderboard for each task and dataset details in the repository are both on the to-do list, so any comparison has to be run by the reader or taken from a paper.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: To-do-list; Citation

limitations.text: The model table contradicts itself on size: Bacformer and Bacformer Large are both listed at 27 M parameters while differing in dimension (480 against 960), so the parameter column cannot be relied on for the large variant.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Benchmarked models

limitations.text: Protocols changed on 2026-05-13: the essential-gene and PPI tasks moved to genus splits and strain clustering was deprecated, so results from before that date are not on the current protocol. The strain clustering scripts remain in the repository.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: News; Task overview

limitations.text: Two tasks are small and one has no training split: essential genes has 9 test genomes and the operon dataset card lists 5 genomes in a test split only, so per-genome medians and means rest on few genomes. The genome-level tasks are the opposite problem, at 36 to 55 GB per modality, needing streaming and a GPU.

run_guide.summary: Install BacBench, embed a task's dataset with the model you want to test, then run that task's evaluation script on the embedding parquet file.
prerequisites: Python 3.10, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and PyTorch Lightning; the repository was developed in python=3.10.
A GPU and considerable disk space: embedding and most full benchmark runs need GPU hardware, and the genome-level datasets run to tens of gigabytes.
Optionally the faesm extra, which needs flash-attention and a CUDA GPU, for fast ESM-2, ESM-C and Bacformer inference.
The code and the task datasets are Apache-2.0.

steps.title: Install the package

The antibiotic-resistance and phenotypic-trait data licences, Apache-2.0, are read from their saved dataset card responses. The dataset web addresses are not printed in any saved file (the README gives dataset identifiers for load_dataset and the API response gives the identifier), so data_url is null on every entry and the identifier is kept in the dataset field.

profile.summary: One paper's benchmark of whether perturbation models get differential expression right, rather than mean expression. Each gene under each held-out perturbation is classified as up-regulated, down-regulated or not differentially expressed, and five deep learning models are compared with three simple classifiers on essential-gene Perturb-seq screens in K562, RPE1, Jurkat and HepG2, under two regimes: unseen perturbations within a cell line, and perturbations seen elsewhere in a held-out cell line. It is for anyone choosing a perturbation model for the downstream task that actually gets used, deciding which genes responded.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Section 1; Section 3.1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is three-class classification: for a gene and a perturbation, predict non-DE, up-regulated or down-regulated. The authors argue this is the decision that matters downstream, because an effect's significance has to be judged against the variability in the data, and that existing benchmarks measure continuous expression accuracy instead, or at best a top-k DE gene overlap score that ignores class-wise performance. Their headline finding is that simple baselines are competitive with and often beat deep learning models on this task, by being more precise while the deep models favour recall, and that better continuous-expression scores do not imply better DE prediction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Section 1; Section 3.1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Four essential-gene Perturb-seq screens are used: K562, RPE1, Jurkat and HepG2. Raw UMI counts are normalised by total counts per cell, scaled to 10,000 and log(1+x) transformed. DE labels come from Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction per perturbation, with a pair counted as DE when the adjusted p-value is below 0.01 and the sign of the log fold change deciding up or down; the same procedure produces the labels from observed expression and the predictions from each deep model's predicted expression. The classes are very unbalanced: per the paper's Table 5, non-DE is 96.61% for K562, 95.96% for RPE1, 97.61% for HepG2 and 98.35% for Jurkat, over 17.61 to 23.03 million pairs per dataset, with 2,057 to 2,393 perturbations and 8,561 to 9,623 genes. Every cell line is scored twice: on the full data, and on the PerturbQA-downsampled subset where non-DE pairs were cut and DE pairs restricted to the most significant, using that paper's own train and test split.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2 and Table 5

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Both tasks score the same held-out 40% of perturbations. For unseen perturbations, a cell line's perturbations are split 60% train and 40% test, and every method trains on that same split and reports on that same test set. For cellular context, a cell line is held out, models train on perturbation and gene pairs from the other cell lines over the 6,641 genes common to all four, and performance is reported on the held-out cell line's 40% test set; STATE is the exception, trained with the held-out line's 60% training set as its official codebase does, which the authors say makes it few-shot rather than zero-shot. The metrics are per-class F1 for up, down and non-DE, macro F1 averaging the three equally, and balanced accuracy averaging per-class recall; alongside these the paper reports continuous metrics (DE overlap at 50, MAE, MSE, global Pearson, Pearson delta, per-gene Pearson) to show that they disagree with the DE metrics. A sparsity calibration step sets predicted expression at or below a gene-specific quantile threshold to zero, with the scaling factor r = 1.

sections.title: How the split is actually made
sections.body: The repository's own code differs in wording from the paper, and the difference matters. The split script takes each perturbation's dominant DE class, merges rare strata into the most common one, and makes a stratified 80/20 split of perturbations with test_size 0.20 and random_state 305, writing a split_80 column. A second step turns 25% of the training perturbations into a calibration set. The preprocessing README then states that the calibration perturbations are merged into the test set for final reporting, which gives the 60/40 train and test split the paper describes. A second 60/40 split, in which the original evaluation perturbations all move to training, exists for robustness.
sections.source_locator: preprocessing/train_test_split.py; preprocessing/README.md steps 2 to 4

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository reproduces the analyses. One conda environment is created from the repository root, with VAE and scVI listing extra requirements in their own folders. The raw h5ad files for the four screens, the processed train and test splits with DE labels, the PerturbQA downsampled data and the embeddings used in the study are all downloadable from addresses the README gives. Each method has its own folder with its own README holding the commands, and there are separate folders for the metrics and for the post-prediction calibration. The preprocessing folder holds the DE calling and split scripts that every model shares.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Environment, Repository layout, Data access; preprocessing/README.md

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Four essential-gene Perturb-seq screens: K562 (17.61M perturbation-gene pairs, 2,057 perturbations, 8,561 genes), RPE1 (20.93M, 2,393, 8,748), HepG2 (23.03M, 2,393, 9,623) and Jurkat (21.25M, 2,393, 8,881). Each is also scored as the PerturbQA-downsampled subset. The cross-cell-line task uses the 6,641 genes common to all four.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 5; Sections 3.1 and 3.2

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: By perturbation, 60% train and 40% test, the same split for every method. The code makes it as a stratified 80/20 split on each perturbation's dominant DE class with random_state 305, then turns a quarter of the training perturbations into a calibration set which is merged back into the test set for reporting. Per-dataset train and test pair counts are in Table 5, for example 10.56M train and 7.05M test pairs for K562. For the cross-cell-line task the training data are the other cell lines, with the held-out line's 40% test set scored; STATE additionally trains on the held-out line's 60% training set. The downsampled arm uses PerturbQA's own split.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Table 5; preprocessing/train_test_split.py; preprocessing/README.md

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Macro F1 (the mean of the up, down and non-DE F1 scores), balanced accuracy (the mean of per-class recall) and per-class F1, all higher is better. Reported alongside them: DE overlap at 50, global and delta and per-gene Pearson correlations (higher is better) and mean absolute error and mean squared error on pseudobulk expression (lower is better).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.5.1 and 3.5.2

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three non-deep-learning methods: a perturbation majority vote that predicts each gene's most common class across training perturbations and ignores perturbation identity, a weighted k-nearest-neighbour classifier on GenePT perturbation embeddings, and a regularised logistic regression on those embeddings. The deep models compared are scVI (sampling and mean), Scouter and a VAE adapted from scGen for the within-cell-line task, with STATE and TranScouter added across cell lines.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 1; Sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split is by perturbation, so a test perturbation is unseen in training, and the cross-cell-line task holds out a whole cell line. The authors flag the one breach themselves: STATE is given the held-out cell line's training perturbations, following its official codebase, which makes its cross-cell-line result few-shot rather than zero-shot and not directly comparable with the others. No sequence or gene-level identity control is described.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Not reported as intervals in the text read: the code's split uses one fixed seed (random_state 305) and the paper reports single values per model, dataset and metric, with a second 60/40 split available in the repository for robustness rather than as error bars.
facts.source_locator: preprocessing/train_test_split.py; preprocessing/README.md step 4

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A perturbation and gene pair, labelled non-DE, up or down; the counts run to tens of millions of pairs per cell line.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1; Table 5

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human: the four screens are human cell lines (K562, RPE1, Jurkat, HepG2), which the paper calls four human cell-line datasets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2; Section 4

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Perturb-seq: CRISPR-based genetic perturbation paired with single-cell RNA sequencing, here the essential-gene screens. Labels are not measured directly but computed from the counts by Wilcoxon rank-sum tests against non-targeting cells with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and no log2 fold-change cutoff.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 1 and Section 3.2; preprocessing/README.md step 1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Normalised expression of the training perturbations, plus a representation of the perturbation. The simple baselines use GenePT large-language-model embeddings of the perturbed gene; the majority vote uses no perturbation information at all; the deep models take the expression data in their own formats. For the cross-cell-line task the input gene space is restricted to the 6,641 genes common to the four cell lines.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 1; Sections 3.1 and 3.3.2

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training on the benchmark's own training split: every method, baseline or deep model, is fitted on the same 60% of perturbations and scored on the same 40%. A post-prediction sparsity calibration is evaluated as a separate condition, and STATE's cross-cell-line runs are few-shot because they see the held-out line's training perturbations.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 and 3.4

strengths.text: The DE labels and the split are computed once and shared: every method is trained on the same 60% of perturbations and reported on the same 40% test set, with the preprocessing code published.
Class-wise results are kept rather than collapsed: per-class F1 for up, down and non-DE alongside macro F1 and balanced accuracy, which matters when non-DE is 96 to 98% of pairs.

Both the full data and the downsampled subset are scored, and the authors report that model performance and ranking on the subsampled data can differ drastically from the full dataset, which is the setting a user faces.
Continuous expression metrics are reported next to the DE metrics, which is how the authors show that the two disagree and that a model can look better on one and worse on the other.

limitations.text: One model is not on the same footing: STATE is trained with the held-out cell line's training perturbations, so its cross-cell-line numbers are few-shot rather than zero-shot, as the authors state.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1

limitations.text: The labels are themselves a statistical call, not a measurement: DE status comes from Wilcoxon tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction at adjusted p below 0.01 and no fold-change cutoff, applied to observed and predicted expression alike, so the benchmark inherits whatever that test does on sparse counts.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2; preprocessing/README.md step 1

limitations.text: Scope is narrow and fixed: four human essential-gene screens, single-gene genetic perturbations, no uncertainty intervals, and one split seed in the published code, so small differences between models should not be read as decisive.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2; preprocessing/train_test_split.py

limitations.text: It is a preprint not certified by peer review, and the data are not redistributed by the benchmark: the h5ad files, the processed splits and the embeddings are served from shared drive links the README gives, and the code repository states no licence.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: page header; README.md: Data access

profile.summary: GPCRrecent is a virtual screening set of 16 G protein-coupled receptors whose first crystal structures were determined after 2022, built by Shen et al. so that the targets postdate AlphaFold3's training data. Each target pairs actives taken from BindingDB with decoys generated by a conditional recurrent neural network at one active to fifty decoys, and a method is scored on how early it ranks the actives. It is for testing whether a structure prediction or docking method still enriches actives on targets it cannot have seen as structures.
profile.summary_source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Zenodo record 16826965

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The set measures early enrichment in virtual screening on targets that are new as structures. Shen et al. built it because DEKOIS2.0 had been released over ten years earlier and its template protein structures might overlap AlphaFold3's training data, so good scores there may reflect memorised structures. Here every target's first crystal structure was released after 2022, which the authors say guarantees temporal separation from AlphaFold3's training samples.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Methods 'Datasets'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: UniProt and BindingDB were queried for targets whose first crystal structure was released after 2022 and which have ligands in BindingDB, giving 47 eligible UniProt entries, mostly GPCRs, and the analysis was then limited to the GPCRs. Actives were taken from BindingDB with IC50, EC50, Ki or Kd below 10 micromolar, excluding peptide-like inhibitors and natural products above 600 molecular weight, and keeping EC50 entries rather than dropping them. After standardisation with RDKit the actives were clustered on Murcko scaffolds and only the most potent member of each cluster was kept; targets with many actives were cut to at most 300 diverse scaffolds by ECFP4 fingerprint, and targets with fewer than 200 actives were removed, leaving 16 GPCRs. Decoys come from a streamlined implementation of TocoDecoy, a conditional recurrent neural network that synthesises property-matched decoys, at one active to fifty decoys. For the protein side, the lowest-resolution structure for each UniProt entry was taken from the PDB and prepared in Schrodinger, and ligands were prepared with LigPrep.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Zenodo record 16826965

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method ranks each target's library and is scored with AUROC, BEDROC with alpha = 80.5, and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%; distributions across the 16 targets are compared in box plots. Shen et al. also report a six-target subset: Boltz-2 used a training cutoff of 2023-6, so only the six targets whose first crystal structures were released after that date (O15552, P0DMS8, P13945, P35348, P46098, Q96RJ0) are temporally clean for it. They warn that the six-target subset is too small for firm statistical conclusions. They also plot how BEDROC changes with each active's minimum Tanimoto similarity to PDB ligands, dropping targets with no actives above the threshold. There is no leaderboard; the authors' own scores are in their Zenodo source data.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Fig. 5 caption; Data availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One dataset of 16 GPCR targets, published as a single archive gpcr.tar.gz on Zenodo record 16826965. Shen et al. also score a six-target subset of it, for Boltz-2's training cutoff. Per-target active and decoy counts are in the paper's Table S1, which was not retrieved.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Zenodo record 16826965

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train, validation or test split: the whole library of each target is ranked and scored. The temporal rule is the selection rule rather than a split: only targets whose first crystal structure was released after 2022, and for the Boltz-2 comparison only the six whose first structures came after 2023-6.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC, BEDROC (alpha = 80.5) and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%, higher is better for all. BEDROC with alpha = 80.5 gives the top 2% of the ranking 80% of the score.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'; Fig. 5 caption

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: As reported by Shen et al.: new docking runs with Glide SP and Gnina (Vina score, CNNscore, CNNaffinity), against Protenix and Boltz-2 confidence scores and rescoring schemes. On this set the methods scored are Protenix and Boltz-2, chosen for their lower memory needs than AlphaFold3; Boltz-2's affinity module is excluded.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Scoring schemes'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: A temporal cut on structures: every target's first crystal structure postdates 2022, which the authors say separates them from AlphaFold3's training samples, and a six-target subset handles Boltz-2's later cutoff. The control does not cover binding data: the authors exclude Boltz-2's affinity module because its training sources, such as BindingDB, overlap this benchmark's own composition, and they say the set cannot show the generalisation of affinity prediction models. They also plot performance against each active's minimum Tanimoto similarity to PDB ligands.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Fig. 5 caption

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None requested. Shen et al. report distributions across targets as box plots and means across targets, with structure prediction run under one fixed random seed (seed = 1); for the six-target subset they say the number of targets precludes robust statistical conclusions.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Fig. 5 caption; Methods 'Complex structure prediction'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A compound in a target's screening library, labelled active (from BindingDB) or decoy (generated); one score per target.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated in the files read. The targets are named by UniProt accession rather than species.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Actives carry measured IC50, EC50, Ki or Kd values below 10 micromolar from BindingDB. The decoys are not assayed: they are synthesised by a conditional recurrent neural network to match the actives' properties.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Not fixed by the benchmark. Co-folding methods take one-dimensional protein and ligand sequences; docking baselines need a prepared 3D structure, and Shen et al. took the lowest-resolution PDB structure per UniProt entry and prepared it in Schrodinger, with the binding box set from the crystallised ligand.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets' and 'Scoring schemes'

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot screening: the methods are run as released, with default or recommended settings, and nothing is trained on the benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Complex structure prediction'

strengths.text: The targets are selected by a date rule on structures, so a co-folding model cannot have seen their crystal structures in training; the authors state this gives complete temporal separation from AlphaFold3's training samples.

The curation rules are printed in full: the activity cut-off, the exclusions, Murcko scaffold clustering with the most potent representative, at most 300 scaffolds per target, a floor of 200 actives, and a fixed one to fifty actives-to-decoys ratio.
The dataset is on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, and the authors' own scores and statistics are published as a separate Zenodo record, so their numbers can be checked.
strengths.source_locator: Zenodo records 16826965 and 17568813; Shen et al.: Data availability

limitations.text: The decoys are generated by a conditional recurrent neural network, not assayed inactives, so enrichment here is not comparable with benchmarks whose negatives were measured. Shen et al. report that a reviewer raised this for both DEKOIS2.0 and GPCRrecent.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

limitations.text: Temporal separation covers structures only. The authors exclude Boltz-2's affinity module because its training data overlap this set's composition, and say the set cannot reflect the generalisation of affinity prediction models.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

limitations.text: It is small and narrow: 16 GPCR targets, or six for a model with a 2023-6 cutoff, and the authors say the six-target subset precludes robust statistical conclusions. Its results also do not carry over from DEKOIS2.0, because dataset composition and decoy generation differ.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

limitations.text: The per-target composition is in the paper's Table S1, part of the supplementary information, which was not retrieved, and the Zenodo record gives only one archive with a one-line description.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Zenodo record 16826965

profile.summary: LIT-PCBA is a virtual screening benchmark of 15 protein target sets whose actives and inactives both come from measured PubChem BioAssay dose-response data, rather than from synthetic decoys. The official page states 7761 actives and 382674 unique inactives, publishes per-target counts, and offers the full data and an AVE-unbiased version. Method developers use it to test whether a model ranks measured actives above measured inactives at a realistic class imbalance.
profile.summary_source_locator: Official page: header and data content table; audit paper: Section 2

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark asks whether a method can pick measured actives out of a large library of measured inactives for each of 15 targets. Because the negatives were assayed rather than generated, the ratio of actives to inactives is as lopsided as a real screen: ADRB2 has 17 actives against 311748 inactives, while ALDH1 has 5363 actives against 101874 inactives. The audit paper describes the intended capability as recovering novel chemotypes, that is finding actives whose chemistry differs from what the model has already seen.
sections.source_locator: Official page: data content table; audit paper: Abstract and Introduction

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each target set is drawn from a PubChem BioAssay identifier and holds measured actives and inactives plus one or more PDB templates; the official table gives the assay identifier, the target, whether the ligands are agonists, antagonists or inhibitors, the active and inactive counts and the number of PDB templates. The audit paper describes three components per target: query ligands taken from co-crystal structures, a training set and a validation set, with training and validation partitioned by the asymmetric validation embedding (AVE) protocol. Its Table 1 prints the per-target split sizes, for example 4020 training and 1343 validation actives for ALDH1. The official page offers both the full data and an AVE-unbiased version.
sections.source_locator: Official page: data content table and download links; audit paper: Section 2 and Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission ranks each target's library, and the ranking is scored for early enrichment. The audit paper describes the usual protocol: the co-crystal query ligands are the fixed inputs, the LIT-PCBA validation split is treated as the held-out test set, and the ranking is scored with measures such as normalised EF1%, average precision, ROC AUC and BEDROC; single-ligand evaluation scores one query at a time and reports the mean across queries, while multi-ligand evaluation ranks by the maximum similarity over all queries, the max-pooling the original paper adopts. Because the active-to-inactive ratio varies so much across targets, both the audit paper and Shen et al. normalise the enrichment factor by each target's theoretical maximum (nEF1% or NEF). There is no central leaderboard; each paper publishes its own numbers.
sections.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2 and Section 3.1.1; Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 15 target sets. The official page states 7761 actives and 382674 unique inactives from high-confidence PubChem BioAssay data, with per-target counts; Shen et al. state 10 030 confirmed actives and 2 798 737 confirmed inactives for the full set. Neither source reconciles the two figures.
facts.source_locator: Official page: header; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Per target: query ligands from co-crystal structures, a training set and a validation set, with training and validation partitioned by the AVE protocol. The audit paper's Table 1 gives the per-target sizes, for example FEN1 with 269 training and 91 validation actives and 263 771 training and 86 947 validation inactives. The official page also publishes an AVE-unbiased version of the data.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2 and Table 1; official page: download links

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Enrichment at the top of the ranking, higher is better. The audit paper names nEF1%, average precision, ROC AUC and BEDROC as the ranking metrics in use and argues for reporting mean, median and the normalised nEF1%. Shen et al. use AUROC, BEDROC (alpha = 80.5), EF at 0.5%, 1% and 5%, and the normalised enrichment factor NEF for this benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2 and Section 3.1.1; Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Not published by the benchmark itself in the sources read. The audit paper supplies a parameter-free memorisation baseline built from 4096-bit ECFP4 fingerprints against the training actives, reaching a median raw EF1% of 4.15 on the validation set under the multi-ligand protocol, and compares it with the CHEESE EspSim and ShapeSim encoders, ECFP4, ROCS and SFX. Shen et al. use Glide and Gnina as baselines on their five-target subset.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 3.1 and Table 2; Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The AVE protocol is the benchmark's own control, and the audit paper reports that it does not hold. It finds 2,491 unique inactives shared between training and validation across the 15 targets, 323 active training-validation pairs at ECFP4 Tanimoto at or above 0.6 in ALDH1 alone, query ligands that also appear in the training or validation set, and near-duplicate query ligands within a set. It concludes that the benchmark in its current form does not measure the ability to recover novel chemotypes and that zero-shot evaluations are also affected.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Abstract; Sections 5.1.1 and 5.1.2

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: The benchmark asks for none in the sources read. The audit paper argues that a single summary statistic is not enough and that mean, median and nEF1% should all be reported, because one outlier target can move the result.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 3.1.1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A compound in a target's library, labelled active or inactive from a dose-response assay; query ligands are compounds taken from co-crystal structures.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2; official page: data content table

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated in the files read. The target list names human proteins such as the beta2 adrenergic receptor, estrogen receptor alpha and cellular tumor antigen p53, but no species column is printed.
facts.source_locator: Official page: data content table

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: PubChem BioAssay dose-response data: both actives and inactives are measured. Shen et al. describe the compounds as derived from real-world screening campaigns and both classes as experimentally verified.
facts.source_locator: Official page: header; Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset' and Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Not fixed by the benchmark. Each target ships PDB templates and query ligands, so ligand-based methods may use the query ligands and structure-based methods the templates; Shen et al. picked one of the recommended PDB entries per target for their docking baselines.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Both are in use. The benchmark provides a training set, so a model may be fitted on it and tested on the validation split; methods may also be run zero-shot from the query ligands or the structures, as Shen et al. do with co-folding methods run at default settings.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2; Shen et al.: Methods 'Complex structure prediction'

strengths.text: Both classes are measured: actives and inactives come from high-confidence PubChem BioAssay data, so enrichment is not an artefact of generated decoys. Shen et al. turned to it for that reason after a reviewer questioned decoy-based sets.
strengths.source_locator: Official page: header; Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

strengths.text: The per-target composition is published on the official page, with the assay identifier, actives, inactives and number of PDB templates for each of the 15 sets, so a reader can see the class imbalance before choosing a metric.
An AVE-unbiased version of the data is published alongside the full data, so the AVE-debiased split can be used without rebuilding it.

limitations.text: Huang, Knight and Naprienko audit the benchmark and conclude it is compromised by leakage: 2,491 unique inactives shared between training and validation, 323 active training-validation analogue pairs at ECFP4 Tanimoto at or above 0.6 in ALDH1 alone, and query ligands repeated in other splits. They report that a parameter-free memorisation baseline matches or exceeds published results and say nearly all published LIT-PCBA results are undermined.
limitations.source_locator: Audit paper: Abstract; Sections 3 and 5.1

limitations.text: The official page and Shen et al. print different totals for the full set (7761 actives and 382674 unique inactives against 10 030 actives and 2 798 737 inactives), and neither explains the difference.
limitations.source_locator: Official page: header; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

limitations.text: Raw EF1% is not comparable across targets here, because the active-to-inactive ratio varies by orders of magnitude; the audit paper and Shen et al. both normalise it, and published numbers using raw EF1% can invert a ranking.
limitations.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 3.1.1 and 3.1.2; Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

limitations.text: Published results are often on subsets, not the 15 targets: Shen et al. scored five targets with fewer than 100 000 compounds each and dropped MTORC1 despite it meeting the size rule, because its recommended structures have ambiguous binding sites.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

profile.summary: This benchmark asks a model to predict the binding affinity of a drug-target pair as a number, on the two kinase affinity data sets used by the DeepDTA paper: Davis, with dissociation constants for 442 proteins and 68 ligands, and KIBA, with combined kinase inhibitor bioactivities for 229 proteins and 2111 drugs. The DeepDTA authors split each data set into six equal parts, held one part out as an independent test set, and used the remaining five parts for five-fold cross validation, and they publish those fold files so that later methods can train and test on the same pairs. It is used by people comparing drug-target affinity regression methods, including methods that read only the protein sequence and the compound SMILES string.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Materials and Methods (Data sets), Experiment Setup; data/README.md: Train and test folds

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is regression: given a drug and a protein target, predict how strongly they bind. The authors argue this is more informative than the binary interaction prediction that earlier work used, because binding strength is continuous and because a binary data set has to invent negative examples. Both data sets are kinase data, so the question is how well a method ranks and estimates affinities across a protein family and a library of inhibitors. The paper's own interest is whether sequence alone is enough: it compares models that read raw protein sequences and SMILES strings against models given precomputed Smith-Waterman protein similarity and PubChem compound similarity.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Materials and Methods (Data sets); Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Davis holds selectivity assays of kinases and their inhibitors with dissociation constants, as interactions of 442 proteins and 68 ligands, 30056 interactions in the form used here. The authors convert the Kd values to a log scale, pKd. They note that the peak at pKd 5 covers more than half of Davis, 20931 of 30056 values, and that these are pairs with very weak affinity or not seen in the primary screen. KIBA combines kinase inhibitor bioactivities from Ki, Kd and IC50 measurements into a single KIBA score; it originally covered 467 targets and 52498 drugs and was filtered by earlier work to drugs and targets with at least 10 interactions, leaving 229 proteins and 2111 drugs and 118254 interactions. Compound SMILES strings come from PubChem and protein sequences from UniProt. Each data set is stored as an affinity matrix with the pairs that have a measurement, and the published fold files hold positions in that matrix: one test fold shared by all five training sets, and five training folds. The data folder also ships drug-drug similarities from PubChem structure clustering and target-target Smith-Waterman similarities, which were used to reproduce the comparison methods.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods (Data sets), Experiment Setup; data/README.md: Similarity files, Binding affinity files, Train and test folds

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method predicts an affinity value for every pair in the test fold. The headline metric is the Concordance Index, which asks whether two randomly chosen pairs are predicted in the same order as their measured affinities, so higher is better. Mean squared error is also reported, where lower is better. The authors fix hyper-parameters by five-fold cross validation on the five training folds, then train the chosen configuration five times, each time on four of the five training folds combined (the cross validation training set, leaving out that round's validation fold), score each of those five models on the same held-out test fold, and report the average with the standard deviation in parentheses. Significance between methods is tested with a paired t test at a 95% confidence interval. The comparison is made fair by giving the baselines the same train and test folds. The repository's own script follows this: it reads the test set and the outer training sets, uses get_cindex as the performance measure, trains with a mean squared error loss, and prints the per-fold test Concordance Index and mean squared error along with their average and standard deviation.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation Metrics, Experiment Setup, Results (Tables 3 and 4); run_experiments.py: nfold_1_2_3_setting_sample, run_regression

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository, install the Python, Keras and TensorFlow versions the README lists, place the data folder under the source directory, and run run_experiments.py with the window sizes, batch size, epoch count, sequence and SMILES length limits and the dataset path for the data set you want. The README's example uses the KIBA data path and problem type 1. The script loads the affinity matrix, finds the positions that have a measurement, reads the published test and training folds, searches the given filter combinations by cross validation, retrains on each of the five four-fold training sets and logs the test Concordance Index and mean squared error.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Requirements, Usage; run_experiments.py: experiment, nfold_1_2_3_setting_sample

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two kinase affinity data sets as used by DeepDTA. Davis, with Kd values, 442 proteins, 68 compounds and 30056 interactions. KIBA, with KIBA scores, 229 proteins, 2111 compounds and 118254 interactions, after earlier work filtered the original 467 targets and 52498 drugs to those with at least 10 interactions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1 and Materials and Methods (Data sets)

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: A random one in six holdout, the same for both data sets. The pairs are divided at random into six equal parts, one part is the independent test set, and the other five parts are the training folds used for five-fold cross validation to choose hyper-parameters. The published fold files give the test fold and the five training folds, and the test fold is the same for all five training sets. Counting the entries of the saved fold files gives 5010 test pairs for Davis and 19709 for KIBA.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup; data/README.md: Train and test folds; the two test_fold_setting1.txt files

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Concordance Index, higher is better, on both data sets, with mean squared error as a second metric, lower is better. The repository script uses get_cindex as the performance measure and trains with a mean squared error loss.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation Metrics and Tables 3 and 4; run_experiments.py: run_regression

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: KronRLS and SimBoost, both given Smith-Waterman protein similarity and PubChem compound similarity. On Davis the paper reports CI 0.871 for KronRLS and 0.872 for SimBoost; on KIBA, 0.782 and 0.836. DeepDTA variants that replace one or both similarity inputs with a convolutional block are also reported, the combined model reaching CI 0.878 on Davis and 0.863 on KIBA.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Baselines; Tables 3 and 4

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None beyond the random split: the pairs are divided at random, so the same drug and the same protein appear in both training and test folds. The authors do not apply a sequence identity cut-off; they report similarity statistics for the data sets instead, that Smith-Waterman similarity between proteins is at most 60 per cent for 99 per cent of KIBA protein pairs and for 92 per cent of Davis protein pairs, and call both data sets non-redundant.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods (Data sets); Experiment Setup

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Five training runs, each on four of the five training folds combined, all scored on the same test fold, reported as an average with the standard deviation in parentheses. Differences between methods are tested with a paired t test at a 95 per cent confidence interval. The repository script computes the average, the mean loss and the standard deviation across the folds.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup, Evaluation Metrics, Tables 3 and 4; run_experiments.py: nfold_1_2_3_setting_sample

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A drug-target pair with a measured affinity. In the published files, one example is a position in the affinity matrix for which a value exists, identified by a drug index and a protein index.
facts.source_locator: data/README.md: Train and test folds, For using the folds; run_experiments.py: experiment

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not reported. The saved files say the proteins are kinases and that their sequences came from UniProt, but they do not name the species the data cover.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods (Data sets)

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Dissociation constants from kinase selectivity assays for Davis, converted to pKd. For KIBA, a score combining kinase inhibitor bioactivities reported as Ki, Kd and IC50 from different sources, then preprocessed by earlier work by negating the scores and shifting them.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods (Data sets); data/README.md: Binding affinity files

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Sequence level inputs are enough: the protein amino acid sequence and the compound SMILES string, with no structures or external features. The data folder also ships precomputed drug-drug PubChem similarities and target-target Smith-Waterman similarities, and the paper reports methods that use those instead.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Results; data/README.md: Similarity files

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training on the benchmark's own training folds. Hyper-parameters are chosen by five-fold cross validation within the training parts, then a model is trained from those parameters five times, each time on four of the five training folds combined, and scored on the held-out test fold. The saved files describe no zero-shot or probing setting.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup

strengths.text: The folds are published, so a later method can train and test on exactly the same drug-target pairs. The DeepDTA authors state they gave their baselines the same train and test folds for the comparison.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup; data/README.md: Train and test folds

strengths.text: Affinity is scored as a continuous value, which avoids the invented negative examples that the authors describe as a problem for binary interaction data sets.
Results are reported as an average over five training runs with a standard deviation, and method differences are tested with a paired t test rather than read off a single run.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup, Evaluation Metrics, Tables 3 and 4

strengths.text: Only sequence level inputs are needed, so the benchmark is open to methods that cannot use a protein-ligand complex structure. The authors note that structure based scoring is limited to the complexes in the PDB.

limitations.text: The split is random over pairs, so a drug or a protein in the test fold can also appear in training. The benchmark as published does not hold out unseen drugs or unseen targets, and the authors name prediction for novel targets and novel pairs as future work.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup; Conclusion

limitations.text: Davis is dominated by one value. The authors report that the peak at pKd 5 is more than half the data set, 20931 of 30056 pairs, and that these are weak or unobserved pairs, so both the metrics and the apparent differences between methods are driven by a large block of near-identical labels.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods (Data sets)

limitations.text: Both data sets are kinases and their inhibitors, so a score here says nothing about other protein families. The labels are also not one assay: KIBA scores merge Ki, Kd and IC50 measurements from different sources.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods (Data sets)

limitations.text: There is no leaderboard and no licence. The saved repository files state no licence for the code or the data, and the only published result is the paper's own tables, so a new score has to be produced by rerunning the comparison methods or taken from those tables. The code also pins old versions, Python 3.4 or later with Keras 2 and TensorFlow 1.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Requirements; data/README.md (no licence section in either file)
