profile.summary: This was a public competition, hosted with Topcoder, on predicting what happens to mouse CD8 T cells in a tumour when a single gene is knocked out. The organisers generated an in vivo Perturb-seq data set of 73 gene knockouts in T cells transferred into a melanoma model, annotated each cell as one of five states, and asked teams to predict the five cell state proportions for held-out knockouts, to rank all expressed genes by two therapy-motivated objective functions, and to propose a new objective function. The top-ranked nominations were then knocked out in a second experiment, so submissions were scored against a prospective screen as well as held-out data. The record is useful to anyone comparing methods that predict perturbation effects on cell state composition rather than full expression profiles.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Machine learning competition section, Methods (Challenge setup and results); README.md: Code for Paper, Contents of this Repository

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The biological question is which gene knockout shifts tumour-infiltrating CD8 T cells away from terminal exhaustion and towards progenitor and other useful states, which matters for checkpoint blockade and CAR T therapies. The challenge turns that into three tasks. Challenge 1 measures accuracy: predict the five-dimensional vector of cell state proportions for knockouts that were measured but withheld. Challenge 2 measures usefulness for picking targets: predict proportions for every expressed gene, rank the untested genes by two objective functions, and be scored against a new experiment that knocked out the nominated genes. Challenge 3 measures the objective function itself: propose a score that ranks perturbations by how close they bring the cell state distribution to a desired one. The organisers point out that most existing benchmarks look like Challenge 1 alone, and that Challenge 2 tests the methods for biological efficacy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Machine learning competition section; Methods (Challenge setup and results)

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The training data come from an in vivo pooled CRISPR knockout screen. Naive CD8 T cells from OT-1 TCR transgenic mice were transduced with a guide library and adoptively transferred into congenic recipient mice, which were injected subcutaneously with B16-OVA melanoma cells one day after the transfer; the tumour-infiltrating T cells were collected 14 days later and sequenced. Screen 1 targeted 73 genes; after merging lanes it held 71,393 cells, and 31,009 remained after quality control for single-guide assignment and mitochondrial content. Leiden clustering gave five populations, annotated as progenitor, effector, terminal exhausted, cycling and other, and each perturbation is summarised by the proportions of those five states. A second experiment, Screen 2, targeted 59 genes, gave 75,227 cells and 25,738 after quality control, and served as the validation screen for Challenge 2. Perturbations with very few cells were dropped, with a cutoff of 32 cells for Screen 1 and 10 for Screen 2, leaving 59 perturbations for Screen 1 and 50 for Screen 2. A published screen of 180 transcription factors in the same mouse model was reannotated with the same five states and used as a third data set, with 173 perturbations after preprocessing. That screen activated the T cells before transfer and harvested them after 7 days rather than 14, and when the five cell states were mapped onto it some clusters could not be assigned. The two example objective functions were defined on the proportion vectors, with the unperturbed Screen 1 proportions as the reference point.
sections.source_locator: Paper: In-vivo single-cell CRISPR screens section, Methods (Data preprocessing and normalization, Cell state annotation, Challenge setup and results); README.md: Contents of this Repository

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: In Challenge 1 a submission is a five-number proportion vector per held-out knockout. Seven knockouts were withheld; three of them, Aqr, Bach2 and Bhlhe40, formed a validation set with up to three submissions and feedback, and the final ranking used the average absolute error over the remaining four, with one final submission. The error is the sum of absolute differences across the five states, so lower is better. In Challenge 2 the predicted proportions for all untested genes are turned into two ranked lists with the ICB and CAR T objective functions. The top-ranked genes from the Challenge 1 winners were knocked out in Screen 2, the measured genes were ranked by the same objectives, and each submission was scored by an area under the curve comparing its predicted ranking with the measured one. That score lies between 0 and 1 and a random ranking is expected to give 0.5. Scores were computed on both the filtered and the unfiltered Screen 2, averaged within each, and the final score was the smaller of the two averages. Challenge 3 submissions were written reports, ranked by single-blind peer review among participants, averaged over reviewer ranks, then reviewed by the organisers. For the follow-up benchmarking of the top 20 methods, the organisers reimplemented them and used cross-fold validation instead of the seven held-out perturbations alone: perturbations were partitioned at random into 6 folds for Screen 1 and the public screen and 5 folds for Screen 2, each fold held out in turn, and the whole procedure repeated 5 times to give a standard deviation.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results, Benchmark on prediction error, Benchmark on ranking genes); run_exp.py

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds the organisers' own benchmarking code, not a submission server. Create the conda environment from environment.yml, get the split data files, and run the per-method scripts in the folder for the screen you want. The baseline script for Screen 1 loads a single AnnData file holding the internal splits, loops over six splits and five repeats for three predictors, nearest neighbour, kernel regression and bagged kernel regression, and prints the mean and standard deviation of the average error. Some data files are not in the repository and have to be downloaded from a Google Drive folder the README links.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Environment setup, Contents of this Repository, Notes; run_exp.py

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Three Perturb-seq data sets of CD8 T cells. Screen 1, the training and Challenge 1 data, 73 targeted genes, 71,393 cells merged and 31,009 after quality control, 59 perturbations passing preprocessing. Screen 2, the validation screen for Challenge 2, 59 targeted genes, 75,227 cells and 25,738 after quality control, 50 perturbations passing preprocessing. A published screen of 180 transcription factors in the same mouse model, with T cells activated before transfer and harvested after 7 days, reannotated with the same cell states except for some clusters that could not be assigned, 173 perturbations passing preprocessing. Challenge 2 also required predictions for the expressed genes measured in Screen 1 that were not among the targets already tested, out of 15,077 measured genes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Data preprocessing and normalization, Benchmark on prediction error, Challenge setup and results); Prediction on a public T cell perturbation dataset; README.md: Contents of this Repository

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Held-out perturbations, and a second experiment. Challenge 1 withheld seven randomly selected knockouts, of which three were a feedback validation set and the final ranking used the other four. Challenge 2 was scored on genes that had never been tested when the submissions were made, knocked out afterwards in Screen 2. The organisers' later benchmark instead used random cross-fold splits over perturbations, 6 folds for Screen 1 and the public screen and 5 for Screen 2, with every perturbation held out once, and for the Screen 1 to Screen 2 transfer they trained on all Screen 1 perturbations and predicted the Screen 2 ones.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results, Benchmark on prediction error, Benchmark on ranking genes)

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Challenge 1: the average absolute error, the sum of absolute differences between predicted and measured proportions across the five cell states, averaged over the held-out knockouts, lower is better. Challenge 2: an area under the curve comparing the predicted ranking of the validated genes with their measured ranking, between 0 and 1 with 0.5 expected at random, higher is better, taken as the minimum of the averaged filtered and unfiltered Screen 2 scores. Challenge 3: averaged reviewer rank from single-blind peer review, lower is better. The follow-up benchmark also reports the absolute error on key states such as progenitor and cycling.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results); Benchmarking top participating methods section

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Two simple baselines in the organisers' benchmark: predict the cell state proportions of the non-targeting control cells, and predict the average proportions over all training perturbations. The paper reports that no other prediction method was significantly better than the averaged perturbation baseline on Screen 1. The 246 team submissions themselves, and the 20 top methods reimplemented by the organisers with nearest neighbour, kernel regression and bagging predictors, are the other reference points.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section; Machine learning competition section; run_exp.py

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The held-out knockouts were withheld from the data given to participants, and Challenge 2 was judged against genes that had not been measured anywhere when the submissions were made, so a prediction could not be copied from the ground truth. The organisers do not describe any control on the external data a team may use for gene features, and the winning methods did draw on public databases and other genome-wide Perturb-seq data sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Machine learning competition section; Methods (Challenge setup and results)

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: In the competition itself, one final submission was scored per team, with no replicates. In the organisers' later benchmark each cross-fold procedure was repeated 5 times to get a standard deviation of the accuracy, and each method was run 5 times for the ranking score. The winning Challenge 3 objective function adds a lower confidence bound term derived from the Hoeffding inequality that accounts for how few cells a perturbation has.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Benchmark on prediction error, Benchmark on ranking genes, Challenge setup and results)

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A single-gene knockout. Each example is one perturbed gene, summarised by a five-dimensional vector of cell state proportions over progenitor, effector, terminally exhausted, cycling and other cells, computed from the single cells carrying a guide for that gene.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results, Implementation of top methods)

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Mouse. The screens used naive CD8 T cells from OT-1 TCR transgenic mice transferred into congenic mice that were then injected with B16-OVA melanoma cells, and the public screen used the same mouse model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: In-vivo single-cell CRISPR screens section; Prediction on a public T cell perturbation dataset

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: In vivo pooled CRISPR knockout screens with single-cell RNA sequencing. Guides were delivered by lentivirus to naive CD8 T cells, the cells were transferred into congenic mice that were injected with B16-OVA melanoma cells one day later, tumour-infiltrating T cells were collected after 14 days, and the reads were processed with Cell Ranger. Cell states come from Leiden clustering of the normalised data annotated with known T cell markers, with Screen 2 and the public screen annotated by transfer from Screen 1 after Harmony batch correction.
facts.source_locator: Paper: In-vivo single-cell CRISPR screens section; Methods (Data preprocessing and normalization, Cell state annotation)

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Anything, including outside data. A method has to map a gene identity to a proportion vector, and the organisers describe the top methods as first building a gene feature representation from the provided Perturb-seq data, from public databases such as STRING, NCBI and gene ontology, or from other genome-wide Perturb-seq data sets, then fitting a map from those features to proportions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section; Methods (Implementation of top methods)

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Fitting on the provided screen. A model is trained on the measured perturbations of Screen 1 and applied to genes it has not seen, with hyper-parameters chosen by cross validation on the training set. The organisers' reimplementations pair each of 15 gene feature sets with a predictor, nearest neighbour, kernel regression or bagging, so the feature source and the predictor can be varied separately.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section; Methods (Implementation of top methods); run_exp.py

strengths.text: Submissions were tested prospectively. The genes the methods nominated were knocked out in a second experiment and the measured ranking was used to score every Challenge 2 submission, which is more than a held-out split can show.

The top 20 methods were reimplemented by the organisers in a common two-step form, so the contribution of the gene features can be separated from the contribution of the predictor, and the same predictor can be compared across 15 feature sets.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Implementation of top methods); Benchmarking top participating methods section

strengths.text: The comparison includes two baselines that are easy to beat by accident, the non-targeting control proportions and the average over training perturbations, and the organisers report that on Screen 1 no other method was significantly better than the averaged perturbation baseline.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section

strengths.text: The same methods were also run on an independent published screen in the same mouse model, reannotated with the same cell states, and the organisers report that the ranking of the feature sets was largely preserved.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Prediction on a public T cell perturbation dataset

limitations.text: The competition scored very few test perturbations. The final Challenge 1 ranking rested on four held-out knockouts, which is why the organisers moved to repeated cross-fold splits for their own analysis.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results, Benchmark on prediction error)

limitations.text: The signal the metric can show is limited. The organisers report that the gap between the best and worst performing feature sets was 7.5%, and that the error per gene tracks how far that perturbation sits from the average training perturbation, so a method can look good mainly by predicting the mean effect.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section

limitations.text: It is one mouse model, one tumour and one cell type, with a restricted T cell receptor repertoire, and the cell state labels are clusters the organisers defined and then transferred to the other screens, so both the task and the labels are specific to this study.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: In-vivo single-cell CRISPR screens section; Methods (Cell state annotation)

limitations.text: Reuse is awkward. The paper is under a Creative Commons licence that forbids commercial use and derivatives, no licence is stated for the code, some data files are only on a Google Drive folder rather than in the repository, and the competition is closed, so there is no live leaderboard to submit to.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: licence statement in the PMC record; README.md: Notes (no licence section in the README)

profile.summary: This is a molecular identification test: given one tandem mass spectrum, a model predicts a molecular fingerprint, and that fingerprint is used to rank a pool of candidate molecules drawn from PubChem for the spectrum's molecular formula. The pool and the fingerprints come from the MIST codebase and its public CANOPUS data set, which the MIST authors have since renamed NPLIB1. The record holds the version of this evaluation reported by the DreaMS paper, whose Extended Data Table 1 prints retrieval accuracy at top 1 to top 200 and the cosine similarity between predicted and true fingerprints for feed-forward, MIST and DreaMS models. It is useful to anyone comparing methods that annotate untargeted metabolomics spectra by database lookup.
profile.summary_source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks), Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction), Extended Data Table 1; MIST README.md: Data

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The capability under test is structure annotation from a single spectrum without a reference spectrum of the same molecule. A model reads the spectrum, outputs a molecular fingerprint, and the fingerprint is compared with the fingerprints of candidate molecules to rank them. What is scored is whether the true molecule appears near the top of that ranking, which is the question a metabolomics analyst actually faces. The evaluation also reports how close the predicted fingerprint is to the true one, which is a different thing: the DreaMS authors note that their model does better at retrieval while scoring lower on fingerprint cosine similarity than MIST, and that the same pattern was reported for SIRIUS against MIST.
sections.source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks); Extended Data Table 1 footnote

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The spectra are the public CANOPUS data set, extracted from GNPS and prepared for the 2021 CANOPUS methods paper, which the MIST repository calls canopus_train and has since renamed NPLIB1. The DreaMS paper describes it as covering 8,000 spectra from 7,000 unique molecules. The candidate pools are built by the MIST codebase: one pool per spectrum, holding positive candidates, which are PubChem molecules sharing the first 14 characters of the InChI key with the true molecule, including the true molecule, and negative candidates, which are molecules with the same molecular formula. The MIST repository stores these pools in an HDF5 file that is not part of the data download because it is larger than 5 GB, and says it is built with the relevant isomers for the data set. Splits are shipped as tables of split name and category with the values train, validation, test or exclude, and the README recommends three named split files for future comparisons.
sections.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction); MIST README.md: Data, Experiments

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model must produce a fingerprint for each test spectrum. The MIST retrieval script computes a distance between the predicted fingerprint and each candidate's fingerprint, cosine distance being one of the options, sorts the candidates by that distance and keeps the top k. The analysis script then finds the rank of the true molecule in each list and reports, for k in 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500, the fraction of spectra whose true molecule is within the first k candidates, so higher is better. Where two candidates tie in distance the script takes the worse of the two positions, which the README describes as a change from the earlier optimistic reporting. The DreaMS paper reports accuracy at top k for k up to 200, in per cent, counting a hit for any candidate that shares the first 14 characters of the true molecule's InChI key, together with the cosine similarity between predicted and true fingerprints, and notes that this cosine similarity is the inverted test loss. The DreaMS authors state that for this benchmark they did not use their own Murcko histogram split rule for deciding when to stop fine-tuning, as they did for their other tasks, but kept the split of the benchmark established by the MIST authors.
sections.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction), Results, Extended Data Table 1 footnote; retrieval_fp.py: get_dist_fn and rank_indices; analyze_rankings.py: run_analysis; MIST README.md: Change log

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install the MIST environment, download the public CANOPUS data, rebuild the retrieval HDF5 file from PubChem because it is not shipped, train a fingerprint model on the data set, then run retrieval and the analysis. The README gives one script for each of these steps in the public data retrieval section, and the analysis step calls analyze_rankings.py on the saved ranking files.
sections.source_locator: MIST README.md: Install and setup, Data, Experiments (Public data retrieval analysis); eval_retrieval.py

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: The public CANOPUS spectra data set in the MIST repository, called canopus_train there and renamed NPLIB1 by its authors, extracted from GNPS and prepared for the 2021 CANOPUS methods paper. The DreaMS paper describes the whole benchmark as 8,000 spectra from 7,000 unique molecules. The candidate molecules come from PubChem and are kept in a retrieval HDF5 file over 5 GB that the repository does not ship.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction); MIST README.md: Data

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: The MIST repository's own splits, kept as tables of split name against the categories train, validation, test or exclude, with three split files the README recommends for comparisons. The DreaMS paper states that for this benchmark it kept the split established by the MIST authors rather than its own Murcko histogram split, which it used for its other tasks. No saved file gives the number of spectra in the test fold.
facts.source_locator: MIST README.md: Data, Experiments (CSI fingerprint comparison); DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks)

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Retrieval accuracy at top k, higher is better, reported in per cent by DreaMS for k of 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200: the share of test spectra for which a positive molecule falls in the first k ranked candidates. The MIST analysis script reports top k accuracy for the same values of k plus 500, but counts a hit only for the exact InChI key from the labels file rather than the 14-character prefix. The secondary metric is the cosine similarity between the predicted and the true fingerprint, higher is better, which DreaMS describes as the inverted test loss.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction), Extended Data Table 1 footnote; analyze_rankings.py: run_analysis

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five reference methods in DreaMS Extended Data Table 1: a feed-forward network predicting fingerprints, with top 1 accuracy 17.309, a feed-forward contrastive model, MIST predicting fingerprints, top 1 29.368, MIST contrastive, and MIST contrastive plus fingerprint, top 1 30.703. DreaMS fingerprint, the paper's own model, reports top 1 32.731. The contrastive variants train with batches of PubChem molecules of the same molecular formula and a noise contrastive estimation loss.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Extended Data Table 1 and its footnote

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split files mark molecules as train, validation, test or exclude, and the MIST README states that test set molecules must be kept out of the augmented training spectra. The DreaMS authors criticise structure-disjoint splitting of spectral libraries as leaky for fingerprint prediction, because closely similar structures end up in different folds, and that is why they designed their Murcko histogram splits, which they did not apply to this benchmark. No saved file states a structural similarity cut-off used for the CANOPUS split itself.
facts.source_locator: MIST README.md: Change log; DreaMS: Methods (Murcko histograms algorithm for splitting molecular datasets)

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None reported. DreaMS Extended Data Table 1 prints a single number per method and metric, with no error bars, seeds or repeated runs, and the MIST README says ensembles were removed from the updated code. The MIST analysis script writes one metric value per k from one ranking file.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Extended Data Table 1; MIST README.md: Change log; analyze_rankings.py

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One tandem mass spectrum with a candidate pool. Each example is a single MS/MS spectrum of one molecule, together with the pool of PubChem candidates assembled for it, and the prediction is a molecular fingerprint used to rank that pool.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction)

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not applicable in the usual sense: the examples are small molecules and their spectra, not sequences from an organism. The spectra come from GNPS and the candidates from PubChem, and no saved file attributes the data to particular species.
facts.source_locator: MIST README.md: Data; DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction)

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Tandem mass spectrometry. The labels are the known molecular structures of library spectra, from which Morgan fingerprints are computed as the prediction target, and the candidate labels are PubChem structures matched by InChI key prefix or molecular formula.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks); Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction)

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The spectrum, and whatever derived features a method chooses. DreaMS predicts fingerprints from the raw spectrum in a single forward pass and notes that this avoids assigning chemical formulas to peaks or building fragmentation trees, while MIST is built on molecular formulas assigned to individual peaks and the repository also feeds in subformula and MAGMa annotations. The retrieval step needs the candidate pool for the spectrum's molecular formula.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks); MIST README.md: Data

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Supervised fine-tuning or training on the benchmark's training split. DreaMS fine-tunes its pre-trained network end to end with a cosine similarity loss on the fingerprints; MIST trains its fingerprint model on the same data, optionally with a contrastive model on top and with augmented spectra from a forward model. There is no zero-shot setting.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction); MIST README.md: Training models, Experiments

strengths.text: The scoring is the question an analyst asks: whether the right structure is in the top k of a candidate list, rather than how close a predicted fingerprint is. The DreaMS authors show these two can disagree, their model ranking better while scoring lower on fingerprint similarity.

The code is public under the MIT licence and the data are publicly downloadable, though no licence is stated for the CANOPUS spectra in the files read here; the candidate pools are built by a published script, and the repository names the split files to compare against, so another group can reproduce the same setup.

Ties are scored conservatively. The current analysis script takes the worst position among candidates tied at the same distance, which the MIST authors adopted in place of their earlier optimistic reporting.
strengths.source_locator: MIST README.md: Change log; analyze_rankings.py: run_analysis

limitations.text: It is small. The DreaMS authors state the benchmark covers 8,000 spectra from 7,000 unique molecules and, citing an assessment of how MIST generalises after training on it, describe their own fine-tuning result as a proof of concept rather than a production-ready fingerprint predictor.
limitations.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction)

limitations.text: The split is the MIST authors' own, and the DreaMS authors argue in the same paper that structure-disjoint splits of spectral libraries leak for fingerprint prediction, since near-identical structures can fall in different folds. They applied their own stricter split rule to their other tasks but not to this one.
limitations.source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks); Methods (Murcko histograms algorithm for splitting molecular datasets)

limitations.text: Rerunning it is heavy and not fully packaged. The retrieval candidate file is over 5 GB and is not distributed, so it has to be rebuilt from PubChem, and the comparison numbers in DreaMS come with no repeats or error bars.
limitations.source_locator: MIST README.md: Data; DreaMS: Extended Data Table 1

limitations.text: The counting rule is not identical between the two sources read here. DreaMS counts a hit when a candidate sharing the first 14 characters of the InChI key is in the top k, while the MIST analysis script looks for the full InChI key from the labels file, so a page or a score should say which rule produced it.
limitations.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction); analyze_rankings.py: run_analysis

profile.summary: This is a dose extrapolation test on the Sci-Plex chemical transcriptomics data. For each of twelve cell line and drug pairs, three cancer cell lines crossed with four HDAC inhibitors, the cells treated at the drug's highest dose are held out, and a model must predict the single-cell expression distribution at that dose from control cells, the lower doses of the same drug and all doses of the other drugs in the same cell line. Expression is reduced to 50 marker genes chosen from the training conditions only. The protocol and the preprocessing come from the Generative Intervention Models paper and its codebase; the record holds the version reported by the PerturbPFN paper, which scores predictions by mean distance, gene-wise Pearson correlation and a 2-Wasserstein distance between the predicted and observed cell distributions.
profile.summary_source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 and Appendix D.1 to D.3; GIM: Appendix D.2

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The question is whether a model can predict what a drug does to cells at a dose it has not seen, without being told the drug's target. Each test case gives the model the control cells, the same drug at lower doses and the other drugs at all doses, then asks for the distribution of expression vectors at the highest dose. The PerturbPFN authors describe this as dose extrapolation under unknown perturbation targets, and point out that the held-out drug is not wholly unseen because its lower doses are in the context. Because the prediction is a distribution over cells rather than a mean, the scoring can catch a model that gets the direction of the response right but the magnitude wrong.
sections.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.2 and D.3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The data are the Sci-Plex single-cell drug perturbation data of Srivatsan et al., restricted by the GIM authors to four drugs of the epigenetic regulation pathway in three human cancer cell lines, A549, K562 and MCF7, which gives twelve cell line and drug settings. The GIM preprocessing script lists the four drugs as dacinostat, givinostat, belinostat and quisinostat 2HCl and the doses as 0, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000, with 10000 as the held-out dose. Cells are normalised to the median count of the unperturbed cells, cells with fewer than 200 counts and genes expressed in fewer than 20 cells are dropped, counts are log transformed, then the top 1000 highly variable genes are taken and reduced to 50 marker genes. The script computes both of those steps on the training data only, scoring every gene against control for each drug with a Wilcoxon test ranked by absolute score, then keeping the 50 genes with the largest sum of absolute scores across the drugs, using the training cells only, so the gene set is specific to each held-out protocol. A code comment says it selects the genes most often among the top 50 marker genes, but the code sums the absolute scores and does not use that count. Perturbation features are one-hot drug and dose codes plus a rescaled dose value, and control cells form the observational regime. The GIM paper states that holding out the highest dose leaves 16 perturbations for training in each setting.
sections.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1 and D.2; GIM: Appendix D.2; preprocess_sciplex_data.py

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method predicts a set of cells for the held-out condition. Three metrics are computed per protocol. Mean distance is the Euclidean distance between the predicted and true mean response, lower is better. Pearson correlation measures gene-wise agreement between those mean responses, higher is better. The 2-Wasserstein distance compares the whole predicted and observed cell distributions, approximated by a debiased entropic Sinkhorn cost with squared Euclidean ground cost, epsilon 0.1, at most 200 iterations and tolerance 10 to the minus 6, computed on equally sized deterministically sampled cell sets, lower is better. For the table, each metric is oriented so that higher is better and min-max normalised across the models being compared within each protocol, then averaged over the twelve protocols, and the three columns are averaged for the overall rank. The PerturbPFN authors say plainly that these normalised scores depend on which models are in the comparison, and give the raw per-protocol distributions only as box plots in a figure. All methods are evaluated on the same held-out cells with the same metric code, and metrics for the baselines were recomputed with that code where prediction arrays were available.
sections.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 (Metrics), Appendix D.3 and D.4, Table 2

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The protocol lives in the GIM repository. Create its conda environment, install the package and the bundled cdt source, download the raw Sci-Plex files into data/sciplex/raw, then run the preprocessing script once per cell line, which produces the twelve data sets with their train and test splits. The repository's shell scripts then run GIM and the baselines on the single-cell data, and a notebook makes the figures. The PerturbPFN paper publishes no code of its own, so its own model cannot be run from the sources read here.
sections.source_locator: GIM README.md: Getting Started, Sciplex-3 Data

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: The Sci-Plex single-cell drug perturbation data of Srivatsan et al., reduced to three cell lines, A549, K562 and MCF7, and four epigenetic pathway drugs, belinostat, dacinostat, givinostat and quisinostat 2HCl, giving twelve cell line and drug protocols. Doses in the preprocessing script are 0, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000. Each protocol uses 50 marker genes chosen from its own training conditions. No saved file gives the number of cells in any protocol.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1; preprocess_sciplex_data.py

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: One held-out condition per protocol: the highest dose of one drug in one cell line. The context, that is the training data, holds the control cells, the lower doses of that drug and all doses of the other drugs in the same cell line. The GIM paper states this leaves 16 perturbations for training in each of the twelve settings. The held-out dose in the code is 10000, which the GIM paper writes as 10 micromolar.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.2; GIM: Appendix D.2; preprocess_sciplex_data.py

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three per protocol: mean distance between predicted and true mean response, lower is better; gene-wise Pearson correlation of those mean responses, higher is better; and a 2-Wasserstein distance between the predicted and observed cell distributions, approximated by a debiased Sinkhorn estimator, lower is better. For the ranking in Table 2 each metric is min-max normalised within a protocol so that higher is better, averaged over the twelve protocols, and the three columns are averaged.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 (Metrics), Appendix D.3

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Six reference points in Table 2: GIM, CondOT, a multilayer perceptron, a random-forest X-Learner, a Naive baseline that reuses the nearest observed lower dose of the held-out drug, and an Observational baseline that predicts the control distribution. On the normalised average score the random-forest X-Learner ranks first at 0.8870, PerturbPFN second at 0.8394, CondOT third, the multilayer perceptron fourth, GIM fifth at 0.6151, Naive sixth and Observational last at 0.0233. GIM is fit separately per protocol with 100,000 optimisation steps, and the table also reports runtime per protocol.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 (Baselines), Table 2, Appendix D.4

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two. The held-out condition is removed from the context, and the gene selection is computed on the training conditions only, both the highly variable gene step and the marker gene ranking, as the preprocessing code shows. There is no control against the model having seen Sci-Plex elsewhere, and the lower doses of the held-out drug remain in the context by design.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1 and D.2; preprocess_sciplex_data.py

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None for the scores. Table 2 prints a standard deviation for runtimes only, and no seeds, repeated runs or intervals for the normalised metric columns. The Wasserstein estimate is made deterministic by sampling equally sized cell sets in a fixed way.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Table 2 caption, Appendix D.3

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A held-out experimental condition, one cell line and drug pair at the highest dose. The prediction is a set of single-cell expression vectors over the protocol's 50 marker genes, and the comparison is between that predicted cell distribution and the observed one.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.1 and D.2

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human. The three cell lines are the human cancer lines A549, K562 and MCF7.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1; GIM: Section 5.1

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Single-cell RNA sequencing of drug-treated cells, from the Sci-Plex chemical transcriptomics experiment of Srivatsan et al., in which cells were treated with small molecules at several doses and profiled at single-cell resolution. The labels are the measured expression counts themselves after normalisation and log transformation.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1 and reference list; GIM: Appendix D.2

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The context cells and the perturbation descriptors. A model reads control cells, the lower doses of the held-out drug and the other drugs' doses in that cell line, with one-hot drug and dose codes plus a rescaled dose value as the perturbation features. Drug targets and mechanisms are not provided.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.1 and D.2

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Either is allowed, and both are in the comparison. GIM is fitted from scratch for each held-out protocol by instance-specific optimisation, while PerturbPFN is applied in context with no parameter updates at test time. The protocol itself only requires that the held-out condition is not in the context.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.4

strengths.text: The whole cell distribution is scored, not only the mean. The PerturbPFN authors argue this matters because a model can correlate well with the true mean response while getting the size of the response wrong, and the Wasserstein column does separate the methods: GIM scores 0.2934 there against 0.8611 on correlation.

The gene selection is computed from the training conditions only, in both the highly variable gene step and the marker ranking, so the 50 genes a method is scored on are not chosen with knowledge of the held-out dose.

The comparison is run on the same held-out cells with one metric implementation, and the baselines' metrics were recomputed with that same code where the predictions were available, rather than copied from their papers.
The protocol is reproducible from a public codebase: the GIM repository ships the preprocessing script that builds the twelve train and test splits and the scripts that run the baselines on them.

limitations.text: The published scores are not comparable with any other study. Table 2 prints only min-max normalised values, and the authors state that these depend on which models are in the comparison. The raw mean distance, correlation and Wasserstein values appear only as box plots in a figure, with no numbers printed.
limitations.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.3, Table 2

limitations.text: It is a narrow slice of Sci-Plex: four HDAC pathway drugs in three cell lines, twelve test conditions in all, and only 50 genes per condition. A result here says little about other compound classes or about genome-wide responses.
limitations.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1

limitations.text: It is dose extrapolation, not unseen drug prediction. The lower doses of the held-out drug stay in the context, which the authors say themselves.
limitations.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.2

limitations.text: No uncertainty is reported for the scores, and the numbers come from one group running every method. Table 2 gives a standard deviation for runtimes only, and no seeds or repeats for the metric columns.
limitations.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Table 2 and Section 4.2 (Baselines)

profile.summary: geneRNIB is an open, continuously updated benchmark for gene regulatory network inference, run as an Open Problems task. A method reads an expression matrix, optionally with chromatin accessibility, and returns a weighted directed network of transcription factor to gene links, capped at 50,000 links by default. The benchmark then scores that network with a fixed pipeline against data the method never saw: held-out perturbation or later-timepoint expression, external transcription factor binding references, gene set collections and a virtual-cell prediction task. Eleven data sets are available, including the 300BCG cohort of blood cells, and the documentation publishes a leaderboard in which scores are normalised per data set, ranked by percentile and averaged so that transcriptomics and multiomics count equally. It is for anyone choosing or publishing a network inference method.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: top, GRN Inference, GRN Evaluation, Component type sections; leaderboard page: Overall score normalization; PerturbPFN: Section 4.3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an inferred regulatory network is any use, judged without a ground-truth human network. Instead of comparing to one reference graph, the pipeline asks several different questions of the same submitted network: do the pathways enriched among a transcription factor's predicted targets match the pathways active in held-out expression data, does the network agree with experimental transcription factor binding references, do regulators chosen from the network predict held-out target gene expression, and can a model constrained by the network predict perturbed expression. The PerturbPFN authors describe this as evaluating both the predictive and the biological utility of the inferred network, and note that it therefore tests whether a learned causal structure transfers to regulatory relationships rather than reproducing a curated graph.
sections.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.3 and Appendix E.3; README.md: Component type metrics

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each data set is split into an inference part, which a method may read, and an evaluation part, which it may not. The repository ships eleven data sets: op, parsebioscience, 300BCG, replogle, xaira_HEK293T, xaira_HCT116, nakatake, norman, MSCIC, soundlife and soundlife_vaccine, and the config file records for each what cells it holds, what kind of perturbation it used, whether inference data are single cell or bulk, the measurement time and the modality. The perturbation types span drugs, chemicals, cytokines, CRISPR knockout, CRISPRa and overexpression, and cells span blood cells and lines such as K562, HEK293T and HCT116. Standard file formats are defined for the expression data, the optional accessibility data, the network prediction and the score, all as AnnData objects. Alongside the data sits a prior folder with supporting files such as the list of known transcription factors and consensus files the metrics use to standardise comparisons. For the 300BCG data set the config records blood cells, chemical perturbation and measurement at time zero and at three months; the PerturbPFN authors describe the official split as inference from baseline profiles of 38 donors, with the three-month profiles and the external references kept for evaluation, and the inference matrix as 380 log-normalised profiles.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Available datasets, File format sections; config.py: DATASET_INFO; datasets documentation page; PerturbPFN: Section 4.3 and Appendix E.1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an AnnData file whose prediction slot holds source, target and weight triples, with a default cap of 50,000 links. The scoring entry point is the all_metrics component: it reads the data set identifier from the evaluation data and runs the list of metrics registered for that data set, so the metric set is not the same for every data set. The code implements regression, Wasserstein distance, structural equation modelling, transcription factor recovery, transcription factor binding, replicate consistency, virtual cell and gene set recovery metrics. For the 300BCG data set the registered list at the commit read here is regression, virtual cell, replicate consistency, transcription factor binding and gene set recovery, with the structural equation metric excluded because that data set has a single perturbation condition. Thresholds in the same file record when a metric counts as meaningful, for example 0.001 for the regression metrics and 0.5 for the Wasserstein ones. The output is a score file listing metric identifiers and values. For the leaderboard, only metrics that pass the applicability criteria for a data set are used, raw scores are clipped at zero and min-max normalised per metric within each data set, methods are then ranked by percentile across all applicable data set and metric pairs, and the overall score is the mean of the per-modality median percentile ranks so that transcriptomics and multiomics weigh equally. Higher is better for all metrics. A method that is not part of geneRNIB must first update the consensus prior with its own network before evaluation.
sections.source_locator: README.md: GRN Evaluation, File format score; all_metrics/helper.py; config.py: DATASETS_METRICS and METRIC_THRESHOLDS; leaderboard page: Overall score normalization

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository with its submodules, then either install Docker, Java and Viash, or create the conda environment for the baseline methods and the evaluation. Download the benchmark data from the public S3 bucket, 24 GB for the core data or a 380 MB test subset to check the setup. Infer a network for one data set with one of the methods in src/methods, writing an AnnData prediction file. Then run the evaluation, either the Docker script or the local all_metrics script, naming the prediction, the data set and where to write the score. The README says the Docker route writes the scores into output/score_uns.yaml. Whole-pipeline scripts exist for running every method and every metric.

The config file records single-cell or bulk RNA for inference, with chromatin accessibility as an optional second modality for the multiomics data sets, and perturbation types that include drugs, chemicals, cytokines, CRISPR knockout, CRISPRa and overexpression. The evaluation also uses external transcription factor binding references: the PerturbPFN authors name UniBind, ChIP-Atlas and ReMap as the references the official scorer used.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The inference expression matrix, the list of candidate transcription factors, and for multiomics data sets an optional chromatin accessibility matrix. The method interface exposes the RNA file, the optional ATAC file, the transcription factor list, the link budget, the layer, the seed and the data set identifier. Evaluation data and reference networks are not inputs.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Open. The benchmark asks only for a network inferred from the inference data, so a method may be fitted on that data, as the correlation and tree-based baselines are, or applied as a pretrained model without gradient updates, as PerturbPFN was. Pretrained single-cell models including Geneformer, scGPT and scPRINT are in the method list.

strengths.text: It does not rest on one reference network. Because no complete human regulatory network exists, the pipeline scores a submission against several independent kinds of evidence, including held-out expression, binding references and gene set activity, and the leaderboard only counts metrics that pass applicability criteria for that data set.

Everything needed to reproduce a score is public and MIT licensed: the code, the file formats, the metric implementations, and the benchmark data in a no-sign-request S3 bucket, with a small test subset for checking a setup first.

The submission format is fixed and the link budget is fixed, so networks of very different density are compared at the same size: a prediction is source, target and weight triples with a default cap of 50,000 links.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: File format GRN prediction, Component type method

strengths.text: The aggregation is written down rather than left implicit: clip at zero, min-max normalise per data set and metric, rank by percentile, then average the per-modality medians so that the more numerous transcriptomics data sets do not outweigh the multiomics ones.

limitations.text: It is a living benchmark, so a score is only meaningful with the revision attached. The metric set per data set is read from a config file at run time, and that file records changes, for example that the structural equation metric is excluded for 300BCG because it has a single perturbation condition and for nakatake because only five control samples remain. A number from an earlier run may not come from the same metric set.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: top; config.py: DATASETS_METRICS; all_metrics/helper.py

limitations.text: The leaderboard score is a relative one. Raw scores are min-max normalised across the methods present and then turned into percentile ranks, so adding or removing methods changes the numbers, and the published overall score cannot be read as an absolute measure of a network's quality.
limitations.source_locator: leaderboard page: Overall score normalization

limitations.text: Running it is heavy. The core data download is 24 GB, the Singularity images for the advanced inference methods are 48 GB, and the README says the pipeline had to be split into separate inference and evaluation steps because the task is resource-intensive.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Download resources, Run the entire pipeline

limitations.text: Evaluating a method from outside the benchmark changes the shared resources: the README requires such a model to update the consensus prior before scoring, which means the prior the metrics use is not fixed across submissions.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: GRN Evaluation

profile.summary: This is one paper's evaluation, not a released suite. For each gene knocked down or activated in a CRISPR screen, every other gene is scored by its link to the perturbed gene, either an attention weight taken from a single-cell foundation model or a Spearman correlation, and the score is used to classify which genes turn out to be differentially expressed. Performance is the per-perturbation area under the ROC curve. The same test is run for three univariate gene-level features, variance, mean expression and dropout rate, and then a conditional test asks whether adding a pairwise edge score to those gene-level features improves prediction. The answer the paper reports is no: gene-level features reach 0.81 to 0.88 against about 0.70 for either edge type, and adding edges changes the area under the curve by about nothing. The evaluation is useful as a sanity check that anyone claiming regulatory signal in attention has to pass.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, Perturbation-first validation and No incremental pairwise value sections; Methods, Perturbation-first validation and Confound decomposition

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The paper calls this Objective B, and keeps it apart from Objective A, which is recovery of curated regulatory interactions. Objective B asks whether a pairwise score between a perturbed gene and another gene predicts that the other gene will be differentially expressed after the perturbation. The author stresses that this is an effect-magnitude question, mixing direct regulation, indirect propagation and how detectable a gene is at all, so the two objectives can disagree: a true direct edge may produce little differential expression, and a non-regulatory feature can score well if it proxies target susceptibility. The evaluation therefore sets a floor rather than a ceiling, that any claimed pairwise regulatory signal must first beat features computed from single genes.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Evaluation framework section; Results, Perturbation-first validation

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The expression data are published CRISPR screens, taken through the scperturb package according to the code repository: the Replogle genome-scale CRISPRi screens in K562, described in the paper as more than 640,000 K562 cells and 2,024 perturbed genes, and in RPE1, Adamson CRISPRa in K562 with 77 perturbations, Tian iPSC neurons with 7, and Shifrut primary T cells with 7. Tabula Sapiens tissues and a brain data set are used for the other objective. Preprocessing is standard Scanpy quality control, genes in at least 3 cells, cells with at least 200 genes, normalisation to 10,000 counts and a log transform, with highly variable gene selection. Labels come from the screens themselves: for each perturbation, a Mann-Whitney test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and a log fold change threshold marks which genes are differentially expressed. The pairwise scores being tested are attention weights from Geneformer V2-316M, averaged over heads within a layer and then over cells, and Spearman correlation edges computed from the same control cells, with absolute value taken because the sign is not comparable. The evaluation universe is 2,000 highly variable genes for K562 and 3,309 for RPE1, where the perturbed genes are forced into the set.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Models and data, Attention extraction, Perturbation-first validation; README.md: Perturbation Datasets, External Data

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Two layers of test. The first is per-perturbation area under the ROC curve: rank all candidate genes for one perturbation by the score under test and ask how well that ranking separates the differentially expressed genes, then compare score types across perturbations with paired tests. On K562 CRISPRi, correlation edges reach 0.696 under the primary settings with 151 perturbations, and all 27 sensitivity conditions give 0.62 to 0.76; Geneformer attention at layer 13 reaches 0.704 on 280 evaluable perturbations, indistinguishable from correlation at 0.703. Variance alone reaches 0.881. The second test is conditional: a data set of 280 by 1,999 perturbation and gene observations, 559,720 pairs with a 2.8 per cent positive rate, five logistic regression models under 5-fold GroupKFold cross validation grouped by perturbation. Gene-level features alone reach 0.895, adding attention changes the area under the curve by minus 0.0004 and adding correlation by minus 0.002. Harder splits were also tried, GroupKFold by target gene and joint gene by perturbation splits, with gradient boosted trees as well as logistic regression and with AUPRC and top-k recall as well as AUROC. Propensity matching, five differential-expression-negative targets matched to each positive one on mean, variance and dropout rate, gives 59,153 matched pairs in which attention retains 0.609 raw discriminability but zero incremental value. All tests use Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 0.05, and bootstrap intervals resample at the perturbation level. A synthetic positive control with a planted network shows the same pipeline detects a real pairwise signal, reporting a change in area under the curve of plus 0.518 in the cleanest variant.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Perturbation-first validation, No incremental pairwise value and Positive control sections; Methods, Perturbation-first validation, Confound decomposition and Statistical framework

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The analysis code is published as a repository, archived on Zenodo. Create the conda environment from the file in src, let the scperturb package download the perturbation data, and run the module scripts: one for the perturbation-first validation and the trivial baselines, another for the RPE1 confound battery. The repository says each module is self-contained, loads data from external sources or precomputed checkpoints in results, and writes outputs back into results, with resume support. Geneformer weights come from Hugging Face. The licence statement asks anyone wanting to reuse the repository to contact the author first.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Environment Setup, External Data, Reproducing Analyses, License; Paper: Data availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Published CRISPR perturbation screens, obtained through scperturb: Replogle K562 CRISPRi, described as more than 640,000 cells and 2,024 perturbed genes, with 280 perturbations evaluable in the attention comparison and 151 under the primary correlation parameterisation; Replogle RPE1 CRISPRi, 1,251 evaluable perturbations and 1,167 in the confound battery, 3,838,263 gene-pair observations; Adamson K562 CRISPRa, 77 perturbations; Tian iPSC neurons, 7; Shifrut primary T cells, 7. The K562 incremental-value table has 280 by 1,999 perturbation and gene observations, 559,720 pairs.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Perturbation-first validation, No incremental pairwise value, Cross-context and RPE1 sections; README.md: Perturbation Datasets

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Cross validation over perturbations, not a fixed train and test release. The main incremental-value test uses 5-fold GroupKFold grouped by perturbation, so a perturbation's pairs sit entirely in one fold. Harder protocols group by target gene, to stop a gene's own propensity leaking between folds, and combine both into a joint cross-gene by cross-perturbation split. A nested cross-validation protocol is used when choosing the best Geneformer layer out of 18. The primary evaluation layer, layer 13, was fixed in advance from a separate brain data set before any K562 perturbation data were examined.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Confound decomposition; Results, Perturbation-first validation and No incremental pairwise value

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per-perturbation AUROC for classifying differentially expressed genes, higher is better, is the primary measure. The conditional test reports the change in AUROC from adding an edge score to the gene-level model, with bootstrap confidence intervals, and the harder protocols also report AUPRC and top-k recall. Paired comparisons use Wilcoxon tests and Cohen's d.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Evaluation framework and No incremental pairwise value; Methods, Statistical framework

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three univariate gene-level features, expression variance, mean expression and dropout rate, plus Spearman correlation edges computed from the same control cells. On K562, the gene-level features reach 0.81 to 0.88 against about 0.70 for attention and correlation, with variance alone at 0.881, and the gene-level logistic model reaches 0.895. On RPE1 the figures are variance 0.866, mean expression 0.851, dropout 0.797, attention 0.747, correlation 0.658, with the gene-level model at 0.942.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Perturbation-first validation and Cross-cell-type generalisation

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Several, and they are the point of the design. Cross validation is grouped by perturbation, and in the harder protocols by target gene, so a gene's own susceptibility cannot leak across folds. Propensity matching pairs each differentially expressed target with five non-targets of similar mean, variance and dropout rate, which removes the gene-level advantage before the edge score is judged. Cross-fitted residualisation removes expression covariates from the edge scores. The primary layer was chosen on an independent data set before the perturbation data were seen. There is no control for the perturbation data having been in the foundation models' pretraining corpora.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Confound decomposition; Results, No incremental pairwise value

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Bootstrap confidence intervals with 200 iterations, resampled at the perturbation level unless stated otherwise, reported for the changes in AUROC. Paired p-values with Benjamini-Hochberg correction at 0.05 across a declared family of 95 confirmatory tests out of 153 in all. A power statement is given for the main null: 559,720 observations give more than 99 per cent power to detect a change in AUROC of 0.005.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Statistical framework; Results, No incremental pairwise value

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A perturbation and gene pair. One example is one candidate gene considered for one perturbed gene, labelled by whether that gene is differentially expressed after the perturbation. The per-perturbation metric then averages over perturbations, each of which contributes a ranking of all other genes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Perturbation-first validation and No incremental pairwise value

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human. The cells are human lines and primary human cells: K562, RPE1 retinal epithelial cells, induced pluripotent stem cell derived neurons and primary T cells, with human tissue atlases used for the other objective.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-context replication; README.md: Perturbation Datasets

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Pooled CRISPR screens read out by single-cell RNA sequencing: CRISPRi knockdown in K562, RPE1, neurons and T cells, and CRISPRa activation in K562. The labels are differential expression calls made from those screens with a Mann-Whitney test, Benjamini-Hochberg correction and a log fold change threshold.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Perturbation-first validation; README.md: Perturbation Datasets

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Control cell expression, and a model's internals. The attention scores are extracted from unperturbed cells by forward hooks on each self-attention module, averaged over heads and cells; the correlation scores come from the same control cells; the gene-level features are statistics of the same expression matrix. The perturbed cells are used only to make the labels.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Attention extraction and edge score computation, Perturbation-first validation

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot for the foundation models, with a small supervised classifier on top of the features. The published checkpoints are read as they are, Geneformer V2-316M and V1-10M and the scGPT whole-human checkpoint, with no fine-tuning; what is fitted is the logistic regression or gradient boosted model that combines gene-level features and edge scores under cross validation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Models and data, Confound decomposition

strengths.text: It makes the baseline do the work. Three features computable from the expression matrix alone, variance, mean and dropout rate, are run through the same pipeline, and they beat both edge types, which turns a vague claim about attention into a measurable comparison.

The null result is backed by a sensitivity check of the pipeline itself. On synthetic data with a planted network, and with expression z-scored so univariate variance carries no information about the truth, the same incremental-value test finds a change in AUROC of plus 0.518, and a shuffled control gives nearly zero.

The confounds are attacked from more than one side: grouped cross validation, harder cross-gene and joint splits, linear and nonlinear models, three metrics, residualisation of expression covariates and propensity matching, and the conclusion is the same each time.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, No incremental pairwise value; Methods, Confound decomposition

strengths.text: The choice that could most easily have been fitted to the result was fixed in advance: layer 13 was pre-specified from an independent brain data set before any K562 perturbation data were examined, and the 18-layer profile is reported as a planned secondary analysis.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Perturbation-first validation; Methods, Perturbation-first validation

limitations.text: Two of the five contexts are too small to say anything. The iPSC neuron and T cell sets have 7 perturbations each, and the paper reports only a trend and a null for them, so the cross-context claim rests on K562 and RPE1.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-context replication; Discussion, Cross-context pattern

limitations.text: The numbers depend on choices that change them, and the gene universes differ between data sets. K562 uses 2,000 highly variable genes and RPE1 3,309 with the perturbed genes forced in, and the paper shows that restricting RPE1 to 2,000 genes changes the attention advantage by plus 0.168, so scores are not comparable across these settings.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Perturbation-first validation; Results, Cross-context replication

limitations.text: The endpoint is not regulation. The author states that this task is dominated by which genes are easy to detect as differentially expressed, and that the same attention edges do recover curated regulatory targets on the other objective, so a poor score here is not evidence that a model has learned nothing about regulation.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Perturbation-first validation and Positive control; Discussion, Endpoint-object mismatch

limitations.text: It is one author's evaluation of two models, with restrictive terms on the code. Only scGPT and Geneformer were tested, with newer single-cell models left for future work, and the repository's licence section asks that anyone wanting to reuse it contacts the author, although the Zenodo archive of the same release records a CC BY 4.0 licence.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Discussion, Limitations; README.md: License; Zenodo record 18701417 metadata
