profile.summary: This is the cell type annotation evaluation published with scTab. A classifier is trained on a corpus built from the CELLxGENE census release 2023-05-15, 22.2 million human cells from 5,052 donors, 56 tissues and 164 cell type labels, and is scored on cells from donors it has never seen. The score is the macro-averaged F1, with a correction from the Cell Ontology so that predicting a finer label than the author annotated is not punished, while predicting a coarser one is. The paper reports this for linear, tree-based and deep models and for three single-cell transformer models, several of them refitted by the authors, and it publishes the processed data with fixed splits and tuned reference models so that others can reuse the same comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Dataset preparation and Ontology-corrected cell type classification

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a classifier can name the cell type of a single cell across the whole human body, not within one tissue, and whether it still does so for donors it has not seen. The authors frame the difficulty as a labelling problem: public corpora annotate at different levels of detail, so an evaluation that treats 164 ontology labels as mutually exclusive rewards a model for copying each study's annotation granularity rather than for telling cell types apart. Their fix is to judge a prediction against the Cell Ontology, which turns the task into predicting a label at least as specific as the author's. A second question the evaluation covers is whether a model knows when it is wrong: uncertainty scores from a deep ensemble are tested for separating correct predictions from incorrect ones, and from cells whose type was never in training.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Ontology-corrected cell type classification and Uncertainty quantification

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The corpus starts from the CELLxGENE census release 2023-05-15, restricted to human data on the 19,331 human protein-coding genes. Five filters follow: only primary data, so that the same cell in an atlas metastudy cannot appear on both sides of the split; only 10x-based assays; the label must be a subtype of the native cell term; each cell type needs at least 5,000 cells and at least 30 donors; and each cell type needs at least seven parent nodes in the ontology, a heuristic to drop very broad labels, which the authors note does not remove all coarse labels. Counts are normalised to 10,000 per cell and log transformed. The result is 22,189,056 cells, 164 cell types, 5,052 donors and 56 tissues, split by donor 70, 15 and 15 per cent into 15,240,192 training, 3,500,032 validation and 3,448,832 test cells. Subsampled training sets are also defined for the scaling experiments, both random and donor-based, from 15 to 100 per cent. The processed corpus is published as a 164 GB download in Merlin dataloader format, with a 0.5 GB minimal subset and the trained checkpoints.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation and Subsampled datasets; Results; README.md: Model checkpoints and training data

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model outputs one label per cell from the 164, and the score is the macro average of the per-class F1 on the held-out donors, so every cell type counts equally regardless of how many cells it has. The ontology correction decides right from wrong: the same label as the author is right, a subtype of the author's label is also right, a parent of the author's label is wrong, and anything else is wrong, with child relations looked up in the Cell Ontology. The paper reports each model as a mean and standard deviation over several fits with different random initialisations, and the supplementary information gives a second version of the same table with bootstrapping across test donors added, which widens the intervals by about an order of magnitude, for example scTab 0.8295 plus or minus 0.0007 over seeds against 0.8300 plus or minus 0.0069 with donor bootstrapping. A separate evaluation aggregates the fine-grained predictions to 31 coarse labels without retraining. Uncertainty is scored by averaging the predicted probabilities of 5 independently trained models, taking one minus the maximum probability as the uncertainty, then measuring the ROC-AUC for separating correct predictions from incorrect ones and from cells of types absent from training, where 1.0 is perfect separation and 0.5 is none. Training and inference cost are reported too, on named hardware.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Ontology-corrected cell type classification, Performance evaluation on coarse cell type labels, Uncertainty quantification; Supplementary Tables 1 and 2

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download the processed corpus, or the 0.5 GB minimal subset for a first try, and the checkpoints. Install the cellnet package from the repository, either inside the Merlin PyTorch container the authors used or with pip plus the GPU requirements file. The repository holds the data loading code, training scripts, and notebooks for training, for creating the data store and for all the evaluation in the paper, with tutorial notebooks for loading data and for running a trained model. A modern GPU is needed; the authors state that on a desktop without GPU acceleration the runtime will probably exceed several days.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model checkpoints and training data, Project structure, Installation, Hardware requirements

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One corpus, built from the CELLxGENE census release 2023-05-15: 22,189,056 human cells, 164 cell types, 5,052 donors, 56 tissues and 249 datasets, on 19,331 protein-coding genes. The test set is 3,448,832 cells, the validation set 3,500,032 and the training set 15,240,192. Subsampled training sets at 15, 30, 50, 70 and 100 per cent, by cells and by donors, are defined for the scaling experiments.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation and Subsampled datasets; Figure 1 caption

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: By donor, fixed and published. 70 per cent of donors go to training and 15 per cent each to validation and test, so a donor appears in exactly one split. The authors chose this over a random cell split, which leaks similar cells, and over a study-based split, which leaves cell types missing from one side. Because every cell type is present in at least 30 donors, each type has 4 to 5 donors in the validation and test sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation; Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Macro-averaged F1 over the 164 cell types, higher is better, computed after the ontology correction. For the uncertainty evaluation, the ROC-AUC for separating the uncertainty scores of two groups of cells, higher is better, with 0.5 meaning no separation. The coarse-label evaluation uses the same macro F1 over 31 aggregated labels.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Ontology-corrected cell type classification, Uncertainty quantification, Performance evaluation on coarse cell type labels

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Nine reported models, all refitted or run by the authors on this corpus. Macro F1 over seeded fits: scTab 0.8295 plus or minus 0.0007, XGBoost 0.8127 plus or minus 0.0005, MLP 0.7971 plus or minus 0.0012, an optimised linear model 0.7848 plus or minus 0.0001, CellTypist retrained on a 1.5 million cell subsample 0.7304 plus or minus 0.0015, scGPT zero-shot 0.7301 plus or minus 0.0035, UCE zero-shot 0.7611 plus or minus 0.0018, scGPT fine-tuned 0.749 from a single run, and CIForm on a 750,000 cell subsample 0.766 from a single run. Tuning matters: with default hyper-parameters XGBoost scores 0.5855 plus or minus 0.0112 and CellTypist 0.6258 plus or minus 0.0036.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-tissue cell type classification requires nonlinear models and Robust benchmarks section; Supplementary Tables 1 and 6

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Three. Only primary data are used, so a cell duplicated into an atlas metastudy cannot appear in both training and test. The split is by donor, not by cell, so no cell from a test donor is seen in training. The ontology correction stops a model from being rewarded for mimicking one study's annotation granularity. The authors give no sequence or expression similarity cut-off beyond this, and note their broad-label filter is only a heuristic, leaving some coarse labels in the corpus.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Dataset preparation

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Repeated fits with different random initialisations, 4 or 5 runs per model, reported as mean and standard deviation, and a second version of the table that also bootstraps across test donors, which gives much wider intervals, for example scTab 0.8300 plus or minus 0.0069 against 0.8295 plus or minus 0.0007 over seeds alone. The two single-run entries, fine-tuned scGPT and CIForm, carry no interval. Model uncertainty itself is estimated with a deep ensemble of 5 networks.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Uncertainty quantification and Statistics and reproducibility; Supplementary Table 1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A single cell. One example is one cell's expression vector over 19,331 protein-coding genes, labelled with the author-provided Cell Ontology term, and the prediction is one of the 164 labels.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation; Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human only. The corpus is the human part of the CELLxGENE census, across 56 tissues.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Single-cell RNA sequencing, restricted to the 10x Genomics family of assays, which the authors list as 10x 5 prime v2 and v1, 10x 3 prime v3, v2 and v1, and the two 10x transcription profiling terms. The labels are the cell type annotations supplied by the original authors and mapped to Cell Ontology terms by the CELLxGENE schema.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation; Results

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The expression vector alone. Models take the normalised, log transformed counts over the 19,331 protein-coding genes; no tissue, donor or assay metadata is described as an input. The published corpus is distributed in the Merlin dataloader format for exactly this input.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation and Data loading infrastructure; README.md: Model checkpoints and training data

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: All three settings appear. Most models are trained from scratch on the training split, including scTab, XGBoost, the MLP and the optimised linear model. CellTypist and CIForm were retrained on subsamples because of memory limits. The transformer models were used both zero-shot, by fitting a logistic regression on frozen embeddings, and fine-tuned, in the case of scGPT on 150,000 cells.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-tissue cell type classification requires nonlinear models; Methods, Model details; Supplementary Table 1

strengths.text: The split is by donor and the data are deduplicated to primary records, which removes the two easiest ways to flatter a cell type classifier.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Dataset preparation

strengths.text: The metric handles the annotation granularity problem explicitly. A finer prediction than the author's label counts as correct and a coarser one as wrong, with the relations taken from the Cell Ontology, so the score is less a test of copying one study's labelling habits.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Ontology-corrected cell type classification

strengths.text: It is published as a reusable benchmark, not only as a result: the processed corpus with fixed splits, a small subset, the trained checkpoints and the data loading code are all downloadable, and the paper argues that tuned reference models matter by showing XGBoost rising from 0.5855 to 0.8127 with tuning.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Robust benchmarks section; README.md: Model checkpoints and training data

strengths.text: The supplementary information reports the same comparison twice, over seeds alone and with bootstrapping across test donors, which shows how much of the apparent precision comes from fixing the test donors.
strengths.source_locator: Supplementary Table 1, parts a and b

limitations.text: The label set is a filtered slice of the ontology, chosen by thresholds the authors describe as data dependent: at least 5,000 cells and 30 donors per type, and at least seven parent nodes. Rare cell types are therefore absent by construction, and the authors say coarse labels remain despite the heuristic.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Dataset preparation

limitations.text: Every comparison number was produced by the scTab authors, and several competitors were handicapped by memory limits: CellTypist was retrained on 1.5 million cells, CIForm on 750,000, and the fine-tuned scGPT on 150,000, with those two reported from a single run and no interval.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-tissue cell type classification requires nonlinear models; Supplementary Table 1

limitations.text: Scores depend on how fine the labels are, so they are not comparable across label sets. The same scTab predictions give 0.897 on 31 coarse labels against 0.830 on the fine-grained ones, and the authors tie the model's advantage to parts of the ontology, mainly immune cells, that happen to be finely resolved.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-tissue cell type classification requires nonlinear models

limitations.text: Reproducing it is expensive and tied to specific infrastructure. The processed corpus is a 164 GB download, the repository states a modern GPU is required and that a desktop run would probably exceed several days, and training times in the supplementary table run from about 10 to 33 hours on A100 class hardware.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Model checkpoints and training data, Hardware requirements; Supplementary Table 2

profile.summary: This is the cell type annotation comparison reported with scFoundation, not a standalone benchmark. Two published single-cell data sets are used, Zheng68K, a peripheral blood mononuclear cell set, and Segerstolpe, a pancreatic set, and seven methods are scored by macro-averaged F1 for assigning a cell type label to each cell. The saved sources print one number per method and data set: scFoundation 0.736 and 0.914, CellTypist 0.725 and 0.812, SingleCellNet 0.598 and 0.806, ACTINN 0.649 and 0.722, scBERT 0.670 and 0.670, Scanpy 0.547 and 0.540, scANVI 0.395 and 0.521. It is useful as a reference point for annotation methods on two well-known data sets, but the splits and the fitting details are not in the files that are open.
profile.summary_source_locator: Supplementary Table 4 and the macro F1 definition in the supplementary notes; README.md: Cell type annotation

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a method can put the right cell type label on each cell of a published data set. Two data sets are used, Zheng68K from blood and Segerstolpe from pancreas, and the comparison puts a foundation model's embedding against dedicated annotation tools and against plain pipelines. Because the score is a macro average over cell types, a method is judged on the rare types as much as the common ones: the per-cell-type table for Zheng68K shows where that bites, with CellTypist scoring an F1 of 0 on CD4-positive T helper 2 cells and scFoundation 0.17, against 0.85 and 0.86 on CD14-positive monocytes.
sections.source_locator: Supplementary Tables 4 and 5; README.md: Cell type annotation

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The two data sets are taken as published, Zheng68K of blood cells and Segerstolpe of pancreatic cells, and the repository describes the task as cell type annotation on pancreatic and blood data. The repository ships the precomputed scFoundation embeddings for this task as a zip file and points to Figshare for the raw gene expression data, saying the embeddings can also be regenerated through the model's API or local code. How the cells were divided into training and test parts, how many cells were used, and which labels were kept are not stated in any of the saved files: the main text of the paper is behind a paywall and was not read. Supplementary Table 5 lists per-cell-type results for 11 Zheng68K cell types, counting its rows, which is the only label list in the saved files.
sections.source_locator: Supplementary Table 5; README.md: data table; annotation/README.md

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The reported metric is the macro F1 score, defined in the supplementary notes as the average of the per-cell-type F1 scores, where each type's F1 is computed from its true positives, false positives and false negatives. Higher is better. Supplementary Table 4 gives one number per method and data set, with no interval, no seed count and no statistical test. A second table reports the same Zheng68K annotation task for three model sizes, 0.705 for the 3M model, 0.714 for the 10M and 0.736 for the 100M, and states that the experimental setting is the same as the cell type annotation downstream task. Supplementary Table 5 breaks Zheng68K down by cell type with precision, recall and F1 for CellTypist and scFoundation.
sections.source_locator: Supplementary notes, Macro F1 score; Supplementary Tables 2, 4 and 5

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository has a folder for this task. Clone it, unzip the bundled annotation data into a data folder, and open the plotting notebook, which the folder README says holds the results. The raw expression data are on Figshare and the embeddings can be regenerated from the model, through its API or the local model code in the repository. The saved files give no training command, no split file and no scoring script for this task.

profile.summary: DUD-E is a virtual screening benchmark: for each of 102 protein targets it supplies a set of known active compounds and, for every active, 50 decoy molecules chosen to match it on physico-chemical properties while being topologically dissimilar. A docking program or scoring model ranks the pooled library for a target, and the benchmark measures how far the actives rise above the decoys, reported as an adjusted logarithmic area under the ROC curve and an enrichment factor at 1 per cent. The actives come from ChEMBL09, or the literature for AmpC beta-lactamase, with affinities of 1 micromolar or better, molecular weight under 600 and fewer than 20 rotatable bonds, clustered to 22,886 ligands, and the decoys from ZINC. It is used to compare docking programs and scoring functions, and a later study shows that machine learning models trained on it can score well without learning anything about binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Characteristics of DUD-E, Methods (Automated Decoy Generation, Docking Metrics); DUD-E home page

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Ligand enrichment: whether a method puts known binders near the top of a library that is otherwise full of molecules that look like them but are not known to bind. The decoys are the point. They are matched to each active on six physico-chemical properties, so a method cannot win by preferring heavy or greasy molecules, and they are topologically dissimilar to the actives, so the task is not fingerprint matching. The target list was chosen for diversity, adding classes such as G protein coupled receptors and ion channels that the original DUD lacked. What the benchmark does not measure, as the authors of a later study showed, is whether a model has learned protein-ligand interaction physics.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results; Chen et al. 2019: Introduction and Discussion; DUD-E home page

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Actives come from ChEMBL09: compounds assigned to a protein target with a confidence score of at least 4 and an affinity of 1 micromolar or better. Raw ligands also had to have a molecular weight under 600 and fewer than 20 rotatable bonds, which gives 66,695 raw ligands. For AmpC beta-lactamase the ChEMBL09 ligands are covalent, so its ligands were compiled by hand from the literature instead. Molecules with no measurable affinity at 30 micromolar or worse are kept as experimental decoys, and the in-between cases are kept separately as marginal. Each target's ligands are clustered to leave 22,886 clustered ligands for chemotype diversity. Targets are defined by UniProt gene prefix with species pooled, and each target gets one X-ray structure, chosen by an automated docking campaign over thousands of PDB entries with preference for resolution, enrichment and the human orthologue, with manual intervention where the automated preparation failed. Decoys are drawn from ZINC: for each unique set of six properties of a protonated ligand, molecular weight, estimated log P, rotatable bonds, hydrogen bond acceptors and donors and net charge, a pool of a few thousand candidates is gathered by widening or narrowing property windows in seven steps, ECFP4 fingerprints are computed, the pool is sorted by maximum Tanimoto similarity to any ligand, the most dissimilar quarter is kept, duplicates are spread evenly over the ligands, and 50 decoys are picked at random. That gives 1,411,214 computational decoys in all.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Characteristics of DUD-E; Methods (ChEMBL and RCSB PDB Data Extraction, Target Selection Docking, Target Preparation, Ligand Clustering, Automated Decoy Generation)

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method ranks the library for one target, actives and decoys together, and the ranking is scored. The paper's primary measure is the adjusted LogAUC at 0.001, which is the area under the ROC curve on a semi-logarithmic x-axis spanning three decades, with the random curve's 14.462 per cent subtracted so that random performance is 0 per cent and higher is better. The ROC-based enrichment factor at 1 per cent is also reported: the percentage of ligands found by the point where 1 per cent of the decoys have been found, which the authors prefer to a traditional enrichment factor. Plain ROC AUC is noted as a common alternative. The authors' own numbers come from docking with DOCK 3.6 using solvent-excluded volume ligand desolvation, with conformations from Omega, and they report per-target LogAUC and enrichment factor values in their target table. Scores are per target; the benchmark defines no single aggregate.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Docking Metrics, Docking Calculations); Table 2

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The data are downloaded from the benchmark's own site, either target by target, by subset such as the G protein coupled receptor or kinase groups, or as one package, and the site says the files can also be browsed directly under its db directory without JavaScript. Each target ships the chosen receptor structure and the active and decoy sets, in mol2 and SDF formats. There is no scoring server: a user docks or scores the molecules with their own program and computes the enrichment metrics themselves. The site also runs a decoy generation service, so the same protocol can be applied to a user's own ligand list for a target that is not in the set.
sections.source_locator: DUD-E home page; Paper: Online Tools for Automated Generation of Further Ligand and Decoy Sets

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One set, split by target: 102 proteins, 22,886 clustered ligands from ChEMBL09 and, for AmpC beta-lactamase, the literature, out of 66,695 raw ligands, an average of 224 ligands per target on the project page, 50 property-matched decoys per active, and 1,411,214 computational decoys in all. Experimental decoys, molecules measured as inactive, number 9,219. Each target also has one chosen X-ray structure.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Characteristics of DUD-E table; DUD-E home page

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None. DUD-E is a test set, not a train and test division: each target is an independent screening problem with its own actives and decoys, and the authors say targets are independent of one another so that they can be added, deleted or replaced. Methods that train on DUD-E, as machine learning work does, have to invent their own split, and Chen et al. show that the usual choice, separating targets by sequence similarity, rests on an untested assumption about their actives.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Online Tools section; Chen et al. 2019: Methods and Discussion

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Adjusted LogAUC at 0.001, higher is better: the ROC area in semi-logarithmic space over three decades, with the random curve's 14.462 per cent subtracted so random is 0. Alongside it the ROC-based enrichment factor at 1 per cent, higher is better, the percentage of ligands recovered when 1 per cent of the decoys have been recovered. Plain ROC AUC is named as a common metric and is what later machine learning work reports.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Docking Metrics; Chen et al. 2019: Introduction

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The authors' own docking runs with DOCK 3.6 and solvent-excluded volume ligand desolvation, reported per target as LogAUC and enrichment factor at 1 per cent, and a comparison against the original DUD on the 37 directly comparable targets. A random background calculation is also described, seeding the DUD-E ligands into a ChEMBL subset of ZINC of 273,375 ligands.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Docking Calculations, Original DUD Comparison); Table 2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Within a target, two. Ligands are clustered by Bemis-Murcko frameworks so that near-identical analogues do not dominate, and decoys are filtered to be topologically dissimilar to the actives, keeping only the most dissimilar quarter of the candidate pool by ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity. There is no control across targets, and no control for a model trained on DUD-E: Chen et al. report that models can separate actives from decoys from the ligand alone, with no receptor, which they attribute to analogue bias among each target's actives and to the way the decoys were chosen.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Ligand Clustering, Automated Decoy Generation); Chen et al. 2019: Results and Discussion

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No replicates or intervals are defined by the benchmark: a target's score is a single ranking of a fixed library. The authors do provide a way to probe one source of variance, since the final decoy pick is random where possible, so several decoy sets can be generated for the same ligands to test whether a method is overfitted to the canonical decoys.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Online Tools for Automated Generation of Further Ligand and Decoy Sets; Methods, Docking Metrics

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A molecule paired with a target: one example is a compound in a target's library, labelled active or decoy, to be scored against that target's single chosen receptor structure. Decoys belong to a specific active, one decoy to one ligand, so filtering a ligand removes its decoys.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Online Tools section, Methods; DUD-E home page

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Mixed and pooled. Targets are defined by UniProt gene prefix with the data from each species combined into one set, and the structure choice gave preference to the human orthologue, so a target can carry ligands measured against several species' proteins. The saved files give no species breakdown.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Methods (Target Preparation)

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Binding and activity measurements from the literature, as collected by ChEMBL: half maximal inhibitory and effective concentrations, inhibition and dissociation constants and their logarithmic variants. An active needs 1 micromolar or better; an experimental decoy needs no measurable affinity at 30 micromolar or worse. The receptor structures are X-ray crystal structures from the PDB.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, ChEMBL and RCSB PDB Data Extraction

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The target's receptor structure and the molecules. Each target ships one prepared X-ray structure and its ligand and decoy sets in mol2 and SDF form, so a method may use the protein structure, the ligand structures, or only the ligands. Chen et al. exploit exactly that freedom, training a ligand-only model as a control.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods; DUD-E home page; Chen et al. 2019: Methods

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: As published, none: DUD-E was built for docking programs, which are not trained on it, and the paper describes using it to test method variants such as a new desolvation model. Later work does train on it, and Chen et al. describe building training and test subsets of DUD-E for convolutional networks, which is the use their study criticises.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Applications to Docking Optimization and Testing; Chen et al. 2019: Introduction and Methods

strengths.text: The decoys are hard by construction. They match each active on six properties including net charge, and only the quarter least similar to the actives by ECFP4 fingerprint is kept, so neither property bias nor fingerprint similarity gives an easy win.

The target list is broader than the benchmark it replaced, adding classes such as G protein coupled receptors and ion channels, and each target's receptor structure was chosen through a systematic docking campaign rather than by hand alone.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Target Selection Docking and Target Preparation

strengths.text: It is extensible rather than frozen. The decoy generation protocol is offered as a service for a user's own ligand list, the raw unclustered sets are published so a different clustering can be used, and the random final pick lets several decoy sets be made for the same ligands to test overfitting.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Online Tools for Automated Generation of Further Ligand and Decoy Sets; DUD-E home page

strengths.text: The metric is designed for screening rather than for overall ranking: the adjusted LogAUC weights the top of the list and is shifted so that random performance reads as zero.

limitations.text: Scores from models trained on DUD-E can be meaningless. Chen et al. report that convolutional network models reach high area under the curve without using the receptor at all, and attribute this to analogue bias among each target's actives and to how the decoys were selected, so performance on DUD-E is not evidence that such a model has learned protein-ligand binding.
limitations.source_locator: Chen et al. 2019: Introduction, Results, Conclusions

limitations.text: The decoys are presumed inactive, not measured inactive. Only 9,219 experimental decoys exist against 1,411,214 computational ones drawn from ZINC, so almost every negative label is an assumption.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Characteristics of DUD-E table; Methods, Automated Decoy Generation

limitations.text: Each target is one receptor structure and one pooled set of species, chosen in part because it already enriched known ligands under automated docking. That selection, which the authors describe, favours targets and structures that docking handles well.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Target Selection Docking and Target Preparation

limitations.text: There is no leaderboard, no submission route and no stated data licence: the project page says only that the set is free to use and provided by the laboratories at UCSF, and it points to a newer version, DUDE-Z, at another address.
limitations.source_locator: DUD-E home page

profile.summary: MF-PCBA is a set of 60 drug screening data sets assembled from PubChem BioAssay, each pairing two measurement qualities for the same project: a large, noisy primary screen at a single concentration, and the much smaller dose-response confirmation of the compounds that came through it. The prediction task is regression on the dose-response values, and the point of the benchmark is whether a model can use the hundreds of thousands of primary measurements to predict the few thousand confirmatory ones better than it could from the confirmatory data alone. The collection holds over 16.6 million unique compound and target interactions and over 1.1 million unique compounds, with five fixed random splits per data set. It is for people building molecular property prediction methods, particularly transfer learning between cheap and expensive measurements.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Methods (MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations); README.md: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether low-quality data helps. In a real screening campaign a library is tested once at a single dose, then the hits are retested over a dose range to get a reliable potency. Machine learning work usually models only the second, small set and throws the first away. MF-PCBA keeps both and asks for predictions of the dose-response values, so a method is judged on whether it can turn hundreds of thousands of noisy single-dose measurements into better predictions of a few thousand reliable ones. The authors describe the training sets for the confirmatory-only task as typically fewer than 2000 instances, against primary screens orders of magnitude larger. They also point out that the relationship between the two is not simply strong: the per-data-set correlation between paired single-dose and dose-response values is printed for every one of the 60 sets, and it includes weak and negative values.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Methods (MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification, Evaluation Strategies), Table 1; README.md: Abstract

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The 60 projects were found by hand, searching PubChem BioAssay for primary and confirmatory screening terms, because the two halves of a campaign may sit in one assay or in two and the formats differ. The assays date from 2008 to 2018. Everything after the selection is automated through PubChem's REST interface: the assay rows are downloaded by identifier, SMILES strings are fetched per compound, replicate primary measurements are averaged by mean, with a median option in the code, and dose-response values reported as half maximal concentrations or their logarithms are converted to pXC50. Four RDKit filtering steps follow: sanitisation, keeping the largest fragment to drop counterions, removing stereochemistry and then deduplicating on SMILES, which makes the task modelling racemic mixtures, and neutralising charges. The paper reports how many compounds each step removed on average. Each finished data set holds the compound identifier, the SMILES string and the single-dose and dose-response activity values, with PubChem's binary activity labels included, and five random 80, 10, 10 splits of the dose-response data are provided with their seeds published.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Data Acquisition, Filtering Steps, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification), Results (Effects of Filtering); README.md: General, Random seeds

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: One model per data set: the authors say they consider only single-task learning, so a separate model is trained for each of the 60 sets. The recommended comparison is between a dose-response-only model, trained on confirmatory data alone, and a model that also uses the primary data, so that any gain can be attributed to the extra modality. The paper's own evaluation uses two ways of adding the primary information: appending the measured single-dose value to the compound's feature vector, and training a graph neural network on all the primary data and appending the embedding it produces, which also works for molecules it never saw. For the dose-response regression the authors recommend the coefficient of determination together with an error metric, mean absolute error or root mean square error; for the classification form of the task, the Matthews correlation coefficient together with the area under the ROC curve. Their reported numbers come from random forests, support vector machines and graph neural networks for the confirmatory step, with graph networks for the primary step, over the five provided splits.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Assay Overlap and Size Considerations, Evaluation Strategies and Multifidelity Modeling)

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The data are not distributed as a file: the repository downloads and rebuilds them from PubChem. Install Python 3.9 or later with pandas, numpy, rdkit, tqdm and scipy, then call the retrieval script with the primary assay identifier, the names of the columns holding the single-dose and dose-response values, the transformation to apply to the dose-response values, the confirmatory assay identifier when it is a separate assay, and an output directory. Ready-made scripts for all 60 data sets are in the retrieve-scripts directory, and the authors note they can be run in parallel. A notebook then splits the dose-response data into train, validation and test sets five times using the published seeds, writing one numbered directory per split. The paper reports that rebuilding one data set of 335,445 primary molecules took 554.52 seconds on the machine described.
sections.source_locator: README.md: General, Provided scripts, Random seeds, Requirements, Example workflow; Paper: Data Availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 60 multifidelity data sets, each a primary single-dose screen paired with its dose-response confirmation, drawn from PubChem BioAssay with assay dates from 2008 to 2018. In total over 16.6 million unique compound and target interactions and over 1.1 million unique compounds. Table 1 of the paper lists every data set with its assay identifiers, assay type, measurement types, unfiltered sizes and the correlation between the paired measurements; primary screen sizes there run to the hundreds of thousands and confirmatory sets to the hundreds or low thousands. The collection is also split into MF-PCBA-23, the previously analysed subset, and the disjoint MF-PCBA-37.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1, Methods (Data Acquisition, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations), Results

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Five random splits per data set, 80 per cent train, 10 per cent validation and 10 per cent test, drawn over the dose-response data only. The seeds are published in the repository as a JSON file with a notebook that applies them, so the same five splits can be reproduced. The primary single-dose data are not split: they are available in full as the low-fidelity source.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; README.md: Random seeds, Example workflow

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: For the regression task, the authors recommend the coefficient of determination together with mean absolute error or root mean square error. For the classification form, using PubChem's binary activity labels, the Matthews correlation coefficient together with the area under the ROC curve. Higher is better for the coefficient of determination, the Matthews coefficient and the area under the curve; lower is better for the error metrics. The benchmark defines no single aggregate score across the 60 data sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation Strategies and Multifidelity Modeling

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The paper's own evaluation: random forests, support vector machines and graph neural networks for the dose-response step, each run as a confirmatory-only model and as a multifidelity model, with a graph neural network trained on the primary data to produce the embeddings for the second augmentation. The authors report this for all 60 data sets, focusing their analysis on the 37 that were new in this work.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation Strategies and Multifidelity Modeling; Results

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Deduplication and an overlap check, but no structural split. Stereochemistry is removed and molecules are deduplicated on SMILES within a data set, so the same structure cannot appear twice. The splits are random over compounds, not by scaffold or by cluster, so analogues can fall on both sides. The authors do check overlap with other collections: no assay in common with the 128 assays of PCBA, 27 confirmatory assays in common with the 1310 assays of an earlier ChEMBL-derived set, and no overlap in primary assays. Overlap between the 60 data sets themselves is limited, with over 75.6 per cent of values missing if all compounds are matched against all primary screens.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Filtering Steps, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations)

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Five splits per data set, whose seeds are published, so a result is reported over five runs rather than one. The paper reports its filtering effects as means with standard deviations, and Table 1 gives a p value alongside each data set's correlation between the paired measurements. The benchmark does not ask for multiple model seeds beyond the five splits.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; Results, Effects of Filtering on Dataset Size; Table 1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A molecule in one screening project. Each row is a compound, identified by its PubChem compound identifier and a SMILES string, carrying a single-dose activity value, a dose-response value, or both, for that project's target. Stereochemistry is stripped, so a row stands for a racemic mixture.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; Filtering Steps

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Mostly inapplicable: the examples are small molecules and the labels are activity against a target or in a cell or organism assay, not sequences from a species. The paper says the assays span biochemical inhibition through to phenotypic experiments on whole organisms, and Table 1 marks each data set's assay type, but no saved file gives a species list.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data Acquisition and Table 1

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: High-throughput screening data from PubChem of two kinds. Primary screens are single-concentration measurements, reported as percent inhibition, percent activity or a B-score at a stated concentration, sometimes with replicates, which are averaged. Confirmatory screens are dose-response measurements reported as half maximal inhibitory, activity or effective concentrations, or their logarithms, all converted to pXC50. Assay types in Table 1 include biochemical, cell-based and whole-organism readouts.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data Acquisition; Table 1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The molecular structure, plus the primary screening data as the extra modality. The authors say any algorithm that works on fixed-dimension vectors applies, naming fingerprints, physical and chemical descriptors and atom and bond encodings, and the multifidelity augmentations add either the measured single-dose value or an embedding learned from the primary screen. No protein structure or sequence is provided.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; Evaluation Strategies

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training from scratch, one model per data set. The authors state they consider only single-task learning, with a separate model for each data set, and the multifidelity setting adds a transfer step: a model trained on the primary screen supplies embeddings to the confirmatory model. There is no zero-shot or pretrained-and-frozen setting defined by the benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations; Evaluation Strategies

strengths.text: It keeps the part of screening data that other collections discard. Each data set pairs the full primary screen with its dose-response confirmation, which is what a real campaign produces, and the authors state no earlier collection explicitly considered screening data of different fidelities.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations; README.md: Abstract

strengths.text: The splits are fixed and published. Five random 80, 10, 10 splits per data set with their seeds in the repository, and a notebook that writes them out, so two groups can score on the same test sets.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; README.md: Random seeds

strengths.text: The curation is reproducible and documented step by step: the filtering is four named RDKit operations, the paper reports how many compounds each removed, and the MIT licensed code rebuilds every data set from PubChem rather than shipping a snapshot.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Filtering Steps; Results, Effects of Filtering; README.md: Provided scripts; LICENSE

strengths.text: The authors state a recommended comparison, confirmatory-only against multifidelity models, and recommended metrics for both the regression and the classification form, which makes two papers' numbers more likely to mean the same thing.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation Strategies and Multifidelity Modeling

limitations.text: The test sets are small and the splits are random over compounds, not structural. Confirmatory training sets are typically fewer than 2000 molecules, a 10 per cent test split is therefore in the hundreds, and nothing stops close analogues from sitting on both sides of a split.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation Strategies; MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification

limitations.text: Chemical information was deliberately thrown away for consistency: stereochemistry is removed and molecules are then merged on their flat structure, so the labels describe racemic mixtures and a method cannot be credited for handling stereochemistry.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Filtering Steps

limitations.text: The selection was manual and the sources are heterogeneous. The authors had to search PubChem by hand because formats and conventions differ, primary screens come at different concentrations and with different readouts, and units for confirmatory values are not always consistent, so comparability across the 60 data sets is limited.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data Acquisition

limitations.text: There is no leaderboard and no distributed data file. Every user rebuilds the data from PubChem with the scripts, which takes minutes per data set and depends on PubChem's current contents, and the benchmark defines no aggregate score over the 60 sets.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Data Availability; README.md: Provided scripts

profile.summary: CycPepNet compares molecular representations and machine learning models on cyclic peptides for three properties: binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life. Each property is posed twice, as regression on the measured value and as classification against a stated threshold, giving 20 tasks. The framework covers those 20 tasks, 45 model configurations, two split methods and five seeds, and its analyses draw on a main pool of 22 configurations. The data come from six published cyclic peptide sources, which the framework does not redistribute: it ships an inventory with each input file's hash, a curator per source, the released split indices and the full archive of run records, so the published tables and figures can be reproduced without retraining. Its own result table shows the point: test root mean square errors on the small binding sets sit close to the mean baseline, while the larger permeability sets are predictable.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: top, Framework definition, Input data, Results and figures; results/learnability.csv

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How far machine learning can get on cyclic peptides, a class where the data are scarce and scattered. Three properties are covered: binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life. Each is set up as a regression on the measured value and as a classification against a fixed cut, an inhibition constant or half maximal concentration at or below 100 nanomolar for binding, a log permeability at or above minus 6, and a half-life of 8 hours or more. Because the model and representation matrix is held fixed across tasks, the comparison is as much about which molecular representation helps as about which model wins, and the framework's own result table compares each selected model against a mean baseline on the same test split.
sections.source_locator: README.md: top, Framework definition; results/learnability.csv

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Six published sources supply the measurements: CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD for permeability, Macrocycle-DB for binding affinity, and PEPlife2, PepMSND and PepTherDia for half-life. Nine exact provider files make up the snapshot and none of them is redistributed; an inventory records each one's size, hash, acquisition address and identity check, and most carry the status that redistribution terms are not established. Each source has its own curator script, and the permeability and half-life combinations are separate curation steps. One function, load_task_table, applies everything that defines a task: the filters, for example a single target and activity type within Macrocycle-DB, dropping missing values, deduplicating on SMILES by averaging replicate measurements and discarding any molecule whose replicates have a coefficient of variation above 1, the base-10 log transform of the target, and the classification threshold. The released splits are generated with an 80, 10, 10 ratio and a fixed seed, in two flavours: a Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints with a cutoff of 0.45, and a random split. The split size table shows how small the sets are: 28 test molecules for the binding task on one target, 19 for the combined half-life task, against 695 for CycPeptMPDB permeability.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Input data, Framework definition; cycpepnet/benchmark.py: load_task_table and generate_all_splits; results/splits_summary.csv; data/sources.csv

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model is trained on the train split, its hyper-parameters are chosen on the validation split, with Optuna over 50 trials for every non-baseline configuration, and it is scored on the test split. Selection is on the primary validation metric and reporting is on test, and the README states that nothing is reselected on a companion metric. The primary metric is the root mean square error for the regression tasks and balanced accuracy for the classification tasks, with Q squared F3 and the area under the ROC curve as companions and the coefficient of determination kept as descriptive. Each result is the mean over five seeds, with a seed standard deviation, a seed confidence interval and a separate test-set confidence interval, and the mean baseline's value on the same split. Root mean square error is never pooled across tasks because it carries each task's units; cross-task summaries use ranks, per-task min-max scores or dimensionless metrics, and the released tables include Friedman and Nemenyi ranks and adjusted p values for the confirmatory comparisons.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Framework definition, Results and figures, Getting started; results/learnability.csv

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Two routes. To check and reproduce the published analysis, install the package on Python 3.12 and run three commands: a verification pass that hashes the released artefacts and validates all 40 splits against the task tables they index, a reproduction pass that runs the analysis stages in order and stops at the first failure, and a comparison pass that checks the regenerated tables against the release to a tolerance of 1e-8. The README says these three need neither of the full environments and write 85 CSV and TeX outputs and 17 figures into a separate directory. To train models, install the locked Pixi environment, which is the one the published results came from, generate the fingerprint cache from the released tables, then call the runner with a task, a model, seeds and a split method. To rebuild the data from scratch, the provider files must be acquired first and verified by hash.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Reproduce the results, Getting started, Train models or rebuild datasets, Input data

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Six published sources behind nine provider files: CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD for permeability, Macrocycle-DB for binding affinity, PEPlife2, PepMSND and PepTherDia for half-life. Ten distinct curated data splits, each used for a regression and a classification task, giving 20 tasks. Test set sizes from the released split table: 28 for Macrocycle-DB OPRM1, 49 for MC4R, 32 for SSTR2, 695 for CycPeptMPDB, 109 for NPMMPD, 288 for the CycPeptMPDB Townsend subset, 92 for the NPMMPD Rzepiela subset, 798 for the combined CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD set, and 19 for the combined half-life set.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Input data, Framework definition; results/splits_summary.csv

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two released split methods per task, both 80, 10, 10 train, validation and test with seed 42: a Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints at a Tanimoto cutoff of 0.45, and a random split. The split indices are released and refer to the task-filtered, deduplicated table, so substituting an input invalidates them. Forty splits in all are validated by the verification command.
facts.source_locator: cycpepnet/benchmark.py: generate_all_splits and generate_random_splits; README.md: Input data, Reproduce the results; results/splits_summary.csv

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Root mean square error, lower is better, as the primary metric for the regression tasks, with Q squared F3 as its companion, higher is better, and the coefficient of determination as a descriptive extra. Balanced accuracy, higher is better, as the primary metric for the classification tasks, with the area under the ROC curve as its companion. Selection uses the primary validation metric. Root mean square error is never pooled across tasks because it is in each task's own units; cross-task comparison uses ranks or dimensionless metrics.
facts.source_locator: results/learnability.csv; README.md: Results and figures

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: A mean predictor is the explicit baseline, and the released result table prints its value on the same test split beside each selected model, for example 1.7469 root mean square error against the selected model's 1.4303 on Macrocycle-DB OPRM1 regression, and 0.5 balanced accuracy for the classification tasks. The comparison set is the model and representation matrix itself: random forests and XGBoost on physicochemical descriptors and several fingerprint families, LSTM and transformer models on SMILES and fragSMILES, graph convolutional and message passing networks, two pretrained graph networks and two pretrained chemical language models, with the analyses drawing on a main pool of 22 configurations.
facts.source_locator: results/learnability.csv; README.md: Framework definition

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Three. A Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints at a 0.45 cutoff is released alongside the random split, so a method can be judged on structurally separated molecules. Duplicate structures are collapsed before splitting, by averaging replicate measurements and dropping molecules whose replicates disagree too much. Hyper-parameters are tuned on the validation split only, and the test split is used for reporting, with no reselection on a companion metric. The fingerprint and graph caches carry manifests that refuse a cache whose ordered SMILES or implementation hash do not match.
facts.source_locator: cycpepnet/benchmark.py: load_task_table and generate_all_splits; README.md: Framework definition, Curated tables

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Five training seeds per configuration, and the released table reports for each task the mean, the standard deviation across seeds, a confidence interval over seeds and a separate confidence interval over the test set, for example a seed interval of 1.3762 to 1.4826 against a test interval of 1.0557 to 1.8049 on the same 28-molecule task. The statistical tests table carries adjusted p values and the multiplicity families behind them, and a separate table records retired inferences and their replacements.
facts.source_locator: results/learnability.csv; README.md: top, Results and figures

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A cyclic peptide, given as a SMILES string, with one measured property value. Tasks are per molecule and per property, and duplicate structures are merged before splitting, so one row is one unique structure within a task.
facts.source_locator: cycpepnet/benchmark.py: load_task_table; README.md: Getting started

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Inapplicable in the usual sense: the examples are synthetic cyclic peptides, not sequences from a species. The binding affinity tasks name human targets, OPRM1, MC4R and SSTR2, in their filters and in the split table.
facts.source_locator: cycpepnet/benchmark.py: task filters; results/splits_summary.csv

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Three kinds of measurement, taken from the published sources: binding affinity as inhibition constants or half maximal inhibitory concentrations, membrane permeability as a log permeability, and half-life in hours. The target values are log transformed where the task says so, and the classification thresholds are applied on the transformed scale, 100 nanomolar for binding, minus 6 for log permeability and 8 hours for half-life.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Framework definition, Input data; cycpepnet/benchmark.py: task definitions

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The molecule, in whichever representation a model family uses. The released matrix covers physicochemical descriptors, several fingerprint families including ECFP, MAP4C, MXFP and HDF, SMILES and fragSMILES strings, and graph objects, and the two pretrained families read graphs and SMILES. No target structure or sequence is given to the model.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Framework definition

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training per task, with pretrained models fine-tuned in the same loop. Every non-baseline configuration tunes its hyper-parameters with Optuna over 50 trials on the validation split, and the matrix includes two pretrained graph networks and two pretrained chemical language models alongside models trained from scratch. The README also shows how to drop in an external model: load the task table and the released split, train on train, choose on val and score test with the framework's own metric functions.

strengths.text: The reproduction path is built in and checked. One command hashes the released artefacts and validates all 40 splits against the task tables, another regenerates the analysis, and a third compares the regenerated tables against the release to a tolerance of 1e-8, all without a GPU or retraining.
Both a structural and a random split are released for every task, with the clustering parameters in the code, so the gap between them can be read directly rather than argued about.

The reporting discipline is unusually explicit: selection on the primary validation metric with no reselection on a companion, no pooling of root mean square error across tasks, and both seed-level and test-level confidence intervals in the released table.

The data provenance is documented rather than assumed. An inventory records every input file with its hash, acquisition address and reviewed licence status, a separate evidence file holds the review, and the README states plainly that verification establishes identity, not redistribution rights.

limitations.text: The test sets are tiny for most tasks. The released split table gives 19 test molecules for the combined half-life task and 28, 32 and 49 for the three binding tasks, and the released result table shows test confidence intervals far wider than the seed intervals, for example 1.0557 to 1.8049 against 1.3762 to 1.4826.
limitations.source_locator: results/splits_summary.csv; results/learnability.csv

limitations.text: The input data cannot simply be downloaded. Nine provider files are needed and none is redistributed; the inventory marks most as having redistribution terms not established, and the README records specific unresolved problems: the NPMMPD snapshot differs from the Figshare version, the PEPlife2 export query has to be recovered, and the PepTherDia selection predicate, scraper and page order have not been recovered.

The README states that only the PepMSND Zenodo deposit carries a verified data licence, CC BY 4.0, that the curated tables are modified derivatives rather than provider archives, and that the MIT code licence does not cover the third-party data.

profile.summary: CellBench is an evaluation of single-cell foundation models used as frozen feature extractors, that is with their weights unchanged and only a light head fitted on top. The authors compare 13 such models with classical methods fitted on the training data itself, across 12 human and mouse cohorts and four genetic perturbation screens. Their reported conclusions are that different models preserve different biological information, that classical baselines stay competitive, that human-pretrained representations transfer to supervised mouse analyses but under a shared decoder none beats simply predicting no change for unseen perturbation targets, and that neither model size nor reported pretraining data volume predicts performance. This page is written from the abstract and metadata alone, because the preprint's full text is on bioRxiv, which this run was not allowed to request.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC record: title and abstract, Summary and In Brief sections

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: What a single-cell foundation model's embedding keeps, and whether it is worth using instead of a method fitted on the data at hand. The authors frame the open question as which biological information the embeddings preserve and when the models beat dataset-fitted methods. Two kinds of task are distinguished in the abstract: representing observed cellular states, which the authors treat as the observational side, and predicting how cells respond to genetic interventions, which they report as a different matter where success on the first does not carry over. A third question is evidential rather than biological: whether a model's apparent advantage survives the removal of cohorts that overlap its own pretraining records.
sections.source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstract, Summary, The Bigger Picture and Highlights sections

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The abstract gives the shape of the data and nothing more: 12 human and mouse cohorts, covering tissues and species, and four genetic perturbation screens. The comparison set is 13 frozen foundation models against classical baselines that are fitted on the training data. The perturbation side is said to include unseen perturbation targets. Nothing in the material that could be fetched names the cohorts, the cell counts, the gene sets, the screens or the splits, so none of those is stated here.
sections.source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstract, Summary and In Brief sections

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Three things can be said from the abstract. First, the backbones are frozen, so what is evaluated is the representation rather than a fine-tuned model, and the comparison is against methods fitted on the training data. Second, the perturbation task is scored on genome-wide absolute error against an explicit reference of predicting no change, and the authors report that under a shared decoder no model improves on that reference for unseen targets. Third, a sensitivity analysis removes cohorts whose sample or donor identifiers match a model's pretraining records, and the authors report that this reduces the annotation advantages while leaving the model rankings largely unchanged. The metrics for the other tasks, the aggregation across cohorts, the number of seeds and the exact splits are not in the material that could be fetched.

intake-403-20261126-benchmark-cellbench-.notes: Coverage is limited and deliberately so. The record's two attached sources are bioRxiv pages for the same DOI, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.04.01.714123v1 and the v2 address; this run was told not to request bioRxiv, and the saved Europe PMC record PPR1216366 marks the preprint isOpenAccess N and inPMC N, so the full text was not available. The page is therefore written from the Europe PMC core record's title, author list, date and structured abstract only. One doubt for a human, the name: Europe PMC serves this DOI as CellBench: task-dependent performance and generalization limits of single-cell foundation models, while the store holds CellBench-LS from v1 and a different v2 title, so the record's name, task field and scope note come from abstracts that the current version has replaced. The released date 2026-04-05 is the Europe PMC first publication date for the preprint.
intake-403-20261126-benchmark-cellbench-.no_run_guide_reason: No code or data address for this benchmark appears in any source that could be fetched. The only open copy of the authors' own text is the Europe PMC abstract, which names no repository, no download and no scoring script, and the preprint itself is on bioRxiv, which this run was told not to request.
